#6639. Buttered Nut Squash

We rate butternut the most affable winter squash—relatively easy to prepare, consistently delicious, and available at most grocery stores. The buttered nut dressing is more than just cheeky wordplay. Bold from brown butter and balsamic vinegar and bright from lemon, the crunchy topping is an excellent foil to the sweetness of roasted squash. Cook the squash a couple hours ahead of time and all you’ll have left to do before dinner is make the dressing.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 425°. Lightly crush 2 tsp. fennel seeds with a mortar and pestle or place on a cutting board and gently crush with a heavy pan. Peel 1 medium butternut squash (about 3 lb.) and halve lengthwise. Scoop out seeds; discard. Cut squash into 2" irregular pieces, aiming for sharp, jagged shapes. Transfer to a large rimmed baking sheet; drizzle with 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil and sprinkle with fennel seeds, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. crushed red pepper flakes. Toss squash to coat, arrange in a single layer, and roast until browned and tender, 30–35 minutes.

Do Ahead: Squash can be roasted 2 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

While the squash is roasting, cook 6 oz. thick-cut bacon, cut into 1" pieces, in a medium skillet over medium heat, stirring often, until browned and mostly crisp, 8–12 minutes. Transfer to a small plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to low; combine 1 cup raw pecans and 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pan. Cook, stirring often, until butter browns and nuts have slightly darkened, 6–8 minutes. Remove from heat. Stir in 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped (this will give it a head start to take off the raw edge), then add bacon, zest and juice of 1 large lemon, 3 sprigs sage, and 2 Tbsp. balsamic vinegar and stir to combine. Taste dressing and season with kosher salt if needed.

Arrange squash on a platter and spoon dressing over.

#6638. BA's Best Pecan Pie

Our classic pecan pie recipe has no chocolate chips, no booze, and no hard-to-find ingredients. Instead of focusing on embellishments, we focused on what matters most: the deep flavor of toasted pecans, a caramelly custard, and a buttery, flaky pie crust.

Brown sugar and a spoonful of dark molasses add depth to the filling, while toasting the pecans before incorporating them makes their flavor stand out and their texture more robust. Blind baking the crust—baking it before adding the filling—helps keep the bottom crisp beneath the gooey custard.

When the pie comes out of the oven, the edges should be set and slightly puffed, but the center should still wobble like Jell-O. It will continue to set as it cools, so resist slicing too soon. Serve it all on its own, or gild it with vanilla ice cream or whipped cream.

Can I make this pecan pie without corn syrup?

Yes. Corn syrup gives this classic pie its perfectly gooey texture, but there are alternatives. Brown rice syrup will add a toasty flavor and can be used in equal parts. Golden syrup, honey, and maple syrup are all too sweet and will change the pie’s flavor and texture.

For a pie developed without any syrup, try our Bourbon-Date Pecan Pie.

Can I use chopped pecans instead of halves?

Yes. We love the crunch you get from pecan halves, but if you’re a chopped pecan person, use about 225 g in place of the 2 cups of halves. Watch closely when toasting; chopped pecans will need less time in the oven.

Yes—bake the pie a day ahead and refrigerate it. Let it cool on a rack for up to 2 hours, then transfer it to the refrigerator to finish cooling before covering. To get a head start on the pastry, refrigerate the dough for up to 3 days or freeze it for up to 2 months.

Pulse 1 Tbsp. sugar, 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 2 cups all-purpose flour in a food processor until combined. Add 5 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 3 Tbsp. chilled lard or vegetable shortening and pulse until mixture resembles coarse meal with a few pieces of butter and lard visible, about fifteen 1-second pulses. With motor running, drizzle in 1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar and 5½ Tbsp. ice water and pulse until dough is still crumbly but just holds together when squeezed (add 1 tsp. water at a time if necessary, but be careful not to overwork dough).

Turn out dough onto a work surface. Knead 1–2 times, pressing just to incorporate any shaggy pieces. Flatten into a 6"-wide disk. Wrap with plastic wrap and chill at least 1 hour.

Preheat oven to 425°. Roll out dough on a lightly floured work surface to a 14" round. Transfer to a 9" pie pan. Pick up edges and allow dough to slump down into dish, letting excess dough hang over dish. Trim, leaving about a 1" overhang. Fold overhang under; pinch and crimp. Chill 30 minutes.

Line dough with parchment paper or foil, leaving some overhang. Fill with pie weights or dried beans. Bake until crust is dry around the edges and just beginning to lightly brown, 25–35 minutes. Carefully remove parchment and weights and reduce oven temperature to 350°. Bake until crust is set and beginning to brown in the center, 10–15 minutes. Transfer to a wire rack and let cool.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 3 days ahead; keep chilled, or freeze up to 2 months. Crust can be baked 1 day ahead; tightly wrap and store at room temperature.

Preheat oven to 350°. Toast 2 cups (225 g) pecan halves on a rimmed baking sheet until browned and fragrant, 8–10 minutes. Let cool.

Reduce oven temperature to 325°. Whisk 4 large eggs, room temperature, beaten to blend, 1 cup light corn syrup, ⅔ cup (packed; 134 g) light brown sugar, 1 Tbsp. robust-flavored (dark) molasses, 1 Tbsp. vanilla extract, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl until smooth. Slowly whisk in 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter, melted, slightly cooled, until combined. Fold in pecans and pour into cooled crust.

Bake pie until edges are set and slightly puffed but center is recessed and wobbles like Jell-O, 55–70 minutes (it will continue to set after baking). Transfer to a wire rack and let cool at least 3 hours before slicing. Serve with vanilla ice cream.

Do Ahead: Pie can be baked 1 day ahead; tightly wrap and chill. Serve warm or at room temperature.

#6637. Cranberry Crackle Salad

Recipe by Susan Bronson, Rhinelander, Wisconsin

Cranberry crackle salad combines crunchy and creamy textures with sweet and tangy flavors. It's a retro-style dessert with a hearty dose of seasonal cheer.

I live in cranberry country (aka northern Wisconsin), and when fresh cranberries hit store shelves, there’s a good chance you’ll find me in the kitchen baking with them. One sweet treat that often finds its way onto our holiday brunch menus is a loaf (or three) of cranberry-orange bread. There’s just something so cozy about the combination of tart cranberries and sweet, bright orange juice—the inspiration for this cranberry crackle salad recipe.

Crackle salad is a variation on retro fluff salad that combines cream cheese, whipped topping and fruit mix-ins with a crunchy, candied “crackle” topping (made with crushed pretzels, chopped pecans, brown sugar and melted butter). In this holiday-inspired crackle salad, the cream mixture is flavored with whole-berry cranberry sauce and orange zest. Fresh orange juice in the crackle adds a subtle citrus flavor, too. This recipe makes enough for a small crowd, and is perfect for sharing at a Thanksgiving potluck or as a fun throwback side dish at holiday gatherings.

Preheat the oven to 400°F. Line a 15x10x1-inch rimmed baking sheet with parchment paper or a silicone baking mat.

In a large bowl, stir together the broken pretzels, chopped pecans and brown sugar. Stir in the melted butter and orange juice to coat.

Spread the pretzel mixture in an even layer on the prepared baking sheet. Bake it for five to eight minutes or until it’s bubbly. Let it cool completely on the baking sheet before breaking it into pieces.

Editor’s Tip: Keep your eye on the crackle as it bakes; it can easily burn if baked too long.

In a large bowl, beat together the softened cream cheese and vanilla. Stir in the cranberry sauce until it’s combined. Gently fold in the whipped topping until it’s incorporated.

Fold in the orange zest. Cover the bowl and refrigerate the mixture for at least one hour.

Just before serving, stir in half of the pretzel mixture. Top the salad with the remaining pretzel mixture to serve. If you like, add sugared cranberries as an additional garnish.

Editor’s Tip: Avoid adding the crunch to the salad too early, as it will soften up over time.

Leftover cranberry crackle salad should be stored in an airtight container in the fridge. It will last for up to three days in the fridge. The crackle will soften over time once added to the salad.

Any extra crackle topping should be stored in an airtight container at room temperature to keep it crunchy. It should keep for up to one week.

You can make the cream mixture and crackle up to two day in advance. Store the salad and crackle separately, and don’t combine them until just before serving the salad.

If you want to dial up the crunch factor even more, allow the baked crackle to cool thoroughly before using it. This will ensure it has the crunchiest texture.

Fresh cranberries are a great option when they are in season. To make this cranberry crackle salad with fresh cranberries, you’ll need a 12-ounce package of whole cranberries. (You could also use frozen whole cranberries, but they need to thaw first.)

In a food processor or blender, pulse the berries until they’re finely chopped. Pour the berries into a large bowl and stir in 1/2 cup of granulated sugar. Cover and refrigerate them for at least one hour or overnight. Use the fresh berry mixture in place of the canned cranberry sauce in this recipe.

This cranberry crackle salad will fit right in with any holiday potluck spread. It’s also a fun retro dessert salad to share at a holiday meal alongside classic savory offerings such as roasted turkey, mashed potatoes and green bean casserole.

#6635. Collard Greens Vinaigrette

For those who might shudder at the thought of eating raw hardy greens like collards or kale, this vibrant side inspired by the French bistro classic leeks vinaigrette is the answer. Simmered past squeaky-raw yet well short of meltingly braised, they offer substantial bite, like al dente pasta. The mustard dressing couldn’t be simpler to make—use it as a base for any salad you might serve this season. It’s punchy enough to stand up to winter vegetables or any sturdy bitter green.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Toast ½ cup raw walnuts on a rimmed baking sheet, tossing halfway through, until golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Meanwhile, cook 2 bunches collard greens, ribs and stems removed, leaves cut into 2" pieces, in a large pot of generously salted boiling water until just tender, 9–11 minutes. Using tongs, immediately transfer to a large bowl of ice water and let cool.

Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ¼ cup white wine vinegar, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, preferably country-style, ⅓ cup extra-virgin olive oil, ¼ cup (packed) coarsely chopped tarragon, 2 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl to combine. Set dressing aside.

Transfer toasted walnuts to a small bowl and drizzle with remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Sprinkle with a generous pinch each of sugar and salt and toss to coat. Taste and add more sugar if needed (nuts should be more sweet than salty). Set seasoned walnuts aside.

Drain collard greens and squeeze gently to remove excess water. Transfer to bowl with reserved dressing and toss to coat evenly. Cover and chill at least 15 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Arrange greens in a shallow bowl or on a platter and spoon any dressing remaining in bowl over. Top with seasoned walnuts and tarragon leaves.

Do Ahead: Walnuts can be toasted and dressing can be made 1 day ahead. Store walnuts airtight at room temperature. Cover dressing and chill.

#6634. Taylor! Lainey! Ella! Kacey! Megan! Backstage at the CMA Awards

“Little Lainey would be losin’ her mind if she knew she was about to be hosting the 60th Annual CMA Awards,” Lainey Wilson said ahead of country music’s biggest night at Nashville’s Bridgestone Arena. Indeed, when Vogue caught up with the chart-topper in a quiet moment leading up to the show, she was incredulous about landing the gig.

“I’m still that little girl from a town of 200 people in Louisiana who just grew up dreamin’ about being a small part of this world of country music,” Wilson said in her signature twang. The feeling of going from the middle of nowhere to the center of the ceremony, and in such a milestone year, is nothing short of surreal, she added. Not only was it the show’s six-decade anniversary and a mega year for the genre, but the night was also set to include a tribute to the late Dolly Parton—and the first CMA performance in 13 years from a certain recently wed crossover superstar.

“I’m just excited to celebrate the ones before, the ones now, and the ones comin’,” Wilson said. “I think the biggest thing for me is being present and being right where my feet are. It’s tryin’ to find that balance.”

On the day of the show, Downtown Nashville was a flurry of activity, fans, hot chicken, and road closures as the capital of country music prepared to step into the national spotlight. The recent FAA ground stop gave some out-of-towners agita, but the delay clouds thankfully parted in time. Music was ringing out from every bar and restaurant on Broadway, most of the time in the form of Langley’s ubiquitous “Choosin’ Texas.” The country queen of 2026 was also nominated for almost every award imaginable. It’s to the point where if Langley miraculously cloned herself, they’d be nominated for Best Duo, too.

“This isn’t a fad: everyone you know can sing along to every word of ‘Choosin’ Texas,’” Brittany Schaffer, the incoming Country Music Association CEO, told Vogue. Just hours earlier, Schaffer bolted out of her hotel at 6 a.m. to help give out the first award of the day live on Good Morning America. (Naturally, “Choosin’ Texas” won for Best Music Video.) Schaffer was also busy contending with the Taylor of it all, as her CMA comeback was a closely held secret.

“A small group of us knew for quite a bit of time in advance of the announcement,” Schaffer revealed with a wink. “Obviously, with this being an anniversary, she is such an important part of country music history, so we certainly started that conversation with her early on. We are just thrilled that she was so excited to join.”

While most major red carpets are hectic affairs, the vibe at Music City Center was decidedly chiller—even when an Oscar de la Renta-clad Swift arrived. A hush fell over the space as phones lifted to capture the moment, even that of the lighting technician. Elsewhere, VIPs tucked into fried green tomato sandwiches and sipped whiskey, seemingly unfazed.

“I had to bring my sister, Leslie,” actor Glen Powell, who’s set to play a country music star in next year’s The Comeback King, told Vogue. “ To share this together…I mean, we’ve been country fans our entire lives. We did these long road trips to the ranch, listening to country music the whole way.” A “starstruck” Leslie chimed in: “Two of our childhood idols, Faith Hill and Tim McGraw, are sitting next to us.”

As the Tennessee sun began to set, a series of Sprinter vans whisked people from the carpet to the arena for a 7 p.m. start time. Backstage, a trophy engraver was waiting to etch the names of future winners into history. Inside the arena, the crowd milled about as a booming voice on the loudspeaker urged, “In respect to Dolly, please take your seats.” It proved to be a subtle teaser, as a tribute featuring Wilson and Vince Gill singing “I Will Always Love You” was about to open the show. Later, Kacey Musgraves and Miranda Lambert lightened the mood with their honky-tonk ode “Horses and Divorces,” from Musgraves’s recent album Middle of Nowhere.

From her dressing room, Musgraves, resplendent in a custom suit by the Los Angeles-based western-wear designer RoseCut, took a breather on the couch. “I think people would be shocked to know how boring my pre-show ritual actually is,” she told Vogue. “It’s pretty chill. I don’t shut myself in a hotel room all day. I try to move and connect with the heartbeat of wherever I’m at.” Alas, a vocal doctor did warn once that she should have “no chocolate, no caffeine, or no booze before a performance. “I’m like, ‘Have you ever been on stage without booze,’” she recalled with a laugh. “So pre-show, the band and I usually do a tequila shot.”

According to Musgraves, a night like tonight is all about reconnecting. “So many of us here spend so much of our time out on the road. It’s really a reunion of sorts, getting to see a lot of people and friends that you haven’t seen in so long.”

One of those friends is Megan Moroney, whom Musgraves was happily sharing a dressing room with. Alongside excitement over her two nominations at the CMAs, Moroney is buzzing about her two recently announced Grammy nods. “It’s been such a crazy year,” Moroney told Vogue as the ceremony blared on a TV in the background. “On the morning of the nominations, my manager came into my bedroom at like 6:30 a.m. and said, ‘We need to turn on the Grammy announcement because I just have a good feeling.’ And I was like, ‘Are you insane?!’”

The show itself played out as expected. Ella Langley cleaned up, making history by winning everything from Entertainer of the Year to Female Vocalist of the Year and Album of the Year, breaking a CMA record for most wins. Even the country stalwarts were impressed. “A highlight for me was hugging Miranda Lambert,” Lady A’s Hillary Scott told Vogue of Langley’s collaborator. “What’s funny is we toured with her and Kenny Chesney twenty years ago, early on in our careers.” Her bandmate, Dave Haywood, added: “Longevity was the goal when we started. So to be here after all of these years is a dream realized for us.”

As the show wrapped up and fans departed the arena, stars grabbed snacks to munch on as they got ready to head back out on the road—including a lollipop-sucking Michael Bublé. “What I love about country music is this,” he mused to Vogue, “when you take away all of the production, all of the lights, and all of the magic tricks, you are left with good souls.”

#6633. The Best Subscription Boxes for Women: Sure to Wow the Women in Your Life

Tested by Katie Bandurski, Emily Way and Paul Rankin

We've tested dozens of subscription services over the years, and these are our favorite subscription boxes for women.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

We tested some of the best subscription boxes to find the ones truly worth gifting. Whether you’re shopping for a woman who has everything or treating yourself to something special, these thoughtfully curated subscriptions make it easy to discover new favorites and enjoy a delightful surprise each month.

Looking for more inspiration? Explore our 2026 Holiday Gift Guide for gifts she’ll love.

BloomsyBox is your one-stop shop when it comes to flower and plant subsctiption boxes. Choose from classic arrangements, large, mixed bouquets or collections of roses in monthly, weekly or bi-weekly deliveries.

“My BloomsyBox arrangement featuring red and white roses arrived expertly arranged, although I quickly trimmed the stems for maximum freshness and plopped them in a clear glass vase,” says tester Madi Koetting. “Despite the less-than-ideal winter weather, my bouquet remained intact for a whopping two and a half weeks. BloomsyBox is another go-to for show-stopping flower delivery.”

I re-tested BloomsyBox in 2026 to ensure quality and consistency. My Garden Soirée bouquet arrived via next-day delivery, with all 30 stems fresh and perfectly intact. BloomsyBox delivery is turly one of the freshest, fullest and most well-preserved flower delivery boxes I’ve ever received, and it would make a wonderful subscription gift for anyone who loves fresh blooms.

Our best chocolate box winner offers our favorite chocolate subscription box, too. I tested the Compartés Chocolate of the Month Club box in February—and it wowed from the moment it arrived. Inside were two chocolate bars and a box of assorted chocolates.

The assortment featured strawberry cream and crème brûlée–filled chocolates. The strawberry cream was exactly what you’d expect—fruity and delicious. The crème brûlée, however, was a surprise, capturing the rich, warm vanilla flavor of the classic dessert with impressive accuracy.

February’s box included two chocolate bars: California Berries, a vegan dark chocolate full of dried berries, and Strawberry Shortcake, a white chocolate bar packed with strawberries and airy, crunchy shortcake pieces.

Tester Paul Rankin’s box included four packets of cured meats, three hard cheeses, one jar of sheep and goat cheese in oil, one sweet lemon ricotta, a box of artisan crisps, a bag of pralined pecans, a bag of dried cherries and, lastly, a tiny jar of blackberry balsamic jam.

The ease and quality of this kit are hard to beat, and buying each item separately would likely cost more than the price of the box, making it an excellent value for giving and receiving alike.

#6632. Pecan Pie Brownies

Making Thanksgiving dinner is already a Herculean task, but adding dessert to your list of responsibilities can feel like almost too much. This pecan pie makes things easy, giving you the perfect sweet treat to serve after a long, filling dinner without adding too much extra work. This seasonal twist on brownies skips the pie crust and combines two classic desserts in one delicious bite. The syrupy pecan pie topping seeps into the brownies, making them rich, flavorful, and just the right amount of moist.

Start by preheating your oven to 325°F. Grab a 9"x9" baking pan, grease it with cooking spray, and line it with parchment paper. Next, make the brownie batter following the directions on the box. Pour it into the pan and bake until the brownies are just a little underdone—poke the center with a tester, and if you see a few moist crumbs, they’re ready (this should take about 20 minutes). While the brownies are baking, grab a medium bowl and whisk together the corn syrup, brown sugar, butter, molasses, vanilla, and salt until nice and smooth. Add the eggs and whisk until everything’s well combined. Then, stir in the pecans so they’re all coated in the mixture.

Once the brownies are out of the oven, bump up the temperature to 350°F. Spoon the pecan mixture over the brownies and spread it out evenly. Pop the pan back in the oven and bake for another 40 to 45 minutes, or until the pecan topping feels springy and has thickened up.

Let the brownies cool down to room temperature first, then pop them in the fridge for about an hour until they’re cold and set.

If you’d like, finish them off with a drizzle of caramel sauce before serving.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

These brownies are the perfect make-ahead dessert for your holiday party. Make them the day before the party, pop them (tightly wrapped or in an airtight container!) into the fridge, and forget about them until ready to serve.

#6631. Listen to BA Bake Club's Podcast on Salt Bread

“These little buns…they look so cute, but they are so rich,” guest contributor, and our deputy food editor, Hana Asbrink explains to BA Bake Club hosts Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic. “You can really just snack on them solo and be so satisfied.”

#6630. Thanksgiving Cornbread

Traditionally, cornbread stuffing requires making cornbread, cubing it and letting it dry out, mixing it with stock, eggs, meat, and aromatics, then transforming it into a stuffing (or dressing). This process produces some truly memorable casseroles, but I have an alternative that streamlines the process without compromising flavor: stuffing cornbread. It still smells enticingly like the classic Thanksgiving side as you set the baking dish on the table. I’ve still packed in a medley of woodsy herbs, sweet onions, vegetal peppers, and savory sausage. And it still slices into lofty servings to perch on your plate next to the sweet potatoes and green beans. It just takes half as long to make.

The intentional two-to-one ratio of cornmeal to flour in this cornbread results in a moist, tender crumb that still has enough structure to hold up against the sturdy mix-ins. The sugar might seem like a lot, but it balances out the savory sausage and aromatics perfectly.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Line a 13x9" baking pan with parchment paper, leaving generous overhang on long sides. Coat pan and parchment with unsalted butter. Melt ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium-low heat, then pour into a small bowl.

Cook 1 green bell pepper, halved, ribs and seeds removed, finely chopped, 1 medium white onion, finely chopped, and 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, in same skillet, stirring occasionally with a wooden spoon, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 1 lb. spicy and/or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and cook, breaking up and stirring occasionally, until browned (it may still be a little raw in the center at this point), about 5 minutes. Remove from heat.

Stir together 4 cups (624 g) fine-ground yellow cornmeal, 2 cups (250 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup (200 g) sugar, 1 Tbsp. plus 1½ tsp. baking powder, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 tsp. baking soda, and ¼ cup finely chopped sage, thyme, and/or rosemary in a large bowl. Gradually pour in 3½ cups buttermilk, then melted butter, stirring constantly until combined. Add 4 large eggs one at a time, mixing to incorporate after each addition. Fold in sausage mixture, then scrape batter into prepared pan.

Bake cornbread, rotating pan front to back halfway through, until golden brown and top springs back when gently pressed, 38–45 minutes. Let cool in pan 15 minutes. Using parchment paper overhang, lift cornbread out of pan and transfer to a cutting board. Cut into 12–18 slices; arrange on a platter.

Do Ahead: Cornbread can be baked 4 hours ahead. Store at room temperature; cut just before serving.

#6629. Ina Garten Just Revealed Her Thanksgiving Menu, and the Sides Are Stealing the Show

Even Ina isn't making everything from scratch this year. Her newly revealed side dishes include some surprisingly simple shortcuts.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

Ina Garten has made her position on Thanksgiving dinner quite clear. The turkey may be the centerpiece, but the side dishes are the real stars. “Thanksgiving is one of those meals where I care more about the sides than the main event!” she recently shared with her followers.

In a recent Instagram post, Ina revealed that she’s especially excited to make several new dishes from her latest cookbook, Simply Ina. There are familiar Thanksgiving favorites with a few clever twists, along with some store-bought shortcuts that prove even the Barefoot Contessa knows when to let someone else do part of the work. It’s a reassuring approach to a meal that can demand a lot of time in the kitchen.

Here’s a look at the six recipes Ina shared, along with similar Taste of Home dishes you can make for your own Thanksgiving dinner.

Ina’s combination of caramelized butternut squash and dried cranberries makes particularly good sense for Thanksgiving. Roasting brings out the squash’s natural sweetness, while the tart cranberries provide some welcome contrast. It’s a colorful alternative to the sweeter squash dishes that tend to find their way onto holiday tables, but one that wouldn’t look out of place next to a generous helping of Ina’s sausage and herb stuffing.

Try a Taste of Home version: Butternut Squash Jumble

Ina has always been a champion of making Thanksgiving easier, and her new turkey gravy takes that philosophy a step further. She’s starting with canned turkey gravy, then dressing it up for a richer, more homemade flavor. It’s a practical shortcut for someone who’s spent years teaching us how to make gravy from scratch. And as Ina points out, nobody wants leftover turkey without gravy, either. Making enough for Friday’s sandwiches is simply good planning.

Try a Taste of Home version: Make-Ahead Turkey Gravy

Mashed potatoes are practically guaranteed a place on the Thanksgiving table, but Ina’s addition of garlic gives this familiar favorite a welcome savory kick. Ina actually starts with Bob Evans prepared mashed potatoes, then dresses them up with garlic confit, butter and half-and-half. With so many sweet, rich dishes competing for space on the plate, garlic mashed potatoes offer a little balance without sacrificing any of the buttery comfort everyone expects.

Try a Taste of Home version: Garlic Mashed Potatoes

Brussels sprouts have come a long way from the boiled vegetables many of us remember from childhood, and Ina’s version pairs them with pecorino, a salty, sharp sheep’s milk cheese. The combination makes sense: The cheese adds richness and a savory bite that complements the sprouts’ slightly bitter flavor. It’s the sort of side dish that might even persuade a few longtime Brussels sprouts skeptics to reconsider.

Try a Taste of Home version: Brussels Sprouts with Garlic & Goat Cheese

Here’s where Ina’s fondness for a good shortcut really comes into play. Her Chunky Cranberry Conserve starts with canned whole-berry cranberry sauce, which she dresses up with grated Granny Smith apple, orange juice and zest, raisins and pecans. The result has more texture and complexity than the contents of the can alone, without requiring you to start from scratch.

There’s something reassuring in knowing Ina Garten is perfectly content to open a can of cranberry sauce on Thanksgiving. If it’s good enough for Ina, the rest of us can probably stop apologizing for it.

Try a Taste of Home version: Cranberry-Apple Chutney

Sweet potatoes are a Thanksgiving staple, but Ina’s combination of maple syrup and chipotle gives them a welcome change of direction. The maple enhances their natural sweetness, while the smoky heat of chipotle keeps the dish firmly on the savory side of dinner.

And there’s another shortcut hiding in this dish. In a recent interview with Cup of Jo, Ina revealed that she uses prepared mashed sweet potatoes from Trader Joe’s, adding chipotle powder, maple syrup, butter and seasonings to make them her own. She figures nobody would know she hadn’t roasted the sweet potatoes herself, and with everything else that needs cooking on Thanksgiving, that’s a shortcut (and a great Trader Joe’s find) worth stealing.

Try a Taste of Home version: Hot Honey Sweet Potatoes

#6628. 10 Best Eye Cream for Dark Circles of 2026, According to Experts

While some people appreciate the natural look of a shadowy under-eye, many of us hope to find a solution—which is where the best eye cream for dark circles comes in. “Not all eye creams are created equal, because not all eye problems are equal,” says board-certified dermatologist Dr. Shereene Idriss. “When a person is looking to treat dark circles, the question is: Why do you have dark circles?”

The answer is different for everyone. For some people, it’s pigment, which can be genetic or the result of tiredness. For others, the skin under the eyes is so thin that the blood vessels underneath show through as a bluish or purple cast. If you’re experiencing puffiness, that can cast its own shadow, especially in the morning. Finally, as we get older, a little volume loss where the lower lid meets the cheek can make the whole area look darker than it really is.

That’s why when it comes to your eye cream, the ingredient list matters. Vitamin C, niacinamide and licorice root are good picks for pigment. Formulas that include retinol and peptides help thin skin look firmer and less see-through over time, and caffeine is every skin expert’s go-to for puffiness. Hollowing is the one thing a cream can’t fix, but the right formula can still make the skin around it look smoother and brighter.

Below, we rounded up the best eye creams that target dark circles—according to dermatologists, estheticians, skin experts, and Vogue editors.

British Vogue’s Jessica Diner uses Medik8’s Crystal Retinal Ceramide Eye Cream.

Vogue’s Kiana Murden uses Chanel’s N° 1 De Revitalizing Eye Serum.

Vogue’s Kiana Murden uses RoC Retinol Correxion Eye Cream.

“Yes, good eye creams formulated with clinically-proven ingredients do work and can provide visible benefits to the skin,” Murphy-Rose admits. “Dark circles caused by vascular congestion can be targeted with caffeine, vitamin K, and arnica. Dark circles caused by true hyperpigmentation can be treated with retinol and vitamin C-containing eye creams that help to brighten and fade discoloration.” And those with more prominent pigmentation around the eye should look to in-office treatments alongside topical solutions. “When dark circles are caused by a loss of volume or other anatomical cause, it can be difficult to achieve a significant improvement with topical therapy alone. Sometimes in office treatments like injectable fillers will bring about the most significant improvement to help this shadowed area reflect more light.”

Do eye creams actually get rid of dark circles?

Though eye creams can soften the appearance of dark circles, they’re (alas) not a one-swipe magic wand. “Eye creams can improve the quality of the skin around your eyes, but they can’t fix every undereye concern,” says Brauer. “Eye creams mainly help to moisturize and protect the skin around your eyes—one of the most delicate areas of skin on your face. The right eye cream can help to minimize dark circles, but they won’t get rid of them permanently.” So, what to do when those dark circles crop up? Read on.

What do dermatologists recommend for dark circles?

Whether dark circles are spurred by a sleepless night, a red-eye flight, or a host of other factors, there are fixes. But your particular path to bright-eyed pertness will be personal. “A lot of what is recommended is dependent upon the underlying cause or causes of the darkness,” Brauer says. “Aging—including thinning skin, bone resorption, and fat-pad changes—sun damage, and allergies are some of the main causes of what one sees in the mirror.” To find the right eye cream for you, Brauer recommends talking it over with a pro. “It’s important to find an eye cream that works for your specific skin type and dermatologic concerns to get the best results,” he says. “The best approach is to speak with a dermatologist to determine what would work best for you.”

In addition to particular eye creams, Brauer has set his patients up with everything from lasers and injectable fillers and prescription medications (such as topical steroids) to brighten the appearance of under-eye circles. He specifies that prescriptions are generally his recommendation for those whose dark under-eye circles are a secondary cause of allergies, while under-eye circles resulting from volume loss are generally best treated with a multifaceted approach that includes injectable fillers and energy-based treatments that incorporate lasers or radiofrequency.

How often should I apply eye cream for dark circles?

To reduce existing dark circles and prevent more gaze-darkening baggage from popping up in the future, Brauer recommends applying eye cream once to twice daily, morning and night. “You can apply it as the first step in your skin-care routine,” he says—issuing a friendly reminder that no morning regime is complete without sunscreen for face. When it comes to applying the eye cream, “Be sure to use your ring finger,” he says, to lightly tap it in. “You want to be gentle when applying cream to this delicate area of skin.”

She explains that the pesky dark circles could be the result of pigmentation or underlying redness and vasculature. “If the dark circles are due to pigmentation, then you want to look for ingredients with brightening effects. Products containing vitamin C, hydroquinone, and kojic acid work best. Also, look for products with retinol in them because retinol can help a person even out pigmentation over time. However, if the dark circles are due to underlying redness or puffiness, then you want to look for eye creams with caffeine or vitamin K, which is an ‘underdog’ and not used as frequently as I wish it were.”

Like many other skin conditions, dark circles can be reduced with lifestyle changes as well. According to board-certified dermatologist Dr. Morgan Rabach, “good sleep, hydration, low salt, and sunscreen under the eye” can make a positive difference because “factors are genetic and environmental.” (On the makeup front, consider layering your tinted moisturizer with SPF beneath your concealer of choice to temporarily veil dark under-eye circles.) For more intensive treatment, Rabach often uses “fillers made from hyaluronic acid to mask the bags and also sometimes undergo under-eye surgery (called a lower blepharoplasty) to remove the eye bag.”

Ingredients to Look for in Dark Circle Treatments

While eye creams tend to make grand promises—advertising their ability to firm, lift, and brighten—sussing out certain ingredients is the surest way to determine a cream’s eye-brightening efficacy. “There are so many factors that contribute to dark circles, including thin, translucent skin from collagen loss, hyperpigmentation, blood vessels and venous pooling, eye bags and puffiness, and lifestyle factors such as stress, lack of sleep, and dehydration,” says Dr. Adazeh Shirazi, a board-certified dermatologist who’s based in California. “Different ingredients help address different causes to reduce the appearance of dark circles.” Herewith, find a cheat sheet of the most powerful ingredients for combatting under-eye circles.

#6627. Pear Salad With Honey-Roasted Seeds

In the midst of a rich meal, something fresh and acidic keeps your taste buds awake. Where lettuce splashed with vinaigrette can feel like an afterthought, a juicy, savory-slanting pear salad is worth making room for on a plate full of turkey and cornbread. This is the antithesis of the haphazardly chunked together fruit salads you find at the supermarket for a brunch or dessert spread. Keep the focus on crisp-tart pears—apples also work—and it’s a welcome accompaniment to the other hearty dishes. Sliced razor-thin (use a mandoline) and fanned out on a platter, the fruit acts as an edible canvas for wisps of cheese and clusters of honey-roasted seeds. Leftovers (if you have any, of course) are delightful spooned over a well-toasted and buttered slice of multigrain bread the next day.

Pick firm green pears (Bartlett and Anjou are fair game; use Asian pears in a pinch) to ensure they hold their shape once sliced—even a little underripe is better than slightly over. After slicing, have a taste: If they are very tart, add 1 tsp. honey to the dressing; if fairly sweet, skip it.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Preheat oven to 325°. Whisk 3 Tbsp. honey, 1 tsp. garlic powder, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, and ¾ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl to combine. Add 1 cup raw sunflower seeds, pumpkin seeds (pepitas), and/or coarsely crushed raw nuts (such as walnuts, almonds, and/or hazelnuts) and stir to coat. Spread out in a single layer on a parchment-lined rimmed baking sheet; reserve bowl.

Bake seed mixture until golden brown, 12–14 minutes. (Honey mixture will puff up a bit but will deflate when you stir.) Toss honey-roasted seeds, then let cool. Toss again just to break up.

Whisk 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice, 1 tsp. Dijon mustard, a pinch of kosher salt, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in reserved bowl. Add 2 lb. firm green pears (such as Bartlett and/or Anjou; about 4 large), cored, thinly sliced, to dressing and gently toss to coat.

Arrange pears on a large flat platter. Scatter honey-roasted seeds over and top with 2 oz. Parmesan, aged white cheddar, or Manchego cheese, shaved.

Do Ahead: Honey-roasted seeds can be made 6 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

#6626. Why Did My Pumpkin Pie Crack and How Can I Fix It?

Here's how to avert dessert disaster before it strikes—with tips for hiding it just in case.

Most cooking mistakes are fixable. When it comes to baking, though, one wrong move can ruin the whole recipe. It’s extra frustrating when you’re trying to make a Norman Rockwell-worthy pumpkin pie for Thanksgiving, and a huge crack splits right through the center. Yes, you can still eat a cracked pumpkin pie, but if you can avoid the crack (or cover it up), all the better. The eyes eat first, as they say!

Pumpkin pie will crack when the eggs are overbeaten, when the filling is overbaked, and when the pie experiences rapid temperature changes. Not to put the blame on one single ingredient, but it all comes down to the eggs—or, rather, how you treat them.

Pumpkin pie is technically a baked custard (like cheesecake), and eggs are thickeners in custards. Overbeating the eggs aerates the filling, which causes it to inflate during baking, then deflate and crack as it cools. Overbaking the filling will tighten the eggs and cause the filling to crack, too. And even if you pull the pie out at just the right moment, the filling can still crack from a rapid temperature change that makes the eggs contract. Ugh. It seems like there’s a lot working against you, but taking preemptive steps reduces your chances of ending up with a cracked pumpkin pie.

These are all the steps I take as a professional baker to reduce the risk of cracking, as well as a few tricks to cover up cracks if they appear.

Seasoned bakers know that whipping eggs aerates them. That’s usually a plus when you want structure in baking recipes, but in pumpkin pie, it’s the catalyst for a cracked filling. The pie’s filling will puff up in the oven, then promptly collapse as the eggs deflate. That structural change causes the filling to crack. It’s the same problem that leads to a cracked cheesecake!

Room-temperature eggs blend into custards much more easily, so take the eggs out of the fridge 30 to 60 minutes before starting, depending on the kitchen temperature. Once you add the eggs to the filling, mix them just until they’re combined.

Even if you use a reliable pumpkin pie recipe with tons of five-star reviews (cough, cough: our pumpkin pie recipe) and follow it to the very letter, it may be the oven that betrays you in the end.

Ovens often have miscalibrated internal thermometers, so even if you set your oven to the recommended 350°F, the real temperature may be significantly higher. Before you realize it, the pumpkin pie is overbaked and already cracked.

Buy an oven thermometer and hang it from one of the oven racks for all your bakes going forward. They usually cost about $10—totally worth the investment!

Have you ever read a recipe with specific oven rack placements? They’re not there as a suggestion; oven rack placement significantly affects your bake. Ovens produce heat from the bottom, and this creates zones as that heat rises: hotter on top and cooler down below.

Since you want your pumpkin pie to bake relatively low and slow, the bottom oven rack is best. The filling cooks evenly, and the pie crust browns beautifully—no cracks and no soggy bottom.

The best way to avoid an overbaked (and therefore cracked) pumpkin pie is to know the signs of doneness. The edges should dome a bit, but the center should be wobbly like Jell-O, not rippling like an ocean wave. The pumpkin pie will continue to bake from the residual heat once the oven is off.

This is where your oven light comes in handy. Don’t open the oven door until you see the edges start to dome, or cool air will rush inside before it’s supposed to. Only when you see the dome should you check for a wobbly center.

Even after meticulously following every single step to avoid a pumpkin pie crack, a rapid change in temperature can undo all that hard work. The shock of removing a pumpkin pie from a hot oven and setting down in a cold November kitchen (or, worse, a 32° fridge) will cause the eggs to contract, leading to a crack.

Once the pie is done baking, turn the oven off and leave the door slightly ajar. If the oven door doesn’t stay open on its own, prop it open with a wooden spoon. Keep the pie in the oven until it’s completely cooled.

So, your pumpkin pie did crack. That’s OK! It happens from time to time, even when you follow all the rules. The good news is that the pie still tastes great. Even better? You can cover up the crack with homemade whipped cream. Pile it in the center or pipe it in a decorative pattern. Use stabilized whipped cream if you want to add the topping a day ahead of time. You can even grate fresh nutmeg on top for dimension.

You can do the same with Swiss meringue. Spread it simply, or pipe it on top for a big, showy decoration. Toast the meringue so it’s beautifully golden brown.

#6624. The Best Cast-Iron Skillets for a Lifetime of Cooking (2026)

For some people there isn’t much of a debate around who makes the best cast-iron skillet. There is a die-hard fan base loyal to the affordable US-made Lodge cast-iron pan that will not hear of any other suggestions.

There are others (cast-iron nerds and collectors) who swear by the superior quality of their vintage pan from Griswold or Wagner that they found at a scrap yard, de-rusted in a bucket with a DIY electrolysis setup, and seasoned with a proprietary oil blend in the furnaces of their bespoke restoration workshop.

To these two camps of people I say: “I don’t want to fight you, and I already know why you feel the way you feel. Please do not send me any angry emails.”

If you’ve been loyal to your own cast-iron pan for years—or decades—I don’t expect to change your mind. My goal is merely to provide recommendations for cast-iron cookware based on side-by-side testing and the input collectively provided by members of our staff. Agree with me and my team or don’t; either way, I’m happy if people are passionate about cooking with cast iron because I too enjoy it a great deal.

Cast-iron frying pans were the original nonstick pans, before ceramic nonstick and PTFE rolled around, and unlike modern nonstick coatings, a cast-iron pan’s surface actually gets more nonstick over time rather than degrading week by week. This is because, through continued cooking, thin layers of oil polymerize to the surface of the pan, creating a glassy nonstick surface that improves with continued use. They are also strong enough to handle metal utensils. The same can’t be said for that Instagram-famous nonstick pan (you know the one).

Yes, there are ways you can damage this seasoning layer, but these pans are far more resilient than lots of people think, and they aren’t actually all that difficult to care for. Talk to cast-iron enthusiasts and they’ll tell you the best way to season a cast-iron skillet is to just keep cooking with it.

And cook with it you can. Cast-iron pans are amazing for fried eggs, skillet hashes, cornbread, and sautéed greens. At a high heat, they do an incredible job searing strip steaks, London broil, and chicken thighs, giving you a burnished crispy exterior.

Bottom line, cast-iron cooking is an absolute joy, and every kitchen tool kit should include some cast iron alongside its stainless-steel and carbon steel pans and enameled Dutch oven.

New in this update: A review of Made In's new cast-iron pan as well as more long-term testing information for our winner.

Size(s): 10.5" (4.5 lb.), 12" (6 lb.), 13.5" (7.5 lb.)Pre-seasoned: Yes

What I loved: Because they’re much more expensive than the Lodges folks got used to, many feel a certain type of way about the new era of smooth, vintage-style cast-iron pans that includes this Lancaster. But when you have the opportunity to test a bunch of these pans side by side, you really get a sense of their differences (however small), and you’d be surprised by the things you notice. It was in this apples-to-apples testing that this pan, manufactured by a small company based in Southeastern Pennsylvania, really set itself apart.

The Lancaster is the lightest cast-iron pan I’ve tested, weighing in at 4 lb. for the No. 8 (10"-diameter) pan. Most cast-iron pans of a similar size are around 5 lb. or more—a seemingly small difference in number that makes a surprisingly big difference in hand. When laid out next to a dozen pans in the Test Kitchen, multiple testers singled out this pan as being the most comfortable to hold and maneuver.

It has thinner walls than a typical cast-iron skillet, which allows it to heat up faster. In testing, it came to temp over one minute faster than pans with thicker walls. We were concerned this would mean a reduction in the level of heat retention you’d want to crisp up the edges of some skillet cornbread, but we didn’t find that to be a problem at all. The cooking surface also demonstrated relatively even heat for a cast-iron pan (you really can’t expect too much from cast iron, though; cold spots are sort of inevitable with the material).

The pan comes pre-seasoned, but as is the case with most smooth cast-iron pans, this seasoning layer isn’t nearly as robust as what you’d find on a conventional Lodge or Victoria pan. The polished surface does aid in the pan’s nonstick properties, though, so we found the pan was exceptionally nonstick right out of the box.

Other testing sites have criticized this style of smooth cast-iron pan for getting stained after cooking, but to that we say: This is the process of seasoning developing on the pan. That staining is a feature, not a bug.

An earlier design of this pan didn’t include a helper handle, a feature we missed but forgave because the pan was already so easy to wield. However, Lancaster recently updated the design to include one—all the better in our book. Check out my full review of the Lancaster No. 8 here.

What I’d leave: The main drawback here is the cost. This pan will set you back $175, a steep price for cookware with a reputation for being budget-friendly. I’ll just say this: People happily pay comparable prices for nonstick ceramic cookware that lasts only a year or two at best. This pan, provided you don’t drop it in an industrial crucible, will last a lifetime.

In the long run: I have more patience than a lot of people when it comes to taking care of pans. So I will concede that the out of the box seasoning isn’t that robust. Some tasks, like searing off meat, can strip the seasoning slightly at first. With the Lancaster, I’ve found that this doesn’t impact the pans overall nonstick-ness. It does, however, mean you have to keep an eye out for rust until it gets a couple uses under its belt.

Below you’ll see two Lancaster pans. The left is four years old and the right is fresh from the box (you can tell because the earlier generation of pans didn’t have the helper handle). These are the pans after searing off two chicken thighs. You can see how the pan on the left has a robust, established seasoning, while the one on the right has some gray patches where the chicken skin pulled off some of that seasoning. From experience (I am the owner of the pan on the left), I can say that all you really need to do is keep cooking with it to get that seasoning back, but if you want to do a whole round of seasoning in the oven yourself, it certainly won’t hurt. Honestly, had I just sautéed some onions in the rendered schmaltz after cooking the chicken, those spots would be taken care of.

For comparison, I seared some chicken thighs in both pans. The factory seasoning might get patchy after the first use. Don’t let that scare you, just keep cooking with it. If you’re really worried about rust, just wipe down the surface of the pan with a tiny bit of neutral oil, buff off the excess, and put it over the heat for a few minutes.

Some people complain about the cosmetic changes to these smooth pans when breaking them in To reiterate: It does not impact the performance of the pan. If it bothers you, I encourage you to think about how it’s a record of use and proof that it’s growing and developing alongside you. Or, if you’re just an unsentimental aesthete, perhaps read up on the concept of wabi-sabi. I personally think that my pan is the most beautiful piece of cookware I own!

If you want a high-quality pan that’s not only a pleasure to cook with, but can serve as a family heirloom for generations to come, consider this one. If you’re just looking for a workhorse that won’t break the bank, go for the budget option below.

Size(s): 4.8" (1.1 lb.), 6.5" (2 lb.), 8" (3.1 lb.), 10" (5.5 lb.), 12" (7.5 lb.)Pre-seasoned: Yes

What I loved: Again, I apologize for snubbing Lodge, as even in our office we have a number of staunch brand loyalists. But in my testing, the Victoria edged out the fan favorite on two separate metrics. Victoria pans are pre-seasoned with flaxseed oil and arrive glossy and exceptionally nonstick. Having a more thorough pre-seasoning is more important on cast-iron pans, as they are prone to sticking early on. We found the Victoria pan’s factory seasoning slicker than Lodge’s, which made frying potatoes and eggs ever so slightly easier. Do all cast-iron seasonings improve with continued use over time? Yes. But we know that some people want as much of a head start as they can get, and this pan offers you the best one.

The other way the Victoria bested the Lodge is in its form factor. The pour spouts on the Victoria are nice and wide, making it easy to pour off oil or other pan juices, and testers found the handle shape slightly more comfortable than the Lodge.

I’ll be honest, though, these differences are pretty small, and if you feel drawn to the Lodge name, I recommend it as well.

What I’d leave: Given it’s bargain pricing, there isn’t much to dislike here. I will note this pan is significantly heavier than the Lancaster pan—a full pound and a half for the same diameter skillet. Heavier skillets are cheaper and easier to produce, so it’s a trade-off you’ll have to accept if you want a less expensive piece of cookware.

1. We had several members of staff handle the pans to get a broad sense of how easy the pans were to maneuver. Then we got to cooking.

2. Using a little bit of oil, we fried eggs sunny-side up and scrambled to see how much (if anything) stuck to the pan.

3. We seared skin-on chicken thighs to get a sense of how evenly heat was distributed around the cooking surface. We also measured how long it took for the pan to reach 375° at medium heat.

4. We washed the pans in hot water, noting any places where seasoning might have worn away.

5. We re-seasoned the pans ourselves in an oven for an hour at 500°.

6. We cooked another round of eggs to observe any changes.

I omitted enameled cast-iron skillets like those made by Le Creuset or Staub because enameled surfaces offer a different experience in terms of both cooking and care. I also chose to exclude any cast-iron griddles or grill pans since they are too different functionally.

Sizing is a bit different from company to company, but I chose to stick with a 10"-diameter skillet—a No. 8 in traditional cast-iron sizing—as it is the most common size available.

I should clarify that cast-iron pans aren’t nonstick in the sense that you can cook an egg in the pan without any oil and slide it around. A really well-seasoned pan that’s a glossy lacquered black from years of use might get close, but the seasoning really just helps food release more easily from the pan—and the more seasoning there is, the less oil you’ll need for food to release.

I evaluated the pans on their out-of-the-box factory seasoning, because having a solid seasoning layer to start with diminishes the amount of time you need to break in a pan. This matters more with cheaper, rough textured cast iron, which is more prone to sticking when it lacks proper seasoning. For polished or vintage-style cast-iron pans (like the Lancaster), factory seasoning is nice, but the smooth surface also aids in preventing sticking, so it isn’t as crucial in the beginning stages of using the pan. That is why, throughout this review you see more emphasis on factory seasoning when discussing budget pans.

Is the pan designed in a way that makes it easy to use?

I counted form and design heavily in how I judged these pans. I wanted the pan to be comfortable and easy to maneuver, so I looked for pans that were lightweight (relatively, we’re talking about iron here) and had handles that were comfortable to grip. If the pan was heavier, I wanted a helper handle for moving it from the cooktop to the oven. I didn’t place an emphasis on whether handle was designed to stay cool, because even a handle billed as “stay cool” will get dangerously hot when cooking for long enough, so I feel it’s better to just make a habit of always using an oven mitt or cloth to grab a cast-iron handle.

Heavy-duty, even-heating, satisfyingly weighty skillets are staples in the BA Test Kitchen because of their versatility. Stainless-steel and carbon steel frying pans get hot quickly, but they don’t always have the heat-retention capabilities of cast iron. And while nonstick pans are nice for scrambled eggs and crispy-skinned fish, many are not oven-safe and should never be exposed to high temperatures, so you can’t sear safely with them.

The Stargazer is a lovely pan. Like the Lancaster, its a vintage-style skillet, so it has a smooth texture that’s easy to clean. The surface develops seasoning well, and the curved lip allows for easy pouring at any angle. Ultimately, it is one of the heavier high-end skillets available on the market, which is why we don’t have it as a winner. However, if weight isn’t a huge concern for you, it is still an excellent pan.

If you know cast-iron pans, you might see the Yeti cast-iron skillet and might find that it looks somewhat familiar. This is because Yeti acquired cult-favorite Butter Pat several years ago. The Yeti skillet is just the Butter Pat by a new name, and apart from the logo, the finish, handle shape, and overall design remain unchanged. This pan has a nice velvety surface that holds on to seasoning very well, while still maintaining a smooth, glossier finish that makes vintage-style pans so desirable. Small gripes: The handle design wasn’t a favorite among testers, and the side walls are a slightly shorter than most other cast-iron pans. It’s also a touch heavier and a couple touches more expensive than our winner. Still, this is an excellent cast-iron pan and makes a great family heirloom.

Lodge Cast-Iron Skillet with Red Mini Silicone Hot Handle Holder, 8"

People who track recommendations like these tend to be shocked that we don’t place the Lodge as our winner or budget pick. It is a fantastic pan, make no mistake. It has a great factory seasoning that’s resilient from the jump, and the 10" costs around twenty bucks—so what gives? When it came down to it, the Victoria pan had a slicker factory seasoning out of the box and a more comfortable handle design.

Another high-end polished cast-iron pan on the list. Smithey pans are gorgeous, so much so that it almost feels wrong cooking with them. However, you should cook with it straight away, as the factory seasoning is a little light on these, and we observed a little bit wearing away after the first couple rounds of cooking prior to us adding an additional layer of seasoning. Senior editor Noah Kaufman has been cooking with the Smithey multiple times a week for a couple years and says that within a few months of regular use and two bouts of seasoning in the oven he no longer worried about stuck eggs or steaks.

Gorgeous as they are, Smithey pans are heavy, though, at 5.8 lb. for the 10" skillet.

This skillet is the second lightest (4.3 lb. at 10") and has a velvety surface that holds on to seasoning a little better than the smooth polished pans. Like the Stargazer, it also has a curved lip instead of a pour spout, but I found that this pan does have a bit of a dribbling problem, which I wasn't crazy about. Still, one member of our team who has now lived with this pan for years loves it and uses it every day.

Lodge Cast-Iron Blacklock Skillet, Triple Seasoned - 10.25"

Lodge released this pan in response to the wave of new and fancy polished pans, and as beautiful (quite beautiful), well-seasoned (three glossy layers), and lightweight as it is (almost even with the Lancaster), our testers found the handle uncomfortable to hold.

Ooni is a pizza oven company, and this pan is really designed for cooking in an oven rather than on the stovetop. It has a detachable handle, which is actually a genius bit of design that makes it easy and comfortable to grab out of a blazing hot pizza oven. But the sides are too shallow for doing more normal cast-iron things like frying chicken or sautéing greens. It is, however, great for cornbread and pizookies.

This is Made In’s official entry into the cast-iron new wave. The pan has a smooth machined surface, nice design touches, like curved sidewalls and a spacious helper handle. The primary handle is nice to hold; however, a longer handle can make a pan feel heavier and add strain on the wrists. This pan is not the lightest, either. I found it difficult to transport the full pan from the stovetop to the oven using only one hand, so consider this a pan for people with meaty forearms. Made In also uses flaxseed oil for the factory seasoning, which is a controversial choice in the cast-iron world. The reason for that controversy is that, while the finish flaxseed oil produces is glossy and attractive, it tends to be brittle. Especially with newer pans, a flaxseed seasoning has a tendency to wear away with regular cooking. After testing, I did notice this pan had some gray (unseasoned) patches after a round of searing meat. Again, not a big deal—just keep cooking with it— but something to keep in mind. All of that being said, I do still think this is a high-quality pan. During the cooking tests, I had absolutely no issues with sticking whatsoever.

This pan is pretty similar to a standard Lodge or Victoria, but with a seasoning that’s not as nonstick out of the box. We did find, however, that it added new layers of seasoning quite well.

The Valor is apparently a favorite in restaurants, but there’s nothing special to it that makes it stand out. If anything, the pour spouts are so small they might as well not be there at all.

We’re all for innovation, which is what Finex sought to do with its octagonal pan and its bulbous handle, but we didn’t really observe any value from the modifications. While the octagonal shape is easier for flipping you could just use a bigger cast-iron pan for anything you want to flip. And its “speed cool” handle was awkward to hold.

Anytime KitchenAid ventures beyond the small appliance space you never quite know what you’re gonna get. In this case, it’s a cast-iron pan that is totally average in every way, except for its minimalist modern design. We think this pan is too expensive for what you’re getting.

“Ooh, a lid!” Was the universal reaction to this cast-iron pan. If you like the idea of having a lid for your pan, then this is your pan. The problem with cast-iron lids, though, is that they don’t benefit from the progressive seasoning development the rest of the pan gets as you cook with it. Lids are only really dealing with evaporative moisture, which makes them even more likely to rust. Smithey, up above, sells glass lids that fit their pans, which, while not as oven-safe, won’t have that rust problem.

This is Victoria’s answer to the high-end polished cast-iron pan. The seasoning is great, but the pan is heavier than the Lancaster, and we didn’t love all the extra design embellishments. The brass insert on the handle had no practical value (it heated up quicker than the surrounding cast iron). Also, all the extra ridges and divots just meant more places for gunk to get stuck in.

Amazon customers really like this pan. It comes with a silicone handle cover and a glass lid, which is nice (glass is a better material for a lid than cast iron). It also has tall 3" sides that make this pan great for frying. Beyond that, though, the pan is heavy and seemed to be barely pre-seasoned.

This is a super polished cast-iron pan with a glossy cooking surface that was nice to work with. However, we noticed quite a few cosmetic issues, like small nicks and rough edges that made it seem like there were some corners cut in the manufacturing process.

Another pan that is just fine. The factory seasoning is minimal, so you’ll have to build that up yourself. There are several better options that are just as affordable from Victoria, Lodge, and others.

This is an affordable pan that looks a lot like a Lodge, but with a lesser factory seasoning.

The seasoning that came on this pan out of the box was pretty bad, and with so many other cheap alternatives that offer much better quality, we don’t see the point in purchasing this pan. It’s also only available in a 15" diameter at the time of writing, which is bigger (and heavier) than most people need.

When you first get your pan, you’ll want to season it. We recommend this even when the pan comes labeled as pre-seasoned. To do this, just lightly rub a bone-dry pan with a thin layer of high-heat neutral vegetable oil and place it upside down in a very hot oven—450°F–500°F should do the trick. Leave for an hour, turn off the heat, let it cool completely in the oven (you should be able to take it out without an oven mitt or towel), rub with a tiny bit more oil, and store. You can season cast iron as many times as you’d like to build up a glossy nonstick surface; when the pan looks dull or dry, it’s time to moisturize.

No, you can’t chuck it in the dishwasher, and you won’t be using your normal hand-wash methods, but a cast-iron skillet really doesn’t require much love. When it’s time to clean up, simply wipe a damp rag across the surface of your pan, then dry it thoroughly. Often, that’ll be enough. But if there are any crusty bits, try pouring coarse salt in there and going at it with a Tawashi scrubber, which has soft bristles that whisk away any detritus. Many will tell you to avoid soap at all costs lest you ruin your careful seasoning, but a little dish soap is fine—just don’t let it sit in hot water. (Read our complete guide to cleaning cast iron.)

For really baked on crumbs, try The Ringer, a handy chain mail scrubber that easily rinses clean between uses. After cleaning your cast iron, be sure to wipe your fry pan very dry—this is key for preventing any rust spots. Then take a teeny bit of neutral cooking oil (like canola or vegetable), smear on a paper towel, and give it a light coating. Take care to get the handle and the bottom as well as the cooking surface, as rust can crop up anywhere. And you’re good to go! It sounds involved, but it really only takes a few minutes. A well-seasoned pan takes virtually no time at all, so dutifully season and you’ll be rewarded.

Tossed your skillet in the sink absentmindedly or left it out in the rain only to find it’s developed a layer of orange rust? Don’t panic—rusting can happen pretty easily if you allow your pan to come into contact with water for an extended period of time (it is made of iron, after all). But that doesn’t mean it’s ruined. A salt scrub will help with most small spots, while a vinegar soak is the cure for more serious cases. (Read more on dealing with pesky cast-iron rust patches.)

If, after all of that, you’re still intimidated by raw cast-iron cookware, you might want to consider an enameled cast-iron skillet. It offers all of the heat retention and distribution of a well-seasoned cast-iron pan, plus it has a porcelain enamel to prevent rusting. Unlike a Le Creuset Dutch oven, enameled cast-iron skillets, like Staub’s, have a dark textured enamel that helps with browning and crisping.

Wilder Davies: I have been Epicurious and Bon Appétit’s resident cookware tester and researcher for over six years. I have cooked with hundreds and hundreds of pans and have asked chefs, materials scientists, and manufacturers far too many questions about things that go clank in the kitchen. I am a big apologist of nonstick alternatives, and strongly believe in a buy-it-for-life ethos when it comes to outfitting your pantry.

#6623. Andrew Scott on Elsinore, the Met Gala, and Why “Shakespeare Is Really for Everybody”

To be or not to be? Andrew Scott knows a thing or two about that question. On Wednesday evening, the Irish actor brought a touch of Shakespearean flair—and plenty of leading-man charisma—to the Museum of Modern Art for the New York premiere of his latest film, Elsinore.

Dressed in a pinstripe suit by Vivienne Westwood, Scott made quite the entrance. Joining him were director Simon Stone, co-star Joe Locke, and members of the film’s creative team, all exchanging warm embraces, big smiles, and the kind of affectionate greetings that made the evening feel less like a formal premiere and more like a particularly well-dressed reunion.

There was plenty to celebrate. Based on a remarkable true story, Elsinore features Scott as Ian Charleson, the Scottish actor best known for his role in Chariots of Fire, during the final months of his life in 1989. As he prepares to take on the titular role of Hamlet at London’s National Theatre, Charleson is privately battling AIDS, though determined to return to the stage despite his deteriorating health. Named after the Danish castle that provides the setting for Shakespeare’s tragedy, the film follows Charleson’s journey toward one final, extraordinary performance, exploring the complicated relationship between art and mortality, and the courage it takes to keep pursuing one’s passion in the face of devastating circumstances.

Also starring Olivia Colman and Luke Thompson, Elsinore finds unexpected lightness in a story shadowed by tragedy. At its heart is a celebration of the transformative power of performance—and of a man whose final act would become one of the most meaningful of his life.

Scott is no stranger to Shakespeare’s most famous prince. His own acclaimed turn as Hamlet in Robert Icke’s 2017 Almeida Theatre production earned him an Olivier Award nomination. His experience with the Bard may make Shakespeare’s lines look effortless, but finding his way into the language is another matter. So what’s his secret? “I always think of it like rap music. If I don’t understand every word when someone is rapping, there’s the energy behind it and the musicality or the velocity of it—and it’s still electrifying,” he told Vogue. “It’s the same with Shakespeare, but I hate the idea that it’s kind of kidnapped by academics. Shakespeare is really for everybody.”

And when it comes to commanding an audience, Scott is something of an expert, though even he admits that some occasions are more nerve-racking than others. Asked whether portraying Hamlet or getting dressed for the Met Gala presents the bigger challenge, he didn’t hesitate. “Playing Hamlet is more intimidating—but only just,” he said with a laugh. “I think with the Met Gala, you always think it’s going to be incredibly intimidating. The stairs are a bit scary, but it’s only clothes! So you’ve just got to have a bit of fun.”

Scott’s greatest challenge in Elsinore was getting beneath the mythology of Charleson and discovering the man himself. What struck him most was the actor’s sense of humor—a quality he was determined to preserve on screen. Despite its emotional weight, Scott insists, this is not a film without comic relief. “It’s a very uplifting and a very funny film,” he said, calling Stephen Beresford’s screenplay “as hysterically funny as it is heartbreaking.”

That humor was also something producer Andrea Occhipinti was keen to protect. His connection to Charleson, however, went far beyond the screen. The two first met in 1984 while working on the television miniseries The Sun Also Rises. As Occhipinti recalled, they became close friends, bonding over the fact that they were the only two gay men in the group. Charleson never disclosed that he was HIV-positive. It was only after his death, when their mutual friend Ethan Silverman shared the story of his final six months, that Occhipinti began to imagine the possibility of a film.

Years later, he found his screenwriter in Beresford and his leading man in Scott. The casting, it seems, was almost written in the stars. Asked what Charleson might have thought of the film and the evening’s celebrations, Occhipinti said he was certain his friend would approve. “Ian would be pleased because Andrew Scott is amazing. He really looks like Ian and he has incredible talent. I think he would have smiled about all of this tonight. He very much was a loving and warm person.”

That celebratory spirit carried into the evening, which brought out a suitably starry crowd. Among those on hand to mark the occasion were Sigourney Weaver, Ben Platt, Dylan Mulvaney, Patricia Clarkson, Katie Couric, François Arnaud of Heated Rivalry, And Just Like That’s Sarita Choudhury, Kate Walsh, and Christopher Meloni.

And no Shakespearean celebration would be complete without a little drama after the curtain fell. The festivities continued at Le Rock, where guests gathered for the after-party, eager to congratulate Scott, exchange a few words, and sing his praises. Over Champagne and conversation, partygoers tucked into sliders and fries, while an impressive seafood display piled high with fresh lobster, oysters, and shrimp provided a lavish centerpiece.

Naturally, Shakespeare had the last word on the evening’s décor, too. Copies of Hamlet were scattered throughout the restaurant, alongside a rather cheeky nod to one of the play’s most memorable scenes. A skull emblazoned with the words “This is what you’ll look like by the end of it”—a joke that also features in the film—added a deliciously irreverent touch. It was a fitting detail for a celebration of a story that finds plenty of laughter amid the tragedy. The party carried on well past midnight, with no one seemingly in a hurry to call it a night.

#6622. Is Cottage Cheese Good for You?

Yes, cottage cheese is good for you! It's packed with protein and calcium, but the kind you buy matters. Here's how to choose the best cottage cheese for cooking, baking and snacking.

I have to admit: I can see why cottage cheese recipes go viral. TikTok trends have turned this humble dairy staple into everything from high-protein flatbread to better-for-you ice cream. Packed with protein and important vitamins and minerals, cottage cheese is an easy way to make everyday meals more satisfying.

As a dietitian and recipe developer, I love an ingredient that’s not only nutritious but also versatile and affordable, and that can help me meet my daily protein goals. There are so many creative ways to use cottage cheese, and a whole new world of options opens up when you whip it smooth. Think: smoothies, creamy dips, pasta sauces, puddings and more!

But as versatile as cottage cheese is, you can’t swap it into every recipe without a little know-how. And with so many milkfat options, the one you buy matters. I’ll share my favorite ways to use it, which varieties work best for different dishes and a few tricks to help you get delicious results every time.

First things first: Here’s why you might want to toss another tub of cottage cheese into your grocery cart.

Cottage cheese is one of my go-to high-protein foods. A half-cup serving packs 12 to 14 grams of protein, roughly the same amount you’d get from two large eggs.

Adding a scoop of cottage cheese to my plate is an easy way to make meals and snacks more satisfying without turning on the stove. I especially like it at breakfast, when it’s all too easy to end up with a meal that’s heavy on carbohydrates but light on protein. A scoop alongside toast and fruit, or blended into pancake batter, gives breakfast a little extra staying power without much effort.

You don’t have to be lifting heavy weights to care about muscle health. Our bodies need plenty of protein to maintain and repair muscle tissue, and that becomes especially important as we get older.

I like to keep cottage cheese on hand for an easy post-workout snack because there’s nothing to prep. Pair it with fruit or whole-grain crackers, and you’ve got protein plus carbohydrates to help muscles refuel and recover after exercise.

The protein in cottage cheese does more than help keep you full and support your muscles—it also plays an important role in keeping your bones strong. Cottage cheese aprovides two minerals that work together to support bone health: phosphorus and calcium.

It’s worth noting that cottage cheese contains less calcium than a serving of milk or Greek yogurt, but it can absolutely contribute to your daily intake. Just be sure to include other calcium-rich foods in your diet, too.

The type of cottage cheese you buy can make a big difference in how your recipes turn out. Like other dairy products, cottage cheese comes in different milkfat percentages, which affects its taste and texture.

I usually reach for 2% or 4% cottage cheese, depending on how I’m using it. Low-fat (2% cottage cheese) is perfect for whipping into dips, spreads and pasta sauces. It contains enough fat to blend smooth and creamy without feeling too heavy.

Full-fat, or 4% cottage cheese, gets my vote for baked goods, casseroles and lasagna fillings. The extra fat adds richness, which is especially helpful if you’re using it in place of sour cream or cream cheese.

I usually skip fat-free cottage cheese for cooking. It tends to be watery with a slightly chalky taste, and the lack of fat can make creamy recipes less satisfying. That extra moisture can also affect the texture of baked dishes, so I prefer cottage cheese with a little more fat for the best results.

For all its nutritional perks, cottage cheese can also pack a lot of sodium. Some brands contain more than 400 milligrams per half-cup serving. Eat a full cup, and you could be getting more than 800 milligrams of sodium (about one-third of the recommended daily limit) from cottage cheese alone.

Too much sodium can raise blood pressure and increase your risk of heart disease, so it’s worth paying attention to how much you’re getting, especially if you eat cottage cheese regularly.

If you’re watching your sodium intake, compare labels and choose a brand that’s lower in sodium. Good Culture is one of my favorite cottage cheese brands. With 380 milligrams of sodium per serving, it’s a little lower than other brands.

I also go easy on added salt when using cottage cheese with salty ingredients like Parmesan or ranch seasoning.

Here are some creative ways to put cottage cheese to work, plus a few kitchen tricks I’ve learned along the way:
