Archaeologists have discovered thousands of stone artifacts in Saudi Arabia, some of which suggest people were using poison-tipped stone tools to hunt large game 125,000 years ago.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists have found what may be the world's oldest poisoned weapons at a 125,000-year-old site on an ancient lakeshore in Saudi Arabia. The stone tools, which were likely used to hunt large animals, had traces of residue from a poisonous tree historically used for its toxins.

"At 125,000 years old, these would be substantially older than the poisoned arrowheads recently identified in South Africa, which date to around 60,000 years ago," study co-author Chris Clarkson, an archaeologist at the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology in Germany and Griffith University in Australia, told Live Science in an email. "But we haven't demonstrated exactly how the poison was prepared or whether it was effective. So I'd describe these as potentially the oldest evidence for poisoned hunting weapons, rather than an unequivocally established first."

In the new study, published Thursday (Nov. 12) in the journal Science, researchers investigated a 125,000-year-old site in southern Saudi Arabia known as 'Uruq Aljelibah, which means "sand dunes of a watering hole," study co-author Frans van Buchem, a geologist at the King Abdullah University of Science and Technology in Saudi Arabia, told Live Science.

Today, the area is "hot, extremely dry, with extensive sand dunes," Clarkson said, located as it is within the Empty Quarter — one of the hottest, driest deserts on Earth. But the scientists found the site was once home to a freshwater lake measuring about 130 square miles (340 square kilometers) and up to 95 feet (29 meters) deep. Fossils there suggest it once supported a rich diversity of flora and fauna, including hippopotamuses, buffalo, ostriches, camels, gazelles, oryx, palms, reeds, trees and shrubs, which early modern humans likely exploited for food and other resources.

"The idea of hippopotamuses and enormous buffalo living around a lake in what is now the Empty Quarter really brings home just how dramatically these landscapes, and global climates, have changed," Clarkson said.

Saudi Arabia is a desert today, but it used to be a lush landscape.

The archaeologists discovered more than 5,500 stone artifacts at the site, along with extraordinarily preserved traces of plant materials, such as fibers, resins and wood. Several of these artifacts were stone points that showed impact damage consistent with hunting large animals, and a microscopic analysis revealed traces of animal tissue near the point tips. The distribution of the stone tools closely matched clusters of animal bones, suggesting that the lakeshore was a focal point for hunting and processing game, according to the study.

"At most Paleolithic sites, we're lucky if we get the stone tools and perhaps a few animal bones," Clarkson said. "Here we can actually begin to reconstruct what those tools were doing and what other materials people were combining with them."

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The researchers found that people may have hunted animals with poison-tipped tools. Several stone points had chemical residues linked with the arrow poison tree (Acokanthera schimperi), which is known historically for its toxins and is native to eastern and central Africa and southern Arabia. African hunters have coated spear tips and arrowheads with extracts from this plant to paralyze or kill game.

It remains unclear how hunters who poisoned their targets might have avoided poisoning themselves upon eating the game.

"The effects of a poison depend on the substance, the dose and how it enters the body," Clarkson said. "A poison introduced directly into a wound doesn't necessarily behave in the same way when swallowed." Hunters throughout history "are known to sometimes remove the meat around the wound before eating the rest of the animal," he added.

These findings emphasize how researchers have often underestimated the technological complexity of early human populations, because so much of what they made was organic and has simply disappeared," Clarkson said. "These weren't just people knocking stone flakes off cores," Clarkson noted. "They were combining stone with wood, plant fibers, resins and potentially toxic substances to make complex tools and weapons."

To have so much evidence for how people were making and using tools in a site like this "is remarkable," Eleanor Scerri, an archaeologist at the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology in Germany who did not take part in this research, told Live Science in an email. "This goes from both the micro-scale, in finding traces of how people hafted spear tips, for instance, up to the bigger scale of the whole site and the very convincing spatial relationship between hunting-related tools and the bones of animals such as hippos."

Sites in Arabia that possess both stone tools and animal bones are rare, Jeffrey Rose, a Paleolithic archaeologist at the University of Algarve in Portugal who did not participate in this study, told Live Science in an email. "This one has thousands of artifacts on an old lakeshore alongside hippo, buffalo and ostrich, and some of the flakes fit back together, so the tools were made on the spot," he said. "It's valuable new data."

The Arabian Peninsula sits between Africa and the rest of Asia and was a major corridor for humans as they dispersed across the world. Recurring spans of increased rainfall could have made its otherwise hostile landscapes more habitable in the past. However, the hot desert that now covers much of Arabia has made it difficult for scientists to excavate many details about this vital bridge during this critical point in human history.

The researchers did not unearth any human remains. Still, they suspect the site most likely belonged to modern humans (our species, Homo sapiens), as opposed to a different human species.

"We know that H. sapiens had already expanded out of Africa and were present in Southwest Asia during this period," Clarkson said. "The age of the site fits with those early movements."

These findings add to growing evidence that wetter intervals in Arabia created migration corridors between Africa and Asia and supported productive habitats capable of sustaining repeated human occupation.

"What our site shows is that people weren't necessarily just passing through these environments," Clarkson said. "They were exploiting them in quite sophisticated ways, using a range of technologies and resources."

But Rose cautioned that all of the stone artifacts found in this study were collected from the surface. "Not one was excavated from the layers that were dated," he said. "The 125,000-year date belongs to the lake, not to the tools. For the tools, it is only a maximum age." Future research at the site should look for stone artifacts sealed in lake beds. "That's hard in Arabia, where wind has stripped most sites down to surface scatters, but it can be done," Rose said.

Clarkson agrees that further work is needed. "I'd really like to keep going back to this site to find more fossils, both animals as well as hopefully human fossils," Clarkson said. "I'd also really like to push the chemical and functional analyses further, particularly the evidence for toxic plant compounds. It would be fascinating to determine exactly which substances were being used, how they might have been prepared and whether they were deliberately applied to hunting weapons."

Future research focusing on the ancient lake margins may reveal more information. "There must be other places where people were living and carrying out activities, and some may preserve better stratified archaeological deposits," Clarkson said.

But the combination of discoveries at this site is amazing, the researchers said.

"I've spent much of my career studying stone tools, and one of the great frustrations is that we're usually only looking at the small fraction of ancient technology that survives," Clarkson said. "Here we have a chance to see much more of the complete technological system."

Clarkson, C., Price, G.J., Kalifi, A., Losi, G., Matheson, C., Al-Jibreen, F., Alsharekh, A.M., Armitage, S.J., Blilou, I., Boivin, N., Breeze, P.S., Drake, N., Duval, M., Gradwell, S., Groucutt, H.W., Guagnin, M., Guzmán, J., Hapiot, L., Martínez-Pillado, V., … van Buchem, F. (2026). Poisoned hunting weapons, megafauna, and plant use at a 125,000-year-old Arabian paleolakeshore. Science. https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aef9342

#6503. Why Do Some People Feel Their Souls Leave Their Bodies at Night? The Answer May Lie in a Hidden Brain State.

Brainwave recordings reveal the strange neural overlap that can make you feel like you’re floating away.

When you have what is known as an out-of-body experience, you may feel as if your mind has left your body, though it hasn’t actually gone anywhere. Maybe you feel like you’re floating or flying. On the darker side, it might be an unsettling experience that makes you feel as if your body no longer belongs to you, or a nightmarish bout of sleep paralysis that leaves you panting and in a cold sweat. How can the brain conjure experiences that sound straight out of science fiction but are really nothing more than illusions?

To make sense of these intangible phenomena, neuroscientist Teresa Campillo-Ferrer of Radboud University in the Netherlands recruited participants for an experiment designed to capture what happens in the brain when the mind seems to wander from the body during sleep. Most of her subjects had already had an out-of-body episode or some other kind of unusual bodily experience (UBE). Some were lucid dreamers, people who can become aware that they are dreaming. Others had dealt with sleep paralysis, which is waking up while the body is still paralyzed as it is during dreaming sleep. Some had even felt that they left their physical body behind and passed through a portal to another realm. Although UBEs can occur during waking hours, Campillo-Ferrer reasoned that she would probably capture more of them in sleeping brains.

“Studying UBEs is essential for understanding the mechanisms underlying bodily awareness, self-perception, and the sense of ‘having a body’ (embodiment) or ‘owning a body’ (body ownership),” she wrote in a study recently published in Consciousness and Cognition. “As such, UBE research has the potential to expand current theories of human self-consciousness and multisensory perception.”

The participants’ main job was simply to relax. Before they drifted off to dreamland, they were fitted with EEG electrodes, practiced pre-sleep meditation, and were given visual stimulation that could help induce lucid dreams and UBEs. Researchers also asked them to move their eyes left and right several times if they noticed anything strange happening, whether or not they were lucid dreaming. This works because even in a semiconscious state, the brain can remember instructions and respond to something unusual. Participants then slept for three hours in soundproof chambers. If the recordings showed the left-right eye signal, participants were either spoken to over an intercom or woken up to describe their experiences. After the sleep session ended, participants also discussed their dreams with the researchers.

The reported UBEs fell into several categories. In vestibular-motor experiences, subjects felt as if they were moving or being moved, such as levitating, spinning, or falling. These sensations can also show up in the opposite way, as heaviness or a feeling of sinking deeper and deeper, like the harrowing scene in A Nightmare on Elm Street where Glen is sucked into his own bed. Flying and other movements that defy the laws of physics also belong in this category. In tactile UBEs, the person feels touch or vibrations from an outside source even though nothing is touching them. In UBEs involving distorted body boundaries, the outer limits of the body blur, so that the body seems to merge with the bed (another very Freddy Krueger moment), shapeshift into another form, or gain a duplicate.

Other UBEs are defined by a lack of bodily sensation or sense of position. These are often associated with feeling detached from the physical body or not knowing where the body actually is. They are similar, though not identical, to out-of-body UBEs, in which participants reported leaving their physical body or realizing, at least while dreaming, that they felt separate from it. Because out-of-body experiences often involve a feeling of levitation, they tend to overlap with the vestibular-motor category, though some involve no sense of movement at all. Sleep paralysis made up another category, and it may be the most frightening. The person is fully aware but can’t move, and sometimes it feels as if they can’t breathe. Still other UBEs stemmed from hallucinations or lucid dreams.

Exactly where UBEs arise in the brain is still unknown. After analyzing EEG patterns, however, the researchers suggest that they happen somewhere in the liminal space between waking and sleeping. In participants whose UBEs were confirmed by the eye-movement signal, slower brainwaves known as delta and theta waves decreased while faster beta and gamma waves surged, especially in the temporal lobes on both sides of the brain. These are the regions that process the sensory information that gives us a sense of existing in our bodies. What makes this pattern striking is that slower waves are linked to sleep, while faster waves are more typical of being awake. It is as if the sleeping and waking brain overlap.

Campillo-Ferrer explained the significance of these findings: “Specific EEG features associated with UBEs appear to reflect the reactivation of EEG activity from levels observed in baseline brain states in which UBEs emerge. [Our] models allowed for precise analysis of neural activity and individual variability, providing new insights into the neural correlates associated with UBEs and their role in bodily self-perception and consciousness.”

#6502. Scientists Discover a Hidden Magnetic Effect That Produces Signals 100 Times Stronger

Antiferromagnets could pave the way for faster, more energy-efficient electronics, but accurately measuring their properties remains a major challenge.

A nearly invisible layer of magnetic material can overwhelm scientific measurements, producing signals more than 100 times stronger than those of the material researchers are trying to study. Scientists at Martin Luther University Halle-Wittenberg (MLU) and the Max Planck Institute for Microstructure Physics discovered this problem while investigating a promising material for ultrafast electronics. Their findings, published in Advanced Materials, also show how to prevent the interference.

The research focuses on antiferromagnets, materials in which neighboring atomic magnetic moments cancel one another out, leaving little or no overall magnetization. Unlike conventional ferromagnets, they are resistant to electromagnetic interference and can switch magnetic states up to 1,000 times faster. These properties could help engineers develop faster electronic components that consume less energy.

The researchers investigated Mn₃Sn, a compound made of manganese and tin that belongs to a special group called chiral antiferromagnets. Its magnetic moments are arranged at 120-degree angles rather than pointing in opposite directions. This arrangement has a property called chirality, meaning it cannot be superimposed on its mirror image simply by rotating or moving it.

“Chiral antiferromagnets combine the advantages of both classes of magnets while minimizing their drawbacks. However, they are often difficult to control,” explains Professor Georg Woltersdorf from the Institute of Physics at MLU and spokesperson for the Cluster of Excellence “Center for Chiral Electronics”.

Researchers in the cluster are exploring ways to use chirality in spintronics, an approach to electronics that exploits the spin of electrons as well as their electrical charge. Spin is an intrinsic form of angular momentum that gives electrons magnetic properties. Controlling it could enable electronic devices that operate at extremely high speeds while using less energy.

To examine Mn₃Sn, the team fabricated layers just a few nanometers thick and combined them with either platinum or a nickel-iron alloy. They then exposed the samples to ultrashort laser pulses and measured the resulting electrical voltages on picosecond timescales, equivalent to trillionths of a second. These measurements allowed the researchers to investigate rapid changes in magnetic order.

However, the samples containing platinum produced unexpected results. The researchers traced the problem to a heating step used during fabrication to repair defects in the crystal structure. During this process, atoms at the interface between the materials reacted to form an unintended ferromagnetic compound.

This thin interfacial layer generated magnetic signals more than 100 times stronger than those produced by Mn₃Sn itself. As a result, the measurements were dominated by the newly formed compound rather than the antiferromagnet the scientists intended to investigate.

“It was only when we modified the process and allowed the Mn₃Sn layer to be cure fully before depositing the platinum that the material remained unchanged. Before that, we had essentially only been measuring a layer that was an unintended result of the sample preparation process,” explains the study’s first author Paul Marschall from the Institute of Physics at MLU.

By completing the heating treatment before adding platinum, the researchers avoided forming the unwanted magnetic compound. Properly prepared samples then allowed them to investigate the actual properties of Mn₃Sn, including how efficiently it converts spin currents into measurable electrical voltages.

When the scientists directed a spin current from the nickel-iron layer into Mn₃Sn, they found that the conversion efficiency was approximately 10% of that typically achieved with platinum. This provided a more reliable assessment of the material’s behavior without the interfering magnetic layer.

“Interfaces are not just a peripheral aspect of spintronics, they are often the actual component. If we want to harness chiral antiferromagnets for technological applications, we must first understand and be able to control what happens within these few atomic layers,” concludes Woltersdorf.

Reference: “Spin Transport Across Interfaces With the Non-Collinear Antiferromagnet Mn3Sn” by Paul A. Marschall, Wolfgang Hoppe, Prajwal Rigvedi, Börge Göbel, Franziska Ziolkowski, Samir Lounis, Banabir Pal, Stuart S. P. Parkin and Georg Woltersdorf, 20 September 2026, Advanced Materials. DOI: 10.1002/adma.75024

The study was funded by the German Research Foundation (DFG).

Re-examining this system through the Flow–Anti-Flow Symmetry Transformation and Topological Vortex Theory reveals that the interface should be understood as a distinct topological vortex phase, whose geometry determines the macroscopic spin-transport response.

The Mn₃Sn/Pt case shows that interface engineering in spintronics is fundamentally geometric. Once the interface is recognized as a topological vortex phase, the distinction between “intrinsic Mn₃Sn signal” and “interfacial artifact” becomes a question of vortex boundary conditions rather than sample quality alone. This perspective turns a persistent experimental ambiguity into a constructive design principle for TVT-based spintronic devices.

Treating an “accident” at a material boundary not as a nuisance to sweep under the rug, but as a clue—or a different purpose waiting to be discovered—flips the whole lens on how these effects get read.

In both lab experiments and hands-on engineering, an unexpected reaction right at the seam often points to something you wouldn’t have set out to test on purpose. Instead of viewing a 100x interfacial signal strictly as contamination that ruins a clean baseline, it can stand on its own as a distinct boundary behavior or show what happens when layer timing and thermal energy are deliberately staggered.

A different target altogether: What looks like a ruined test of a base material can point to a much stronger or faster response coming from the interface itself—worth studying for what that seam actually does rather than tossing it aside.

Timing as a deliberate lever: When letting one layer lag behind another before coupling and heating produces a big jump, that lag becomes a tunable variable rather than just a procedural slip.

Testing assumptions at the seam: A surprise at the boundary forces a closer look at what is really happening where two surfaces meet, instead of treating the interface as a passive divider.

Viewed alongside standard material science and cosmology as a complementary lens, seeing that 100x boundary jump through intersecting temporal torsional knots binding and accumulating at an interface lines right up with how structure forms out of geometry, timing, and tension.

Binding Instead of Passing Through: Rather than slipping past each other with minimal friction, overlapping phase and impedance gradients lock them into a bound configuration right at the seam—much like a tight dual-helix weave under tension.

Why Accumulation Happens: Once a bound knot or interfacial phase locks in, it acts as a local anchor where rotational structure and energy accumulate instead of scattering out. #6501. Black Holes and Their Mysterious Bright Structures Explained

Astrophysical jets launched from black holes aren't shy. They announce their presence with enormous blasts of energy that extend extreme distances into space. They're the most long-lasting and luminous sources of electromagnetic energy in the Universe.

Supermassive black holes (SMBH) emit the largest astrophysical jets, and they come from active galactic nuclei (AGN) which are SMBH that are actively accreting material. As material gathers in an accretion disk around a SMBH, it rotates and heats up. Some of the material is ejected out of the black hole in the powerful jets.

These jets are impossible to ignore. No astrophysicist could feign their interest. Exactly how these powerful expressions of cosmic energy are created isn't clear, though some things are known.

Astrophysicists know that they're powered by a SMBH's rotational energy and their extremely powerful magnetic fields. They know that they move at relativistic speeds. And they know that they can inject gigantic amounts of energy into the intergalactic medium, heating up gas and introducing turbulence, two things that act against star formation.

One thing that puzzles researchers is how the different regions in a black hole jet have different brightnesses. The expectation is that the center of the jets would be brightest, because this is where energy is most concentrated. But when researchers examine the jets coming from the SMBH in Centaurus A, the closest radio galaxy to Earth, that's not what they see.

Since it's so close and so bright, Centaurus A is one of those natural laboratories for extreme physics that makes astrophysicists' eyes light up. They've been observing the jets in Centaurus A in detail for many years. Observations with the Event Horizon Telescope spanning a decade have revealed that its jets are brighter at their edges than in their centers, in a phenomenon called limb brightening. Why is that?

New research in Astronomy and Astrophysics has an explanation. It's titled "Probing anisotropic particle acceleration and limb brightening in Centaurus Aâs jet." The lead author is Felix Glaser, Master's student at the Chair of Astronomy at the University of WÃ¼rzburg in Germany.

"Relativistic jets are among the most fascinating phenomena in the universe, and recent high-resolution very long baseline interferometric (VLBI) observations, including the Global mm-VLBI Array and the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT), are able to resolve their structure close to their launching site," the authors write. The combined observations show the black holes with brighter limbs are not only found in Centaurus A, but in M 87 and 3C 84, too.

This image shows four different looks at the central region of M 87. The top image from the Hubble is in visible light. The other three are all in polarised light. The lines mark the orientation of polarisation, which is related to the magnetic field in the regions imaged. Though the researchers focused on Centaurus A, this image highlights how magnetic fields and polarity influence astrophysical jets. Image Credit: EHT Collaboration; ALMA (ESO/NAOJ/NRAO), Goddi et al.; NASA, ESA and the Hubble Heritage Team (STScI/AURA); VLBA (NRAO), Kravchenko et al.; J. C. Algaba, I. MartÃ­-Vidal

Each of these three galaxies are different from one another, making it difficult to understand the cause of their limb brightening. "Therefore, as a pilot study, we aimed to model the EHT observations of Cen A," the authors explain. It's the closest, so that makes sense.

This is a composite image of Centaurus A, with the individual images and their wavelenghts on the right. The image is from the Hubble (visible), Chandra (X-ray), Spitzer (infrared), and the Very Large Array (radio). Image Credit: NASA, CXC, SAO, Astrophotography by Rolf Olsen, NASA-JPL, Caltech, NRAO, AUI, NSF, UOH, M. Hardcastle

The researchers performed a magnetohydrodynamic simulation of an accreting supermassive black hole and how it launched it jets to observe the plasma dynamics involved. Since these jets are relativistic, the simulation included general relativistic effects. They also adjusted their simulation to match the properties of Centaurus A. "In order to match our model to the EHT observations, we adjust several free parameters..." the authors write, including black hole mass and the viewing angle.

The simulation successfully mimicked the recent observations of Centaurus A with the EHT.

"Our results demonstrate that the edge-brightening observed in Cen A can be naturally reproduced by an anisotropic particle distribution," the researchers write.

That means that the electrons emitted in the jets aren't distributed evenly over pitch angles. Pitch angles are the difference between the magnetic field and each electron's velocity. This is where synchrotron radiation enters the picture. Synchrotron radiation is when particles are forced to follow the curve of a magnetic field.

The emission of synchrotron radiation is strongly dependent on the pitch angle. So as a result, the observed brightness of the radiation changes depending on the viewing angle of the magnetic field the particles are forced to follow.

This figure from the research shows the synthetic polarized intensity images of our Cen A model at four representative frequencies: 86 GHz (panel A), 230 GHz (panel B), 680 GHz (panel C), and 3 THz (panel D). Each one zooms in closer and shows more detail in the model. Image Credit: Glaser et al. 2026.

âWhat is truly amazing is that microscopic plasma effects can shape structures on vastly larger scales,â said Dr. Christian Fromm, leader of the Computational Astrophysics Group. âFuture observations will reveal even more of these plasma signatures, making it increasingly important to include realistic plasma physics in our models already today and to further investigate the highly nonlinear effects of relativistic plasma.â

This figure shows how microscopic plasma effects can shape the large-scale structure of black hole jets. The hot accretion flow surrounding the supermassive black hole is shown in red, the relativistic jets in blue, and the magnetic field structure by gray helical field lines. Colored particles and arrows illustrate the motion of accelerated particles along the jet. Top right: The Event Horizon Telescope image of the inner jet of Centaurus A at a wavelength of 1.3 mm. Bottom right: The synthetic EHT observation generated from the new plasma-informed model. (Image Credit: Christian M. Fromm, Janssen et al. 2021 and Glaser et al. 2026)

âCen A is our closest window into the physics of relativistic jets,â said lead author Glaser. âThe fact that our plasma-informed model reproduces the observed edge brightening suggests that we are capturing an important piece of the underlying physics. These processes may not be unique to Cen A, but could be common in relativistic jets throughout the Universe.â

This study makes real progress in understanding the details of astrophysical jets, and how they exhibit things like limb brightening. It links the small scale of plasma physics with the jets and their characteristics. It's all because of a focused, multi-disciplinary effort.

âBy bringing together expertise in high-resolution observations, numerical simulations, and plasma physics, we are making progress toward understanding how black holes launch powerful jets and how these jets produce the radiation we observe. The new study is an excellent example of this approach,â said Fromm.

New telescopes are coming online that will take this work even further. The Square Kilometre Array will be the world's largest and highest-resolution radio telescope when it comes online in 2027. Updates to the Very Large Array will also drive progress when they're completed in 2031.

This work may affect more than our understanding of black hole jets. On a detailed plasma physics level, there are similarities between the jets and fusion. If we ever have a functioning fusion reactor, it will involve extremely powerful artificial magnets to generate powerful fields that confine the plasma.

This illustration shows some of the "D"-shaped toroidal field magnets in the ITER international nuclear fusion research and engineering project being built in France. Each magnet weighs 330 tons, and their job is to confine the plasma inside ITER's vacuum vessel. Lessons learned by studying plasma physics in black hole jets are applicable to fusion reactors. Image Credit: ITER Consortium.

âA black hole and a fusion reactor may sound like completely different worldsâbut both are governed by the physics of plasma,â says Professor Karl Mannheim, holder of the Chair of Astronomy at the University of WÃ¼rzburg. âAt Centaurus A, we can study plasma under conditions that cannot be created on Earth. These insights not only help us understand the Universe, but may also contribute to the development of future fusion energy.â

#6500. Scientists Discover Mysterious Toxic Chemicals Floating in the Air Above America

Scientists conducting atmospheric research in rural Oklahoma unexpectedly detected a toxic class of industrial chemicals never before measured in the air of the Western Hemisphere.

Toxic industrial chemicals used in everything from metalworking fluids to plastics have turned up in an unexpected place: the air above rural Oklahoma farmland.

Researchers detected medium-chain chlorinated paraffins (MCCPs) in the region while investigating an entirely different atmospheric process, marking the first reported detection of these pollutants in North American air.

The University of Colorado Boulder researchers identified the pollutants during a 2023 field campaign near Lamont, Oklahoma. Their findings, published in ACS Environmental Au, also reveal how atmospheric MCCP concentrations fluctuate with temperature.

Using a nitrate chemical ionization mass spectrometer, the team continuously monitored air at an agricultural site for nearly a month. While examining the chemical signatures in the measurements, CU Boulder chemistry PhD student Daniel Katz noticed unusual isotopic patterns that he eventually identified as MCCPs.

“It’s very exciting as a scientist to find something unexpected like this that we weren’t looking for,” said Katz, the study’s lead author. “We’re starting to learn more about this toxic, organic pollutant that we know is out there, and which we need to understand better.”

The instrument detected 18 groups of gaseous MCCPs. Their estimated average concentration was approximately 3.1 nanograms per cubic meter, although the researchers consider this a lower-bound estimate. Concentrations were substantially higher than those reported in remote polar regions, suggesting nearby sources may be contributing to the pollution.

The researchers also observed a consistent daily cycle: gaseous MCCP concentrations increased during warmer daylight hours and declined at night. Their analysis suggests that temperature controls how these chemicals move between the gas phase and airborne particles, potentially affecting how long they remain in the atmosphere and how far they travel.

MCCPs are widely used in metalworking fluids, PVC manufacturing, and textiles. They can enter wastewater and accumulate in sewage sludge, which is sometimes processed into biosolid fertilizer and spread on agricultural fields. Researchers suspect this practice could explain some of the pollution detected in Oklahoma, although they have not confirmed its source.

“When sewage sludges are spread across the fields, those toxic compounds could be released into the air,” Katz said. “We can’t show directly that that’s happening, but we think it’s a reasonable way that they could be winding up in the air. Sewage sludge fertilizers have been shown to release similar compounds.”

MCCPs are chemically related to short-chain chlorinated paraffins (SCCPs), which have faced restrictions because of their toxicity, environmental persistence, and potential to accumulate in living organisms. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency began regulating SCCPs in 2009, and the Stockholm Convention added them to its list of persistent organic pollutants in 2017.

Researchers suspect restrictions on SCCPs may have encouraged greater use of MCCPs as substitutes, potentially increasing their environmental presence.

“We always have these unintended consequences of regulation, where you regulate something, and then there’s still a need for the products that those were in,” said Ellie Browne, CU Boulder chemistry professor, CIRES Fellow, and study co-author. “So they get replaced by something.”

Although the team identified MCCPs in Oklahoma’s air, their exact source remains unknown. Wind measurements suggest several possible sources in the surrounding region, while the observed temperature fluctuations indicate that interactions with airborne particles influence their concentrations. The researchers also detected compounds consistent with products formed when MCCPs undergo atmospheric oxidation.

Further measurements across different seasons and locations could establish how widespread these chemicals are and clarify their atmospheric transport, chemical reactions, and environmental persistence.

“We identified them, but we still don’t know exactly what they do when they are in the atmosphere, and they need to be investigated further,” Katz said. “I think it’s important that we continue to have governmental agencies that are capable of evaluating the science and regulating these chemicals as necessary for public health and safety.”

Reference: “Real-Time Measurements of Gas-Phase Medium-Chain Chlorinated Paraffins Reveal Daily Changes in Gas-Particle Partitioning Controlled by Ambient Temperature” by Daniel John Katz, Bri Dobson, Mitchell Alton, Harald Stark, Douglas R. Worsnop, Manjula R. Canagaratna and Eleanor C. Browne, 16 July 2025, ACS Environmental Au. DOI: 10.1021/acsenvironau.5c00038

3.1 ng/m³ is a scientifically interesting detection (unexpected in the Western Hemisphere, possible biosolids link, temperature-dependent behavior) that contributes to understanding environmental baselines, but it is far below levels associated with health effects under current reference values. I am surprised that the article did not mention that the measured levels of MCCPs were thousands of times lower than the lowest level for health concerns.

Your link to municipal biosolids applications is a very long stretch and seems to be intended to sensationalize your article. This reduces the credibility of the article significantly.

A common antibiotic may be linked to a higher risk of miscarriage and stillbirth when used early in pregnancy, a new study suggests.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Taking doxycycline, a commonly prescribed antibiotic, during the first trimester of pregnancy may increase the risk of pregnancy loss, a new study suggests.

The antibiotic is broad-spectrum, meaning it targets a wide range of bacteria. It's often used to treat acne, respiratory infections and sexually transmitted infections, such as chlamydia and syphilis. Doctors generally avoid prescribing the drug during the second and third trimesters because it belongs to a class of antibiotics that can bind to calcium in developing bones. Animal studies suggest that this may disrupt fetal bone development.

However, evidence on doxycycline's safety during early pregnancy has been mixed and limited. The new study, published Tuesday (Nov. 10) in the journal Annals of Internal Medicine, provides clearer evidence of a link between doxycycline use in the first trimester and pregnancy loss.

"I would advise physicians to carefully consider the benefit-risk balance when prescribing doxycycline to women who are pregnant or planning a pregnancy," study first author Almut Winterstein, a pharmacist and drug-safety researcher at the University of Florida, told Live Science in an email.

Using information from two U.S. insurance databases, the researchers analyzed 224,870 pregnancies in people ages 12 to 55. More than 218,230 of these patients were treated for respiratory tract infections, and over 6,630 were treated for acne, between conception and the end of the first trimester. About 4,385 of the women filled a prescription for doxycycline during that time frame, while the others received an alternative antibiotic.

Among women with respiratory infections, those prescribed doxycycline had a 40% to 54% higher risk of pregnancy loss, compared with those prescribed amoxicillin, another broad-spectrum antibiotic in a different class. The exact level of risk varied between the two databases.

The researchers also compared the doxycycline users against women prescribed macrolides, the class of antibiotics that includes azithromycin (or "Z-Pak"). Again, the doxycycline users saw a higher risk — 39% and 36% higher, respectively.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Among the patients treated for acne, doxycycline users had a 49% higher risk of pregnancy loss in one database than those given the antibiotic clindamycin. In the second database, though, the difference wasn't statistically significant. Winterstein said that may be because there were fewer patients included in that analysis.

Overall, doxycycline was associated with seven to 11 additional pregnancy losses per 100 pregnancies, compared with the other antibiotic options assessed, the researchers reported.

The researchers examined the risk associated with taking various antibiotics in the first 12 weeks of pregnancy.

It is not yet clear how the drug might contribute to pregnancy loss. Because the study was observational, it cannot prove that the antibiotic itself caused those losses, which included miscarriages and stillbirths. (Miscarriage is pregnancy loss before 20 weeks of pregnancy, whereas stillbirth refers to pregnancy loss after the 20th week.)

Animal studies hint that doxycycline could interfere with early placental development, potentially making it harder for the placenta to support a growing pregnancy, Luke Grzeskowiak, an associate professor and clinical pharmacist at Flinders University in Australia who was not involved in the study, said in an email.

The study authors also noted in their report that the drug may have direct effects on the developing embryo. But these explanations remain hypothetical; the researchers have not established that either mechanism occurs in humans.

"Pregnancy loss affects around one in four pregnancies and can happen for many reasons," Grzeskowiak noted. Although doxycycline exposure may add to that risk, taking the antibiotic does not necessarily mean pregnancy loss will occur. The available data suggests that it is just one risk factor among many.

Because doxycycline may be prescribed before a pregnancy is recognized, doctors should consider the possibility of pregnancy when prescribing this drug to women of reproductive age, particularly those who are sexually active, Grzeskowiak suggested. That does not mean doctors should avoid prescribing the antibiotic to these women, he emphasized; rather, clinicians should consider pregnancy plans and medical history when choosing a treatment.

In some cases, doxycycline may still be the best option for a severe infection, Winterstein told Live Science, and that infection could itself put a pregnancy at risk. But for less-serious infections, safer alternatives may be available, she said.

#6497. Computer Simulations Provide the Best Explanation for Those "Little Red Dots" Yet!

When the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) made its famous observations of several deep fields in the cosmos, astronomers were surprised to see numerous galaxies that defied expectations. These galaxies were bright and red - earning them the nickname Little Red Dots (LRDs) - and far more abundant than cosmological models predicted. Scientists theorized that these were early quasars, galaxies with active galactic nuclei (AGNs) powered by the "seeds" that would grow to become supermassive black holes (SMBHs).

However, this also conflicted with cosmological models, as it seemed unlikely that many galaxies could have formed with massive black holes less than one billion years after the Big Bang. This led scientists to consider various theories, compact collections of stars, "dusty" galaxies, supermassive stars, and "black hole stars." While the more recent Direct Collapse Black Holes (DCBHs) theory offered the most compelling argument to date, new simulations by an international team of astronomers indicate that they may be the remnants of collapsed supermassive primordial stars.

The study was led by Dr. Daniel Whalen from the University of Portsmouth's Institute of Cosmology and Gravitation. His colleagues included researchers from United Arab Emirates University, the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, the Institute for Astronomy and Royal Observatory at the University of Edinburgh, and the Harvard & Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics (CfA). The paper detailing their findings was published in the The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

The little red dots could represent galaxies in an evolutionary phase predating the luminous quasar phase. Credit: NASA/ESA/CSA/ISTA)/ETH Zurich/NAOJ

Previous attempts to explain the rapid formation, abundance, and spectral characteristics of LRDs all suffered from the same issue. While each explained some characteristics, none could account for everything the JWST revealed in its deep field surveys. Then came the DCBHs theory, which argues that SMBH seeds formed directly from massive clouds of cold gas. While this theory did fit Webb's observations nicely, it still faces numerous theoretical and environmental challenges.

For starters, the core premise of the DCBH theory is that a massive cloud of cold gas could collapse under its own gravity. However, gas tends to fragment into smaller clouds as it cools, leading to a cluster of primordial (Population III) stars instead of a black hole seed. To prevent fragmentation, the gas cloud must remain hot, requiring a very specific amount of Lyman-Werner (LW) radiation from a synchronized star-forming galaxy in its vicinity to destroy the main coolant - i.e., molecular hydrogen (Hâ).

This raises additional problems, including the self-shielding nature of molecular hydrogen. As a gas cloud becomes increasingly dense, its outer layers absorb the LW radiation, shielding the inner core. This means that the critical amount of radiation required to suppress cooling across the entire cloud would be much higher. Even if the SMBH seed did manage to form, the radiative pressure it would emit (plus mechanical feedback from the disk and jets) would slow the accretion rate, significantly slowing further growth.

Whalen and his team found another explanation borne out by advanced cosmological simulations. As he said in a University of Portsmouth press release:

LRDs have been one of the most surprising discoveries made by the James Webb Space Telescope. They are compact, only a few hundred light-years across, but are as bright as much larger galaxies, and their unusual V-shaped spectra have defied the usual astrophysical explanations. Their lack of detectable X-ray and radio emissions has left astronomers struggling to explain what they are.

Artist's impression of a galaxy forming stars within powerful outflows of material blasted out from supermassive black holes at its core. Credit: ESO/M. Kornmesser

Based on their simulations, the team produced a model showing that LRDs are most likely galaxies with AGN powered by massive black holes that formed through the collapse of supermassive primordial stars. What's more, their model suggests that the black holes are largely concealed by dense, massive discs of the gas that created them. These gaseous envelopes trap high-energy X-rays while allowing some visible, ultraviolet, and infrared light to escape, which fits with the unusual light signatures detected by the JWST.

The simulations also explain another long-standing mystery about LRDs: that a large cluster of stars in the disks of these small galaxies produces the blue part of the spectrum Webb observed. These disks, according to the models, contain around 100 million stars densely packed into regions measuring only 500 light-years in diameter, matching what astronomers observed in LRDs. Based on the available data, the team further concludes the black holes at the center of these primordial galaxies are only about 10 million Solar masses.

This is a few orders of magnitude less than previous estimates, which indicated a maximum of 100 million Solar masses. While this research is unlikely to be the final word on the nature of LRDs, it offers what is (to date) the most fitting explanation that matches the observations. "What makes this discovery so exciting is that we may be witnessing the birth of the first supermassive black holes," said Whalen. "For decades, simulations have predicted that these objects should exist, and now the James Webb Space Telescope may finally be allowing us to see them."

Further Reading: University of Portsmouth, The Astrophysical Journal Letters

#6496. The 4 Best Laser Printers For Your Home and Small Office

If you print a lot of professional-grade documents, a laser printer is a worthy investment.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Laser printers, known for printing crisp, professional-looking documents quickly, are generally considered big, expensive machines designed for large offices. While some larger models live up to that reputation, plenty of compact options fit into your home office if you print files often.

While more expensive than an inkjet printer, most laser printers are a better long-term investment, with lower operating costs and designs built for heavy-duty printing. That said, choosing the right one at a glance can be tricky, and may vary based on your needs.

Printers aren’t the most exciting tech products, and many folks see them as frustrating, unreliable machines that require constant repair or replacement and are increasingly unnecessary for the average person in the digital age. While that may be true for some, they remain essential for workers who need to print contracts or create physical records, and students who need hard copies of their homework. With a little research, you can find a good laser printer that makes life easier and lasts a long time.

The recommended printers are based on my personal experience and knowledge of printers, as well as research from reputable publications, including PCMag and The Wirecutter. I looked for printers with performance and features that suit both home and small office users, with price and value in mind. I also spent months testing the best overall pick and using it as my everyday printer to ensure it’s a worthy recommendation.

I have been reviewing tech products for 25 years, including computing peripherals such as inkjet and laser printers. As an editor at Computer Shopper magazine, I helped develop the printer testing methodology used in the reviews. I then brought that expertise to publications such as Digital Trends and Business Insider, applying real-world usage that resonates with shoppers in the evaluation.

There’s no perfect laser printer, but if you’re looking for a reliable, easy-to-use unit that produces high-quality prints, the HP LaserJet Pro MFP 3101sdw fits the bill. I’ve been using this printer for several months and found that it’s an ideal fit for my home office. It also has plenty of advanced features that would make it a good fit for a small business.

With a 35ppm print speed, the 3101sdw is fast for its intended audience. When connected to a typical home Wi-Fi network, it takes about 5 seconds from pressing print to outputting the first page. Printed text looks good even at lower-quality settings, with small fonts staying sharp and legible. I found the scan quality more than adequate for everyday use, but 300 dpi is too low for designers, photographers, and other creative users. It also runs quiet, which is always a nice bonus.

Anybody who needs to make copies will find the ADF-equipped scanner handy, while the 2.7-inch touchscreen makes setup easy. It took me less than 10 minutes to get it up and running. Whether you connect via USB, Ethernet, or Wi-Fi, the printer responds quickly. It also has a USB port for quick prints or saving scans to a flash drive.

While the 3101sdw is small enough to fit on a large desk, it’s more practical to put it on its own stand. I wouldn’t call it “lightweight,” but I could carry it down five floors without much effort. It won’t win any design awards, either, which is too bad because HP generally knows how to make great-looking products.

The paper tray has an average 250-page capacity, but a notable drawback is that it has no manual feed tray. I didn’t find this an issue, but if you need to, say, print on envelopes, it could be problematic because you'd have to switch out the paper in the main tray. Another expert reviewer dinged the 3101sdw for lacking a fax function, but my workaround is to use the HP Smart companion app to scan and send (but not receive) faxes.

The 3101sdw offers stronger print quality, a better build, and ease of use. It’s hard to say how long mechanical devices like this will last, but HP’s printers are known for their reliability—I have a LaserJet from the 1990s that’s still going strong.

In my experience, Brother makes affordable laser printers that consistently deliver solid performance and text quality. At 36ppm and under $200, the HL-L2460DW is a strong basic option for a home or small office. Despite its barebones design, it has useful features like double-sided printing, Ethernet connectivity, wireless printing, a generous 250-page paper capacity, and a mobile app. Plus, it’s lightweight and doesn’t take up too much space.

The HL-L2460DW supports a 1,200-page standard-yield toner cartridge or 3,000-page high-yield toner cartridge, but comes with a starter cartridge that only yields 700 pages out of the box. (This is typical of printer manufacturers.) If you plan to print a lot, I’d recommend buying a high-yield cartridge right when you buy the printer.

This is a “budget” option, though, so this printer comes with a few caveats. I don’t love the small LCD display, which has a basic interface that doesn’t display much info and doesn’t feel as well-made. The basic operation means there’s no scanning, copying, faxing, ADF, or other multi-function capabilities. Plus, black-and-white graphics and images don’t look as good as text. User reviews have also complained about its reliability. Still, given its balance of price, speed, and print quality, the HL-L2460DW is a good value regardless of budget.

If it’s for personal use and you only plan to use it every so often, I’d steer you toward a different model, the HL-L2420DW, which has a 30ppm speed and every aforementioned feature except Ethernet. It’s perfect for casual printing, and it costs $50 less.

Most offices shy away from color laser printers because they are expensive to buy and maintain, and employees often use them to make wasteful prints. Likewise, at home, you’re probably better off going with a color inkjet printer. That said, if you truly need color prints, I love the HP Color LaserJet Pro MFP 3301fdw, which delivers excellent print quality and attractive features like glossy paper support. It’s a strong, if pricey, complement to any office.

Despite its compact footprint, the 3301fdw has a 50-page duplexing ADF and a 250-page paper tray. It’s not the fastest color laser printer, but its 26ppm speed is more than adequate for home or small business use.

Print quality is where HP’s laser printers excel. You can expect documents with crisp text and well-saturated, natural-looking color graphics and photos. Unlike most laser printers, the 3301fdw is compatible with select HP glossy paper, so you can make photo prints. They don’t really compare to inkjet photo printers, but it’s fine in most cases.

Like our overall pick, the 3301fdw is a breeze to set up via its 4.3-inch color touchscreen. For connectivity, it supports USB, Ethernet, and Wi-Fi, which covers most home and office networks.

You may have guessed the printer’s big con is that it’s pricey to operate. Whether you’re using the standard or high-yield toner options, the cost per page is high. If you’re looking to spend a little less, I’d look at the Brother MFC-L3380CDW, which has a comparable feature set to the 3301fdw and a lower operating cost. You’re compromising a bit on print quality and performance, though, which is why the HP leads the pack.

A true small-business laser printer needs to be a workhorse. It should offer a robust, office-centric range of features, print fast, support multiple users, hold enough paper, and have a high duty cycle. Experts agree that Brother makes some of the best laser printers for offices, and the monochrome MFC-L2900DW multi-function model is a particularly good option.

Imagine the L2900DW as an enhanced version of the HL-L2460DW. It shares a similar design, small footprint, and print engine, but features a high-capacity 50-page ADF for copying or scanning multi-page documents. The L2900DW also has a single-page duplexing scanner for two-sided pages. There’s even a fax function.

A large 3.5-inch touchscreen makes setup and on-device operation easy without a computer, while USB, Wi-Fi, and Ethernet give you options for connecting. Combined with a fast 36ppm speed, sharp text print quality, low operating cost, and the option to use high-yield cartridges, you’ve got a very capable all-in-one laser printer.

Graphics don’t look as sharp as text, but that shouldn’t matter if your office prints mainly documents. While its 250-page paper tray is adequate for a small business, expect to reload often if multiple users print often. This model offers no option for a larger or expandable paper tray.

The ADF has a scanner resolution of just 600 dpi, but that is plenty for text documents; the flatbed scanner has 1,200 dpi, which is fine for color images. The output tray’s 100-page capacity is low for heavy usage. One missing feature is a front USB port, which is handy for printing or faxing documents from a flash drive or saving scans to one.

If you need to support a large number of workers, consider stepping up to Brother’s MFC-L5915DW. It has a 70-page ADF and a 5-inch LCD, and you can expand its paper capacity beyond the standard 250 pages. With a faster 50ppm speed, support for 18,000-page high-yield cartridges, and a higher duty cycle, it’s an ideal choice for busy offices. It’s a big jump in price, which is why I went with the L2900DW, but it may cost less to operate in the long run.

Whether for the office or your home, a laser printer is a good option if you often print many multi-page documents. If you need a home printer for occasional printing, a more affordable inkjet printer may make more sense. Again, a laser printer costs more up front but pays dividends in the long run as a professional tool or a home tech staple. If you’re on the fence about what to buy, here are the things I look at when I evaluate laser printers:

Most prints from a laser printer are black-and-white text documents, and most models deliver decent print quality. If you need to print impactful pages with photos and charts, a color laser printer can print higher-quality graphics. Even the best monochrome printers we’ve tested and researched can’t match the detail and clarity of color ink toner. For example, if you have a multi-colored pie chart, a monochrome reproduction can only do so much to separate the different color shading.

Keep in mind, though, that even the cheapest color laser printer will be expensive, and its print quality may not rival that of higher-end models. They also do not support specialty media like glossy photo paper.

A basic laser printer’s sole function is to print documents, and that’s enough for most people. It’s generally compact and fits on a desk. But if you run a small business or work remotely in a home office, you may want a multi-function, “all-in-one” printer that scans and copies, too, among other tasks. Multi-function printers are far more useful, but they’re larger and cost more due to the extra hardware inside.

“Yield” refers to the estimated number of pages you can get out of a single toner cartridge. Most laser printers should get around 1,500 pages from a toner cartridge, while high-yield cartridges should last 3,000 pages or more.

Toner cartridges are expensive, especially for color printers, but they offer a better cost per page than ink. My rule of thumb is that high-yield toners will save you money in the long run.

Similarly, a laser printer’s “duty cycle” rating refers to the maximum number of prints per month that the manufacturer recommends to keep it in proper working order. Basic laser printers have a duty cycle of around 5,000 pages or less, while heavy-duty models have ratings of 10,000 or higher. Printing beyond the rated duty cycle can lead to breakdowns, more maintenance, or a shorter lifespan.

For personal use or small businesses that print occasionally, 25 to 30 pages per minute (ppm) should be fine. Small offices with a few employees that print often may want a faster printer with a speed of 35 to 40 ppm. In a larger office, I’d look for at least 40 ppm, if not more. Keep in mind that manufacturers measure speeds under ideal conditions, and real-world results may not always match. Expect a small discrepancy of a few pages.

Most printers rely primarily on a USB cable to connect to your computer, but a hard-wired connection alone isn’t practical in today’s world of wireless laptops, phones, and tablets. I recommend choosing a printer with a wireless connection compatible with your most-used devices, such as Wi-Fi or Apple AirPrint. Some laser printers also support Ethernet for a high-speed hard-wired connection. Office-focused machines may include a front USB port so you can plug in a flash drive with the files you need to print.

Most laser printers have a paper tray that holds 250 pages, which is enough for personal and small business use. Some compact printers may have a smaller capacity–around 150 pages. If you expect to print a lot, consider a model with a higher-capacity tray or support for multiple trays, and look for an output tray large enough to hold everything you print out. All printers also have a multi-purpose tray for manually feeding non-standard paper like envelopes.

In addition to the essentials, there are some features that I look for which are nice to have, but won’t make or break a printer:

Depending on the model, it can be basic or advanced. Depending on your use case, you may consider some or all of these essential. That said, they aren't universal, and some printers work well without them.

Laser printers use toner, a powder heated onto paper, while inkjet printers spray ink droplets. Laser printers are considered superior for their speed and print quality, but they are expensive to purchase and maintain. Inkjet printers offer color printing and affordability, but prints need time to dry, and the cost per page can be higher with heavy use.

However, the best modern inkjet printers today are fast and deliver great-looking prints, especially photos. They also support different paper types and sizes. Laser printers can also print in color, but they're pricey. Beyond speed, their advantages include consistent print quality and long-term reliability.

Which technology is better ultimately depends on your needs. Most people will find an inkjet printer sufficient and more versatile, but those who print often may find a laser printer more economical in the long run. In an ideal setup, consider an affordable laser printer for frequent print jobs and a good inkjet printer for color documents and photos.

Color laser printers can print photos and graphics on standard paper, but if you want to print on photo paper, an inkjet is the better choice, especially one that supports multi-color ink tanks. Laser printers aren’t designed for photo-quality reproduction, and generally don’t work with specialty paper. (As we discussed, some HP models are compatible with select glossy paper.)

Depending on usage and maintenance, a laser printer can last for many years. It’s a mechanical device, though, so there’s no guarantee that it won’t break down and require service. Here are a few tips to keep your printer running as efficiently as possible and maximize its lifespan:

#6495. Scientists Discover 15,000-Year-Old Clay Figures That Rewrite the History of Human Art

Clay figurines from the Middle East suggest that artistic traditions were already being shared across generations before farming, possibly with children taking part in their creation.

Long before agriculture transformed life in the Middle East, people were already shaping clay into figures that reflected the world around them. Some resembled birds, mammals, and humans, while others carried traces of red or orange coloring. One fragment may even depict the facial markings of a mountain gazelle.

These small artifacts, originally excavated from three sites in present-day Israel, date back roughly 15,000 to 11,500 years. Researchers believe they provide the earliest known evidence of a clay figurine-making tradition in the region, suggesting that people were using the material for symbolic expression much earlier than previously thought.

At the time, the region was home to Natufian communities, hunter-gatherers who had begun living in permanent settlements before the development of agriculture. Archaeologists already knew that Natufian people made figurines, although most previously discovered examples were fashioned from bone or stone.

Clay figurines, by contrast, were generally believed to have become common during the Neolithic period, when the agricultural revolution began around 11,500 years ago. The newly identified objects suggest that the practice had much deeper roots, revealing a wider range of artistic expression among these early communities.

The findings also raise questions about how cultural traditions developed before farming. The researchers suggest that Natufian artistic practices were more varied and complex than previously recognized, and that some aspects of the region’s later Neolithic culture may have originated thousands of years earlier.

The research, published November 11, 2026, in the open-access journal PLOS One, was conducted by Dr. Laurent Davin of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem in Israel and colleagues. Beyond revealing an earlier history of clay figurines, the study offers clues about how creative practices and cultural knowledge may have passed between generations.

“These discoveries change how we understand the beginnings of artistic expression in the first villages of humanity. Thousands of years before agriculture and pottery emerged, people were already using clay to create figures, as part of their beliefs and knowledge of the natural world. What is particularly fascinating is the evidence that children were involved in making these objects, suggesting that creativity and cultural knowledge were shared across generations,” said Davin.

Reference: “Modelling symbols among the first-sedentary communities: Emergence of clay figurines in Epipaleolithic Southwest Asia” by Laurent Davin, Marion Sindel, Mina Weinstein-Evron, Reuven Yeshurun, Daniel Kaufman, Leore Grosman, Anna Belfer-Cohen, Hamoudi Khalaily and François R. Valla, 11 November 2026, PLOS ONE. DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0360388

This research was supported by the Israel Academy of Sciences and Humanities, Council for Higher Education, Computational Archaeology Laboratory at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Fondation des Treilles, Fondation Fyssen, Irene Levi Sala Care Archaeological Foundation, Israel Science Foundation (grants 511/22 and 703/23), French Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs, Wenner–Gren Foundation, Centre de Recherche Français à Jérusalem, and National Geographic Foundation.

Scientists on China's Tiangong space station used a laser trap to cool a clump of atoms to just above absolute zero, setting a new record.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have cooled atoms to the coldest temperature ever recorded, using a laser trap aboard China's Tiangong space station.

Tiangong included an experiment in which atoms were cooled to 10 picokelvins, which is barely above absolute zero, the coldest theoretical temperature possible in physics. Absolute zero is minus 459.67 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 273.15 degrees Celsius) and the threshold at which all particles in an object are believed to stop moving.

Scientists hit the mark using "optical tweezers," known more formally as an optical-dipole trap (ODT), which hold atoms in a laser beam," the scientists reported Nov. 5 in the journal Science.

The team placed 20,000 rubidium atoms in the trap in order to restrict their motion. This reduced motion, along with the weightlessness induced by the low-gravity environment aboard the space station, caused the cloud of atoms to cool to much lower temperatures than are possible on Earth.

The experiment's results could help improve future space-based research, the team said.

"This record-low temperature could stimulate a new generation of ODT-based experiments in quantum simulation and precision measurements in space," the researchers wrote in the paper.

Despite this achievement, it's doubtful that scientists could ever hit absolute zero. One interpretation of the third law of thermodynamics, which looks at how systems behave when they approach absolute zero, is that the particles would always have a bit of entropy (disorder) associated with them, making absolute zero unachievable.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"One version of the third law states that it would require an infinite number of steps to reach absolute zero, which means you will never get there," Saibal Mitra, a professor of physics at Missouri State University, told Live Science in a 2024 interview.

The second law of thermodynamics, which states that entropy always increases, would also be violated if scientists could reach absolute zero, he added. "If you had a heat sink at absolute zero, then you could build a machine that was 100% efficient," Mitra said.

That said, space makes it easier to get close to absolute zero because microgravity allows atoms to "float" and become more efficient at cooling, Science News reported. The researchers took their weightless collection of atoms and created a quantum state of matter known as a Bose-Einstein condensate, in which very cold atoms clump and create a "fifth state" of matter as they behave akin to a single atom.

Tiangong's very cold clump follows similar experiments on the International Space Station that reached 52 picokelvins and from a weightless fall induced by a drop from a tall tower, in which atoms hit 38 picokelvins, Science News added.

#6493. Microscopic Space Dust Reveals A Hidden Reservoir Of "Heavy Water" Beyond Neptune

Astronomers can find valuable information in even the tiniest objects. That was certainly the case recently when twelve dust grains collected by a high-altitude aircraft helped solve a mystery about the birth of our Solar System. Or at least that is the argument in a new paper published in Science Advances by researchers at NASAâs Johnson Space Center and UCLA. According to the paper, the region beyond Neptune once had a massive isolated reservoir of âheavy waterâ that never mixed in with the inner planets.

In this context âheavy waterâ doesnât mean the type formed with deuterium, like the kind used in nuclear reactors. Instead, it refers to a heavier version of the other element in good old H2O - oxygen. Most of the universeâs oxygen atoms are an isotope called oxygen-16, with eight protons and eight neutrons. However, a small percentage weighs in a bit heavier - oxygen-17 and oxygen-18, which carry an extra neutron or two, respectively.

In 2011, NASAâs Genesis mission caught particles in the solar wind that showed the Sun housed an overwhelming amount of regular oxygen-16. However, Earth, Mars, and the asteroid belt seemed to have much more of the heavier oxygen isotopes. Which meant thereâs a mismatch between what we see inside the Sun and what the planets were formed out of. Scientists have been attempting to explain why for years.

Fraser explains the important of cosmic dust to life on Earth.

The most common explanation of why is known as carbon monoxide self-shielding. Around 4.5 billion years ago, when our Solar System hadnât fully formed yet, ultraviolet light from the Sun blew apart carbon monoxide molecules at the outer edges of the protoplanetary disk of gas and dust. Because oxygen-16 was the most prominent in the disk, the carbon monoxide particles that were made out of it would absorb much of the UV light that was directed at the disk, breaking the ones that were closest the light source (i.e. the Sun) apart. They eventually reformed with hydrogen to make âregularâ water.

However, that left other wavelengths of UV free to travel into the farther reaches of the protoplanetary disk. And some of those wavelengths were particularly good at breaking apart carbon monoxide molecules that had formed with oxygen-17 and oxygen-18. So, in the outer disk, those heavier isotopes made up a higher percentage of the free-floating ions that eventually bonded to hydrogen, in their case creating âheavyâ water.

That makes sense from a theoretical standpoint at least, but proving this âheavy waterâ reservoir exists has been tricky. Almost all the meteorites we have found were formed in the main asteroid belt - not far enough out to capture particles of the reservoir. Some cometary sample missions, such as Rosetta and Stardust, have tried to capture water samples from these ambassadors of the outer solar system, but their method of capture resulted in the water-bearing materials melting, leaving no trace of their isotopic configuration.

Enter the new paper. Lead author Lindsay Keller and his team turned to interplanetary dust particles (IDPs). These microscopic grains are formed when comets and other icy bodies out in the Kuiper belt, the area past Neptune, collide and break apart. Some of the grains that result from those collisions are pulled inward by the Sunâs gravity, eventually intersecting the orbits of the inner planets - including Earth.

During their journey, they are subjected to extreme amounts of high energy particles from solar flares, which leaves microscopic scars on them called solar energetic particle tracks. Previous studies had proven that one way to prove a piece of dust had traveled from the Kuiper Belt is that have around a hundred times more energetic particle tracks, due to their much longer time in interplanetary space, than particles from asteroids do. In other words, if you can count the radiation tracks, you can prove whether a grain of dust came from beyond Neptune or not.

That is exactly what they proved with twelve dust grains collected during NASAâs Cosmic Dust program - an ongoing airborne sampling program running out of Johnson Space Center since 1981. Shockingly, the collected particles still had lots of clays, like saponite, which are made with water, as well as iron-nickel sulfides and around four times as much carbon as would be expected for a primitive meteorite. The minerals proved that liquid water once flowed inside its parent Kuiper Belt object, either heated by radioactive decay or the kinetic energy of another impact.

Using a specialized microscope, the researchers measured the exact oxygen isotope ratios in the clays in the samples. They then worked back through chemical modeling to determine the original recipe for the water on the parent rock that formed the grains. They found that the primordial Kuiper Belt objects these grains came from were extraordinarily enriched with oxygen-17 and oxygen-18 - definitively proving that the reservoir of heavy water does exist out beyond Neptune.

Fraser talks about how there was liquid water on the asteroid Ryugu.

As a consequence, they also, tangentially, provided a significant bump to the carbon monoxide self-shielding theory. And also noted the similarities to a specific unusual meteorite known as Acfer 094, which they hint might actually be a meteor from the Kuiper Belt itself. But there was one final mystery the paper needed to resolve - if there was all this heavy water out in the outer solar system, why didnât it migrate in when the planets were forming?

The authors offer a simple explanation - Saturn. As Saturn grew in the early solar system, its gravity created a high-pressure ridge in the protoplanetary disk, acting as an invisible barrier to keep lightweight material from being pulled too far in towards the Sun. So, thanks to around a dozen specks of dust, we now have a more clearly defined picture of what our solar system looked like in the very early days of its formation - and it seems we can thank our giant ringed neighbor for some of how Earth ended up with its current isotopic balance.

#6491. Tiny Grains of Sand Could Reveal What the Weather Was Like on Mars Billions of Years Ago

Scientists have discovered a surprising connection between sand grain size and the winds that shape dunes on Earth and Mars.

The size of a sand grain could reveal how fast the wind was blowing when a desert dune formed, even billions of years ago. Stanford University researchers have discovered that dunes on Earth and Mars are primarily shaped by winds traveling just above the minimum speed needed to move sand. Their findings offer a way to reconstruct ancient winds using sediment preserved in planetary landscapes.

Windblown dunes and ripples have been identified on Venus, Mars, Saturn’s moon Titan, and even a comet orbiting the sun. Their shapes and patterns provide evidence of prevailing wind directions and how consistently winds have blown, but determining wind speeds has been much more difficult.

In a study published November 16 in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, researchers demonstrated that the wind speeds responsible for most dune formation are closely linked to the median size of the sand grains. Stronger winds can transport larger particles, while finer grains generally require less force to move.

The relationship depends on a critical threshold: the wind must be strong enough to set sand grains in motion along the ground. Although faster winds can transport more sediment, the researchers found that winds only modestly exceeding this threshold account for much of the sand movement that builds dunes.

The research builds on a hypothesis proposed by University of Pennsylvania scientists in 2010, suggesting that dunes develop mainly under winds slightly stronger than those needed to initiate sand transport. “Since then, nobody’s really looked at this idea, even though it’s really powerful because it tells you something about the environmental conditions that formed the dune fields that we see on not just Earth and Mars, but on a variety of other planetary bodies,” said lead author Colin Marvin, who conducted the research as a PhD student at Stanford.

To test the idea, the team examined 30 years of wind observations alongside sand grain measurements from 24 dune fields worldwide. The sites encompassed different dune shapes, sizes, and environments, including Coral Pink Sand Dunes State Park in Utah and the ancient desert landscapes of Namibia.

For each location, the researchers calculated which wind speed transported the greatest amount of sand over time. Across all 24 fields, that speed was closely associated with grain size and remained only slightly above the threshold required to move the sediment.

The team next examined measurements from a Martian dune field, where the relationship between sand size and the winds responsible for dune formation was similar to that observed on Earth. This held despite major differences in atmospheric pressure, gravity, and sediment density between the two planets.

The results suggest that the same basic process may govern dune formation on other worlds, provided loose sediment is abundant and stronger winds become progressively less frequent. Marvin described dunes as a “great recorder of what happens on a planet’s surface, and particularly the interactions between what’s happening in the atmosphere of a planet and what’s happening on the surface.”

Because sand grains can survive long after the winds that transported them have disappeared, the relationship could help scientists estimate ancient wind speeds from sedimentary rocks. It may also provide a way to test models of atmospheric circulation during periods when Earth’s atmosphere differed substantially from its present state.

The discovery could help researchers “better reconstruct winds and climates through time, on Earth and beyond,” said senior author Mathieu Lapôtre, associate professor of Earth and planetary sciences at the Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability. “It works for modern dunes and for sandstones dating back three billion years.”

Such reconstructions could be used to investigate the atmospheric histories of both Earth and Mars. According to Lapôtre, the research is already moving in that direction. “Colin is actively working on that, actually. He’s already pushing on to the next steps.”

The study was supported by a National Science Foundation CAREER grant.
