#6489. Fermi’s 14-Year All-Sky Map Bridges Astronomy’s Elusive "MeV Gap"

Gamma rays, the most high-energy type of electromagnetic radiation in the universe, have always had a blind spot. Weâve always had trouble measuring them in the âmega-electron voltâ (MeV) energy range, which astronomers have taken to calling the âMeV gapâ. But a new paper from an international group of scientists working with the Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT) Collaboration recently published a paper in The Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series that takes a stab at closing that gap by identifying 450 cosmic sources in the 20-200 MeV range, providing the clearest view of low-energy gamma rays ever.

The âgapâ comes from a technological blind spot. Scientists have plenty of tools in the lower energy spectra, such as the Chandra X-ray observatory, that can capture radiation at the x-ray end of the electromagnetic spectrum. They also have a great number of tools at the high end of gamma ray spectroscopy, including the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope, which is capable of finding higher end ones.

But why are low energy gamma rays so hard to catch? Gamma rays notoriously pass right through mirrors and every other attempt to reflect them. Telescopes like Fermi-LAT can be thought of more as particle detectors in orbit rather than traditional telescopes. They track what happens when a gamma-ray photon hits layers of tungsten and silicon inside their chassis.

At high energies - around 1 giga-electron volt (GeV), the damage done to those layers is catastrophic enough to be able to trace a line back to a source. However, at the lower 20-200 MeV range, the photons scatter much more randomly, making it difficult to track where precisely they came from. Fermi-LAT is only capable of tracking a single 20 MeV photon to a patch of the sky about 20 degrees wide - more than forty times the size of the full moon. Combine that with a massive amount of background radiation caused by everything from the Sun to distant galaxies, and it can be a real pain to pick out the direction of any one particular source.

However, Fermi-LAT has been operating now for almost two decades, and with that much data thereâs some math that can help. The researchers combined 14 years worth of collected data with some advanced statistical modeling techniques to pinpoint 450 distinct gamma-ray sources, what they are calling the Second Catalog of Low-Energy Fermi-LAT Sources, or 2FLE. Cross-checking them with other radio, optical, and X-ray data showed known counterparts for 377 of those objects.

The vast majority of those objects - 325 of them - are far outside the Milky Way. Almost half of the entire group of objects consist of flat-spectrum radio quasars (FSRQs), a very extreme type of active galactic nuclei. FSRQs represent a type of âblazarâ - a supermassive black hole that is pointing one of its twin jets of plasma directly at Earth. The 2FLE catalog confirms that FSRQ blazars pump out the majority of their energy at this 20-200 MeV spectral window.

Fraser and Pamela discuss the differnet "colors" of gamma rays.

Closer to home, the catalogue includes 52 sources from inside the Milky Way. Most of them are pulsars - the spinning leftovers left behind when a supermassive star explodes into a supernova. But one intriguing outlier was gamma rays that appear to be coming from M2, a globular cluster, which would mark the first time itâs ever been observed at gamma-ray energies.

Perhaps the most intriguing part of the paper, though, are the 73 sources that donât have a clear counterpart at other energies. 60 of those appear to be brand new gamma-ray discoveries. And while some of those signals might turn out to be overlapping signals from neighboring objects, it's likely there are at least some truly new exotic cosmic accelerators in the dataset awaiting follow-up observations. One particular mystery source seems to align with an object called 2FLE J0340.8+5258, which seems to also have been detected by an observatory in China, and appears to be capable of generating light across nine orders of magnitude in energy.

Fermi-LAT itself seems to have reached its limit with this new data set. The researchers have likely squeezed everything they could out of the decades of data of this satellite, which was originally launched in 2008. However, there are other gamma-ray missions coming online, including NASAâs Compton Spectrometer and Imager (COSI), which is designed specifically to look for gamma rays in the 0.2-5 MeV range using a special type of germanium detector that has only become available in the last few years. Combining that new data with the decades worth of Fermi might finally shed some light on one of the longest-standing blind spots in the extreme physics of the universe.

Over 300 Live Science readers responded to a recent poll about whether they'd train themselves to lucid dream if they could.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Lucid dreaming describes when you realize you're in a dream as it's unfolding. Sometimes, people can control the content of their dreams from this state of awareness.

Recently, researchers claimed that they found a way to "train" people to lucid dream by having them meditate and complete virtual-reality-augmented exercises while they were awake. Following the release of that study, Live Science asked its readers whether they would learn to lucid dream if they could.

Over 300 readers weighed in, with 77% saying "Yes, I'd want to try to control my dreams." Additionally, 17% of respondents said "No, I already lucid dream enough without training," 3% said "No, I don't see the point," and the final 3% said they weren't sure.

In the comments, one reader shared that they'd once experimented with hypnagogic napping, a technique famously used by Thomas Edison and Salvador Dalí in which the famous luminaries would wake themselves up just as they were drifting to sleep. Edison claimed that this helped him access a creative sweet spot at the edge of sleep and wakefulness.

"When I was experimenting with the hypnagogic state (using the Edison method) I started having spontaneous lucid dreams," the reader wrote. "I can confidently say, that there were some of the most profound experiences of my life, so the answer is definitely yes."

Another reader reported having lucid dreams "about once or twice a year," adding that they typically wake up shortly after realizing it's a dream. "My most recent one was of my recently deceased wife. I became very sad when I realized she wasn't supposed to be there," the reader wrote. "I hugged her and told her I don't want to be without her. She replied that I could live a long life if I took care of myself (This was a very typical response from her...lol). I feel very blessed to have had that dream."

Other readers chimed in on Facebook. "Already have it [lucid dreaming], but if I didn't I would certainly practice to do so," one wrote. "Hell yes," another said, in response to the idea of training themselves to lucid dream.

Other readers noted that they already lucid dream quite often or that they can consistently control their dreams, with one even saying that all of their dreams are lucid. Another said, "Some nights I interrupt it [my dream] like Monty Python — 'Too silly!' and start over."

But while one person compared lucid dreaming to "writing and directing your own movie," another noted that "lucid dreams can be boring, repetitive, annoying." So while many people would practice lucid dreaming if they could, not everyone sees the appeal.

#6487. What Is a Thought Made Of? Scientists Reveal Why Human Consciousness May Be Beyond the Reach of AI

A familiar song can pull you back decades in an instant, and the chemistry behind that rush of memory may hold clues to what separates human minds from AI.

How does the brain turn a collection of memories into thoughts, emotions, and the experience of being conscious? Scientists have spent decades studying how neurons communicate through electrical and chemical signals, yet the physical processes that allow us to recall experiences, attach feelings to them, and give them meaning remain incompletely understood.

A new scientific review suggests that part of the answer may lie in the complex chemistry surrounding brain cells. Rather than viewing memory primarily as a product of neuronal activity, the researchers propose that interactions among neurons, supporting brain cells, and molecules in their surrounding environment could play a fundamental role in shaping thought and conscious experience.

Dr. Gerard Marx of MX Biotech Ltd. and Prof. Chaim Gilon of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem’s Department of Chemistry present their theory in Consciousness, Memory, and Intelligence: A Mechanistic Perspective. Building on earlier research into how experiences might be physically stored in the brain, they examine whether the chemistry of memory could help explain the origins of thought and consciousness.

Their proposal also raises a question about artificial intelligence: If human memory and emotion depend on the chemistry of living cells, can computers ever develop consciousness simply by becoming more powerful?

Scientists have long studied how neurons communicate to form and retrieve memories. But Marx and Gilon suggest that important parts of this process may also occur in the molecular environment surrounding brain cells.

Their model, called the Tripartite Mechanism of Memory, involves three interacting components: brain cells, particularly neurons and astrocytes; the molecular material surrounding those cells; and chemicals such as metal ions, neurotransmitters, and gliotransmitters.

According to the theory, these components could allow the brain to chemically encode and retrieve information. Rather than serving only as a support structure, the environment surrounding brain cells may actively participate in memory storage.

Astrocytes, star-shaped cells that interact closely with neurons, play a central role in the proposed mechanism. The researchers suggest that coordinated activity among these cells, neurons, and surrounding molecules could contribute to how memories are formed and processed.

A familiar song can bring back memories from decades ago, complete with feelings that seemed long forgotten. Such experiences show that remembering involves more than retrieving information.

Marx and Gilon propose that the emotional content of memories may be linked to their chemical encoding. In their model, signaling molecules, including neurotransmitters and gliotransmitters, help connect stored information with the feelings associated with an experience.

The researchers also suggest that retrieving and interpreting these chemically stored memories may contribute to the emergence of thought. In this view, memory is not simply a record of past events but an active process through which the brain assigns meaning to experience.

Computers and brains both store and process information, but the underlying mechanisms differ. While computers rely on electronic hardware, biological memory involves living cells and complex chemical interactions.

Marx and Gilon argue that this distinction could matter for consciousness. AI systems can perform increasingly sophisticated intellectual tasks, but their ability to process information does not establish that they experience thoughts or emotions.

For example, an AI system can identify a familiar song and describe the memories or feelings it might evoke in a person. Whether such a system could actually experience nostalgia is a different question.

The researchers suggest that if consciousness depends partly on the biochemical processes involved in human memory, greater computational power alone may not be sufficient to reproduce it.

The proposed model offers a possible connection between memory, emotion, and thought, but it does not establish how physical processes in the brain produce conscious experience.

The authors acknowledge that consciousness remains poorly understood and do not claim to have demonstrated that AI cannot become conscious.

Instead, their work suggests that investigating the chemical mechanisms of memory could help explain how stored experiences acquire emotional meaning and contribute to thought. Whether those processes are essential for consciousness remains an open question.

Reference: “Consciousness, Memory and Intelligence: A Mechanistic Perspective” by Gerard Marx and Chaim Gilon, 4 August 2026, International Journal of Psychiatry Research. DOI: 10.33425/2641-4317.1251

Not helpful! A lot of “what-if’s” and projections based on no real understanding of how our brain forms memories, how they are stored, what creates consciousness.

I made an abstract brain model – that does everything – learn, feel, sex and reproduction, experience – years ago. many years ago. But, does anyone care?

It’s becoming clear that with all the brain and consciousness theories out there, the proof will be in the pudding. By this I mean, can any particular theory be used to create a human adult level conscious machine. My bet is on the late Gerald Edelman’s Extended Theory of Neuronal Group Selection. The lead group in robotics based on this theory is the Neurorobotics Lab at UC at Irvine. Dr. Edelman distinguished between primary consciousness, which came first in evolution, and that humans share with other conscious animals, and higher-order consciousness, which came to only humans with the acquisition of sophisticated language (especially math and logic). A machine with only primary consciousness will probably have to come first.

What I find special about the TNGS is the Darwin series of automata created at the Neurosciences Institute by Dr. Edelman and his colleagues in the 1990’s and 2000’s. These machines perform in the real world, not in a restricted simulated world, and display convincing physical behavior indicative of higher psychological functions necessary for consciousness, such as perceptual categorization, memory, and learning. They are based on realistic models of the parts of the biological brain that the theory claims subserve these functions. The extended TNGS allows for the emergence of consciousness based only on further evolutionary development of the brain areas responsible for these functions, in a parsimonious way. No other research I’ve encountered is anywhere near as convincing.

I post because on almost every video and article about the brain and consciousness that I encounter, the attitude seems to be that we still know next to nothing about how the brain and consciousness work; that there’s lots of data but no unifying theory. I believe the extended TNGS is that theory. My motivation is to keep that theory in front of the public. And obviously, I consider it the route to a truly conscious machine, primary and higher-order.

My advice to people who want to create a conscious machine is to seriously ground themselves in the extended TNGS and the Darwin automata first, and proceed from there, by applying to Jeff Krichmar’s lab at UC Irvine, possibly. Dr. Edelman’s roadmap to a conscious machine is at https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.10461, and here is a video of Jeff Krichmar talking about some of the Darwin automata, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=J7Uh9phc1Ow

The more time I’ve spent working with this pressure washer, the more I enjoy it. I tasked the Greenworks Pro GPW3002A with several jobs: to clean off muddy concrete, remove moss from brick, address dirty vinyl siding, and wash my truck after a road trip that left it streaked with gunk and smashed insects.

The high gpm made quick work of tasks like cleaning off an outdoor fireplace while the 15-degree nozzle provided plenty of power for getting mildew-covered concrete looking like new. If you’ll be laying soapy prewash on a house or large deck, this is the tool for you. Its large soap dispenser—a full gallon in size—makes it a go-to for those types of time-consuming jobs.

The GPW3002A has a larger footprint than other electric pressure washers so you’ll need to make space for it in your garage or shed. At 51 pounds, it’s also heavy especially for an electric model.

If you want to avoid the fumes, fuel, and maintenance of a gas-powered pressure washer but you don’t want to sacrifice powerful cleaning performance, this Greenworks is the tool for you.

The Sun Joe SPX3000 has been a go-to budget pressure washer for years, and after testing it ourselves, it’s easy to see why. Despite costing less than many competitors, it delivers surprisingly capable cleaning performance along with several features that are uncommon at this price point.

Its 2,030-psi and 1.2-gpm output won’t replace a heavy-duty gas machine, but it’s more than sufficient for typical homeowner tasks like washing patio furniture, rinsing muddy walkways, cleaning siding, or refreshing a dirty driveway after winter. We also appreciated how approachable the overall design feels. The controls are intuitive, the oversized front dial is easy to operate even with wet hands, and the large top handle makes the unit simple to pull around the yard or lift onto a shelf for storage.

Sun Joe also includes several genuinely useful upgrades, including dual removable detergent tanks, brass fittings, and a steel-reinforced hose that feels more durable than expected at this price. The automatic pump shutoff is another thoughtful addition, helping extend pump life by preventing the motor from constantly running between cleaning passes.

The biggest drawback we encountered was stability. Because the unit uses an upright design, it can feel somewhat tippy on uneven ground or rough terrain, making it best suited for use on pavement, patios, and flatter surfaces. Still, for homeowners looking for an affordable electric pressure washer that doesn’t feel stripped down or flimsy, the SPX3000 remains one of the strongest values in the category.

The Kärcher K 3000 E feels like it was built for homeowners who’ve outgrown entry-level pressure washers but aren’t interested in the upkeep that comes with a gas engine. During recent testing, its induction motor impressed us with noticeably quieter operation than the shrill universal motors found on many budget models, while it still delivered the kind of pressure that quickly strips algae from concrete and pressure-treated wood, blasts years of grime from retaining walls, and makes short work of weathered fencing and siding. If your summer cleanup checklist includes more than just washing your car, this machine has the muscle to keep up.

Like with many high-pressure electric models, there’s a tradeoff. The 1.1-gpm flow rate means rinsing large patios or long stretches of siding takes a little longer than it would with a machine with a higher flow rate. For most homeowners, though, that’s an easy compromise considering the cleaning performance, push-button convenience, and freedom from mixing fuel or changing engine oil.

We also appreciated Kärcher’s attention to detail. The 35-foot high-pressure hose gave us plenty of working range before we had to move the machine, and onboard storage keeps the wand, hose, nozzles, and power cord organized between projects. Five quick-connect nozzles—including a turbo tip—make it easy to switch from washing patio furniture to tackling those annoying oil stains in the driveway without needing to dig around for accessories.

If you want an electric pressure washer that comes as close as we’ve seen to replacing a residential gas model, the K 3000 E is one of the best options available today.

DeWalt’s 3000 Max feels designed for homeowners who are tired of underpowered electric pressure washers but don’t want to deal with the noise, maintenance, and fuel odors that come with gas-powered models. During testing, we primarily used it on heavily soiled concrete, where it had no trouble stripping away moss, embedded grime, and greasy buildup that weaker electric units often struggle to remove.

At 3,000 psi, this washer delivers serious cleaning force. It provides the kind of concentrated power that makes quick work of stubborn surfaces like retaining walls, garage floors, and heavily weathered patios. Compared to entry-level electric models, the jump in cleaning performance is immediately noticeable, especially on neglected concrete.

The trade-off comes in water volume. Its 1.1-gpm flow rate is relatively low, so while it excels at loosening grime, rinsing larger areas can require a bit more patience. Even so, many homeowners will likely find that compromise worthwhile considering the quieter operation and lower maintenance requirements compared to a gas machine.

We were also impressed with the overall design. The suitcase-style frame feels rugged without becoming overly bulky, and the telescoping handle makes it easy to maneuver around a property or store neatly in a garage corner. DeWalt also clearly put thought into onboard storage, with dedicated spaces for the hose, wand, power cord, nozzles, and included foam cannon to keep everything organized between jobs.

If portability is a bigger priority than outright cleaning power, the smaller DeWalt DWPW2600 remains a strong option. But if you’re looking for an electric pressure washer that comes impressively close to gas-level performance, the 3000 Max is one of the toughest and most capable you can buy.

The Kärcher Cube is the smallest and lightest pressure washer we recommend, measuring 15.1 by 12.6 by 11.8 inches and weighing just 19 pounds. Those compact dimensions, combined with its easy-to-grab handle, made it one of the most portable pressure washers we tested—and easily one of the simplest to pick up and carry out the door.

Despite its small footprint, we found storage somewhat awkward. The wand has to be unscrewed from the handle before stowing, and while there’s onboard storage for the hose and power cord, there’s no dedicated spindle or reel to keep them neatly organized.

We were initially concerned that a pressure washer this compact might feel underpowered, but it exceeded our expectations. Although it runs a bit louder than some competing electric models at 87 decibels, it performed well across a variety of our cleaning tasks, from clearing muddy concrete to washing out gutters.

For shoppers prioritizing portability and space-saving design without sacrificing cleaning power, the Kärcher Cube K1800PS is an excellent choice. It’s especially well-suited for anyone who needs a pressure washer that’s easy to carry, store, or keep tucked away in a garage or truck bed.

The Worx WG644 Hydroshot barely feels like a traditional pressure washer at all—and that’s exactly what we liked most about using it. Instead of dragging around a wheeled base unit, hose bundle, and extension cord, this cordless handheld model functions more like a high-powered cleaning wand that’s easy to grab for quick cleanup jobs around the house.

Its portability is one of its biggest strengths. We found it especially useful for rinsing muddy tools, washing outdoor furniture, spraying off vehicles, and handling smaller messes that don’t justify hauling out a full-size pressure washer. Compared to other cordless models we tested, the Hydroshot also felt noticeably better balanced in hand. The rear-mounted battery helps counterbalance the weight of the wand, reducing wrist fatigue and making it more comfortable to use during longer cleaning sessions.

Worx also includes a surprisingly useful feature: an onboard battery life indicator. It’s a small touch, but when working cordless, being able to quickly check remaining runtime without guessing makes a meaningful difference.

Of course, that portability comes with trade-offs. The Hydroshot doesn’t provide the same cleaning force or water volume as a corded electric model, and runtime is naturally limited by battery capacity. But approached as a light-duty convenience tool rather than a heavy-duty driveway-cleaning machine, it becomes extremely practical.

The Giraffe Grandfalls Pro was another pressure washer that impressed us. Initially, we had reservations about how practical a wall-mounted pressure washer would be. While the concept makes sense for garages or dedicated workspaces, we are more accustomed to hauling pressure washers to job sites or wheeling them around a yard.

In practice, though, the wall-mounted design felt surprisingly freeing rather than restrictive. Mounted near the center of his property, the unit’s 100-foot hose was able to reach nearly the entire home and yard without needing to reposition the washer itself. Instead of wrestling with a wheeled unit, extension cords, and tangled hoses, we could simply walk while the hose extended and auto-retracted smoothly. Without a bulky washer body to drag around, it was also easier to move quickly around structures or even work from a rooftop while cleaning siding.

Naturally, real-world reach will depend on property size and mounting location. The unit is designed for outdoor exposure, so it can be mounted directly to the side of a home near a hose bib and outlet.

Also impressive was how quietly it operated. Even when mounted indoors on hardboard spanning an empty wall bay—which effectively amplified sound—it registered just 76 decibels. Mounted outdoors or on a brick wall, Giraffe’s claimed 68 decibels figure seems plausible. At longer distances, the noise faded so much that using the pressure washer at the full 100-foot extension almost felt strange because the pump was barely audible.

The biggest drawback, we discovered, is lower-than-expected water output. Although the unit advertises “Max” specs of 3,700 psi and 1.6 gpm, its rated performance is 2,700 psi and 1.2 gpm, which aligned with our testing. Anyone expecting power comparable to a gas pressure washer may come away disappointed. In practice, the machine performs better when judged as a convenient and capable electric model rather than against inflated peak numbers.

Electric pressure washers are best for light work and small jobs like washing down driveways and sidewalks or gently cleaning decks, patio furniture, or aluminum siding—figure projects that take 30 minutes max.

They can also remove debris from cars and gravel bikes if you have a light touch and use a white nozzle, which has the widest spray and thus is least likely to damage delicate surfaces. (If cleaning a car is your main objective, though, you may be better served investing in a cordless pressure washer.)

When comparing electric pressure washers, two specifications matter most: psi (pounds per square inch) and gpm (gallons per minute). The former, psi, measures pressure, while gpm measures water flow. Together, they determine how quickly and effectively a machine can clean.

For most household jobs—washing cars, windows, grills, outdoor furniture, or light-duty siding—look for a unit in the 1,500 to 2,000 psi range with at least 1.2 to 1.4 gpm. That’s more than enough for routine maintenance and general cleanup. If you’re regularly tackling concrete, brick, or heavily weathered decking, stepping up to a 2,000-plus-psi model with higher flow will make the work noticeably faster.

Higher psi isn’t always better, though. Too much pressure can damage paint and erode wood grain if you’re not careful. In practice, the right nozzle and steady movement matter every bit as much as raw power.

Most electric pressure washers include a set of quick-connect spray tips designed for different surfaces. A narrow, high-pressure tip helps blast away stubborn dirt and grime, while wide-angle tips are better for siding, vehicles, and general cleaning as they “fan” the water rather than direct it like a jet. Some models now include adjustable spray wands or turbo nozzles that rotate the stream for faster coverage on hard surfaces like concrete and stone.

Detergent tanks and foam cannons are increasingly common as well—and very useful. Being able to lay a coating of soap evenly over the surface before pressure rinsing makes a huge difference when washing vehicles, siding, and outdoor furniture. For larger flatwork areas like patios and driveways, surface cleaner attachments can really speed things up while delivering better results than a standard wand.

Beyond raw cleaning power, usability is what separates an okay pressure washer from one you’ll actually reach for time and again. I prefer long hoses, wheels that are solid and stable, and smart onboard storage. These factors make a huge difference in my overall work time, especially where keeping track of the various components is concerned. And longer cords and hoses simply mean I’m moving the unit less.

Compact vertical units store easily on a garage shelf or in the corner, while larger cart-style models tend to be more stable and easier to roll across uneven ground. If you’ll be working around a driveway, yard, or job site, it’s smart to choose a washer with an appropriate wheel size and construction to meet your anticipated needs.

Gas pressure washers make sense if heavy-duty work—stripping paint, cleaning large concrete areas, or prepping exterior surfaces for finishing—is in your anticipated scope of work. But for the majority of homeowners, electric models are the more practical choice. They start instantly, require minimal upkeep, and are easier to live with on a day-to-day basis.

If your typical jobs involve vehicles, siding, decks, fencing, tools, and the occasional driveway or gutter cleanup, a good electric pressure washer will handle it without much fuss. And with the performance gap between electric and gas continuing to shrink, there’s less reason than ever to deal with the noise and maintenance of a gas engine unless you feel you truly need that extra power. For most homes and garages, an electric pressure washer has become one of the most useful and versatile outdoor tools you can own.

Because they generally aren’t as powerful, electric pressure washers are generally safer to use than gas pressure washers on a wide variety of surfaces. That said, they can still damage sensitive surfaces if you use them incorrectly.

You could also injure yourself or someone you’re working with if you aren’t careful. Even a relatively low-pressure stream can result in lacerations or bruising to your skin. As a safety precaution, you should always wear closed-toe shoes and proper eye protection.

To protect yourself and your stuff, always start with one of the less powerful nozzles—green or white—which have wide spray angles that decrease the intensity of the water stream. If they can’t get the job done, you can either try moving the wand closer to the cleaning surface (your manual will give you the best idea of the specific distance) or move up to a yellow or red nozzle. These produce narrower streams that can gouge more delicate surfaces, so give yourself enough space (about three feet) to evaluate their effect on the cleaning surface before slowly moving forward.

Another no-no: Never use a pressure washer on anything electrical, which will likely damage its components. Just because your outdoor speakers are weatherproof doesn’t mean they can withstand a high-impact blast from a pressure washer.

If you’re new to pressure washing and want to ensure you don’t damage the surface you’re cleaning, take the time to better understand the machine’s capabilities before diving right in.

Start about 10 feet away with the widest nozzle available, and as you get a feel for how the spray affects the surface you’re cleaning, gradually increase pressure by switching to a more focused tip, or by simply walking closer to the surface. Keep in mind that different types of surfaces may require their own approach: The pressure you need to blast grime off of a trash can could potentially strip or damage a more delicate material like painted wood.

The movement of an electric pressure washer’s stream also affects its cleaning effectiveness—the longer the stream is focused on the same place, the more debris it removes. In order to prevent unsightly streaks and potential damage to your surface, it’s important to keep the nozzle moving as you go, maintaining even, consistent coverage.

In order to work as comfortably, effectively, and safely as possible, adopt a stance that allows you to handle the kickback of your pressure washer, especially at its highest settings. When using your washer, keep your feet shoulder-width apart and at a slight angle to the surface being cleaned. A slight bend at the knees also helps to minimize lower back fatigue during longer jobs. As you move around, always reposition yourself—and the machine if needed—instead of overreaching, which can lead to loss of balance or control.

A former residential remodeler and maintenance manager, Dan Stout has worked in nearly every part of the construction and DIY industry, from project planning and permitting to plumbing, drywall, carpentry, and more. He loves to write about the weird history of everyday objects, and to help readers make informed decisions about their homes.

#6485. Extremely Accurate Measurements of a Pair of Flaring Red Dwarfs

About 59 light years away, a binary pair of red dwarfs are orbiting a common center of gravity. Unlike stars like our Sun, which are relatively radio-quiet, red dwarfs (M dwarfs) can produce strong radio emissions. A team of astronomers used that to their advantage to take precision measurements of a binary pair of M dwarfs about 59 million light years from Earth. They determined the stars' orbits and masses with uncommon accuracy.

One fundamental fact about low and intermediate mass stars, including M dwarfs, is that they rotate more rapidly when they're younger. Stars inherit angular momentum from their formation in gas clouds, and since M dwarfs are so small, that momentum is concentrated, making them spin rapidly. They eventually slow down, but this initial rapid rotation makes them very active.

The fast rotation generates powerful magnetic dynamos, and young M dwarfs exhibit very large sunspots and more frequent, powerful stellar flares.

One subset of young M dwarfs is even more extreme. They're called Complex Periodic Variable (CPV) stars, and they're very young, between about 10 and 100 million years old. They're M dwarfs that display complex, periodical optical light curves with sharp drops rather than smooth drops found in most stellar light curves. Their drops aren't simple; there can be multiple dips and peaks during a single rotation. Astrophysicists call their light curves multi-harmonic, and the patterns repeat across multiple rotations.

This image shows CPV light curves for three typical CPV stars found by TESS. Notice the sharp drops in the curves rather than typical smooth drops found in other stellar light curves. Image Credit: Bouma et al. 2023. AnJ

The binary system in this research is named DG CVn, and one of them is a CPV star. Though CPV stars have complex light curves generated by their youthful, rapid rotation, their youthfulness also means they're radio loud. In fact, since both of these stars are young M dwarfs, they're both radio loud. That helped the researchers measure them with such accuracy.

The measurments of DG CVn are in new research in Astronomy and Astrophysics titled "Accurate dynamical mass and orbit determination of the M dwarf binary DG CVn using astrometric very long baseline interferometry." The lead author is Paul VLBI , a network system engineer at the Joint Institute for Very Long Baseline Interferometry ERIC (JIVE), and a Leiden Observatory PhD student. It's noteworthy that this is the first mass measurement of a system with a CPV star.

"We present the first dynamical mass measurement of a binary containing a CPV star." - Boven et al. 2026.

The astronomers' results are based on observations that spanned 18 years. Observations with the National Science Foundationâs Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA) between 2023 and 2025 were especially important in their precise results. The VLBA is a system of 10 radiotelescopes across the USA, each one measuring 25 meters. The 10 dishes work as an interferometer, and the VLBA has the longest baseline in the world, up to 8,611 km long.

"Astrometry through very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) allows the monitoring of radio-loud stars and the detection of any reflex motion due to stellar or substellar companions," the authors write. Reflex motion is the characteristic gravitational wobble induced in a star when a companion tugs on it.

That wobble is often used to detect unseeable exoplanets orbiting stars. Even a small planet can make its star wobble, and that's at the heart of the radial velocity method of detecting exoplanet. The DG CVn system was actually found when astronomers were searching for exoplanets with the radial velocity method. But the system exhibited a more powerful and complex wobble than an exoplanet would.

âWe were really lucky to hear about this object when we had developed tools with which we could explain these motions,â said Boven. âBut the real surprise came when we also detected the second radio-loud dwarf in the observations we did to confirm our model. It really allowed us to measure the system very precisely.â

Measuring reflex motion accurately with the VLBI let the astronomers track the stars' paths, including the tiny wobbles, which in turn let them understand the mass of the stars with extreme precision.

This figure from the research shows the VLBI detections of both members of DG CVn, and their modeled motion across the sky. The dates mark the predicted positions of DG CVn B over time. The inset image shows recent observations when both sources were detected. Image Credit: Boven et al. 2026. A&A.

"In our recent observations, we reliably detected both binary components," the authors write. "A unique and accurate determination of the 1647.647 Â± 0.027 day orbit, with a parallax distance of 18.1851 Â± 0.0033 pc (about 59 light years), is presented. The dynamical masses were estimated with a precision of 0.16% from the sampled posteriors."

The pair of stars orbit each other every 4.511 years on an elongated elliptical orbit. When they're closest to one another, they're only separated by 0.59 astronomical units. DG CVn A is the more massive of the pair with 0.39 solar masses, while DG CVn B has 0.36 solar masses. The pair is close enough to measure their distance with parallax, which gives accurate measurements.

The red dwarfs and their radio emissions are central to this work. The stars are simply too close together from this distance to be separated in optical observations. But the VLBA can pinpoint their locations with extreme accuracy. All of this work let the researchers characterize the system in clear detail, following the motions of both stars through the sky separately.

âDG CVn is a beautiful example of what precise radio astrometry can reveal,â said Jay Blanchard, NSF National Radio Astronomy Observatory astronomer and study co-author. âBy following these two stars over many years, we can see their orbital motion directly and use that motion to determine properties that would otherwise be extremely difficult to measure.â

These accurate measurements also tell astronomers about their planetary systems. Planets form in protoplanetary disks around stars, and since these stars are so close together, that limits the size of their disks. Smaller disks mean smaller planets, so that limits the size of any exoplanets in the system. It's also extremely unlikely that any long-period planets are orbiting either star.

According to the researchers' estimates, an exoplanet in orbit around one of the stars could only be in a stable orbit if its orbital period was less than approximately 23 days. For a circumbinary planet orbiting both stars, the orbital period would have to be at least about 36 years. These approximations are also important, because they can refine the understanding of how exoplanets can form and survive in binary star systems.

Gaia's Data Release 4 is due in a couple of weeks, and it will include binary star parameters for the mission's complete survey. But that data alone won't be able to differentiate between binaries where both are low mass stars, and binaries where one might be a massive planet. But the VLBI will be able to address that. "Astrometric follow-up of selected detections with VLBI can help to differentiate between binary star systems and reflex motion due to large exoplanets (or even both)," the authors write.

"We have presented a complete binary orbital solution with high accuracy based on VLBI astrometry of a binary that is difficult to resolve for optical telescopes on the ground or in orbit," the authors write. "The absolute astrometry provided by VLBI allowed the individual dynamical masses to be determined with high accuracy. These results show that VLBI is well suited for studying the orbits of radio-loud stars."

The results also show how powerful the combination of archival observations and new observations can be. "The value of combining archival and recent VLBI astrometric observations has been demonstrated. It resulted in a highly accurate determination of the system composition, orbit, position, and distance," the authors write. "We present the first dynamical mass measurement of a binary containing a CPV star."

The VLBI network of radio dishes is about to have a growth spurt when the Square Kilometre Array and the Next Generation Very Large Array come online. That will improve the system's reach and precision.

"In the future, we hope to make measurements precise enough to detect planets in orbit around such radio-loud dwarfs,â said Huib van Langevelde, chief scientist a the Joint Institute for Very Long Baseline Interferometry and Leiden Observatory professor. âWe think that when the ngVLA and the SKA become part of the VLBI network, we can do even more precise measurements, for many more, more distant stars.â

A new AI model, called Brain-IT, can transform brain scans into images and reverse the process, turning images into what they'd look like as brain activity.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

An artificial intelligence (AI) tool can use brain scans to recreate the images people looked at with eerie accuracy.

The system, called Brain-IT, uses data from functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to measure activity in the visual cortex, the part of the brain that processes visual input. A computer model then predicts both the broad layout of an image and high-level information about its content. It then passes those predictions to an AI image generator, researchers explained in a study uploaded to the preprint database arXiv. The research was presented at the ICLR 2026 conference, held April 23-25, and publicized by its authors in September.

Brain-IT builds on an approach called the Universal Brain Encoder. That model begins with an image and then predicts the fMRI response that would be expected in individual "voxels" ‪—‬ small 3D units ‪—‬ in a brain scan.

"The key idea is that every voxel, a tiny cube of brain tissue, gets its own learned vector that captures what it cares about in images," said study first author Roman Beliy, a doctoral candidate in the Department of Computer Science and Applied Mathematics at the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel.

Some voxels may be tuned to relatively simple elements of an image, such as edges, textures or locations. Others might be responding to higher-level abstract categories, like faces, bodies or scenes.

Traditional image-to-fMRI systems have generally been custom trained for each participant and dataset. The Universal Brain Encoder is more flexible. It learns from data from multiple people and can transfer information across participants, datasets or different MRI systems with varying magnetic-field strengths, according to the study.

A voxel can determine which parts of an image are relevant to it based on its learned profile, essentially saying, "I recognize edges. Which parts of this image are edges?"

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The Universal Brain Encoder starts with an image and predicts brain activity; Brain-IT starts with measured brain activity and reconstructs the image the person saw. In other words,it asks "based on this brain activity, what was the subject looking at?". It sorts thousands of tiny brain-scan measurements from the visual cortex into 128 groups based on the kinds of visual information they tend to carry.

The system then lets those groups share clues with one another, allowing it to combine, for example, information about a scene's shape, color and possible objects, to build a more complete picture of the image, Beliy explained.

The decoder produces two types of visual predictions. One captures semantic information ‪—‬ the features associated with what is likely in a scene; for an image of a dog standing in grass, for instance, this would include things like the features of a dog and an outdoor, grassy setting. The other captures structural information, like the broad visual layout or how forms are arranged.

In the above example, this would be aspects like the outline of the dog or where it was positioned in the frame. The structural prediction gives the generator a starting point for the image, rather than beginning from pure noise, while the semantic info guides an image generator that removes the remaining static until the image emerges.

Although the new tool can recreate what people see, it can't reproduce memories or imagined scenes.

"We're not reading people's thoughts," study co-author Michal Irani, a computer scientist at the Weizmann Institute of Science, told Live Science. "The images we do manage to recover from fMRI require people's cooperation and full intended collaboration."

The original image of a baseball game (left) and the reconstruction (right) generated by the Brain-IT AI model based on the brain activity of a person viewing the image.

Brain-IT's synthetic images were compared with the images that participants saw. Brain-IT surpassed prior leading methods on standard objective reconstruction metrics and produced more faithful results, the study authors wrote. The system shined when limited fMRI data from a new participant was available, with just one hour of data from a new participant producing results as accurately as earlier approaches that had been trained on 40 hours of recordings.

A high-scoring or realistic-looking output should not be mistaken for a perfect copy of what someone saw, however.

In the final stage of processing, the system uses an off-the-shelf diffusion generator trained on massive numbers of images. Models like this generate plausible images and can smooth textures, sharpen facial features or fill in missing details.

Beliy said this "beautification" can make reconstructions more polished and convincing and introduce details that don't necessarily come from the brain data itself. In other words, the scan constrains the generated picture, but the AI model supplies some of its realism from learned patterns in photographs.

While the new system produces impressive results for seen images, it can't be used to reconstruct an imagined or remembered image.

"Brain-IT relies on how the brain processes a seen image," Irani said. "Information flows from the eyes to the primary visual cortex and onward through a series of visual areas that recognize objects and scenes."

In a controlled experiment, researchers also know precisely which image was shown, giving the model a target during training and evaluation. In contrast, memories and imagined images do not offer the same clean reference. They can be vague and shaped by brain networks involved in memory and thought, with only partial and weaker reactivation of visual regions, Irani said. One limitation that would prevent this technology from being widely deployed is that the only way to get reliable results is from fMRI scanning, which is cumbersome and expensive. The team is currently experimenting with using easier-to-collect electroencephalogram (EEG) data, which is obtained via electrodes on the head, but that work is in the very preliminary stages, according to Irani.

The new system could help brain researchers better understand which visual information is represented in different brain regions, how those regions interact and how individuals’ patterns differ. Such tools could eventually reveal differences in visual processing that could help clinicians spot neurological, neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions.

"There are numerous useful medical applications which we are currently striving toward," Irani said. "These include using our brain encoder/decoder to detect and analyze brain disorders such as MS, PTSD, autism and psychiatric disorders."

Beliy, R., Zalcher, A., Kogman, J., Wasserman, N., & Irani, M. (2025, October 29). Brain-IT: Image Reconstruction from fMRI via Brain-Interaction Transformer. arXiv.org. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.25976

#6483. These Remote Atolls Are Among the Last Places on Earth Humans Haven’t Touched. Here’s What Scientists Found.

Bikar and Bokak sit so far from people that they may show us what the ocean looked like before humans.

There are few havens on Earth as pristine as the Bikar and Bokak atolls. Formed from sunken volcanoes around which coral reefs grew, these atolls in the Ratak chain of the Marshall Islands teem with life and remain uninhabited by humans. Rainbows of fish swim among corals and sea anemones, while sharks glide silently through the water in pursuit of prey. Until recently, even marine biologists had rarely explored these habitats in depth.

That began to change when Alan Friedlander set out across an impossibly blue swath of ocean and led his team into paradise. Friedlander is a marine ecologist at the University of Hawai’i who served as chief scientist for National Geographic’s Pristine Seas program on the expedition, and he takes a special interest in remote and protected regions of the ocean. The people of the Marshall Islands have known Bikar and Bokak for generations, but the atolls had never been comprehensively surveyed when Friedlander and his team arrived. For the Marshallese, the ocean is home even more than the land is. Their survival depends on the health of the fragile reef ecosystems around the country’s 1,225 islands and islets, only some of which are inhabited.

The opportunity came in 2023, when Pristine Seas was invited to join the Marshall Islands Marine Resources Authority in surveying Bikar and Bokak, which are safeguarded by the Utirik Atoll community. Friedlander and his team received a traditional blessing and farewell on Utirik before sailing north to Bikar, which lies about 72 miles (116 km) from the nearest inhabited atoll. Bokak is even more isolated, about 239 miles (385 km) away. This remoteness is part of the reason the atolls have remained relatively untouched by human influence. Friedlander wanted to carry out an ecological assessment of everything from the land habitats to the reefs and the open sea. That meant studying the structure and biodiversity of these ecosystems, documenting how well they had been preserved and how the two atolls differed, and identifying the conservation measures they would need in the future.

“The remote northern atolls of Bikar and Bokak represent some of the least disturbed coral reef ecosystems remaining in the tropical Pacific,” Friedlander and his co-authors wrote in a study recently published in Frontiers in Marine Science. “Both atolls are uninhabited and geographically isolated from major population centers and industrial development. Previous expeditions documented portions of their terrestrial habitats, seabird colonies, sea turtles, and shallow coral reefs.”

The team’s first stop was Bikar, which curves across the water like a crescent moon. There, the researchers used a variety of sampling methods, including scuba surveys, photography, underwater video, deep-sea cameras, and a submarine, to record which species were present and in what numbers. Polynesian rats, which humans introduced, were sometimes seen scurrying through the island’s old-growth Pisonia forests. Even so, native species still thrive. Seabirds such as masked boobies, great frigatebirds, black noddies, and white terns filled the skies, while shorebirds like the migratory Pacific golden plover pecked at the sand in search of small invertebrates. Bikar’s beaches are also a nesting ground for green sea turtles; the team recorded 132 nest pits there. Its reefs are full of fish, including several species of snapper and grouper. Giant clams, which host photosynthetic algae, filter the water and are vital to the health of the reef.

Farther north and even more isolated, Bokak is an oasis that has seen very little human interference. Its drier, savanna-like landscape is covered in tufts of bunchgrass and tree heliotropes, which bear clusters of small white flowers. Many of the seabirds that soar over Bikar are also found on Bokak. Bokak’s waters are even richer than Bikar’s: its reefs are dominated by coral and hold more fish by weight. Friedlander dove in to investigate. He came across a school of humphead parrotfish, a threatened species once thought to have nearly vanished from the islands. He also saw an unusual reversal of the typical food pyramid. Reef sharks and black jacks outweigh their prey in total biomass. Because these top predators feed so often, they keep energy and nutrients moving quickly through the reef, which helps the ecosystem run efficiently.

After Bokak, Friedlander’s team had one more location to survey, and it offered a sharp contrast. From 1946 to 1958, Bikini Atoll was a center of U.S. nuclear testing, starting with Operation Crossroads. When the islanders were evacuated before the first tests, they took only a few changes of clothes, not knowing that they would never be able to resettle their home for good. The series of detonations devastated the atoll. From the ocean’s glassy surface, Bikini seems to be ringed by cities of coral. But divers who swam closer found that many of these formations, which had taken thousands of years to grow, were little more than skeletons. Still, Bikini Atoll is not without hope. After searching long enough, Friedlander found patches of live coral that had settled on the dead reef and were swarming with fish. It was a sign of how resilient life can be.

Even Bikar and Bokak can’t fully escape what is happening elsewhere. Their remoteness protects them from most direct human pressures, but climate change is slowly reaching them, too. When the water gets too hot, corals expel the symbiotic algae that feed them and give them their bright colors, a process known as coral bleaching. Leftover radiation from the nuclear-testing era is still a source of contamination in the region. Meanwhile, currents carry in trash from other countries, and plastics break down into microplastics. People are responding with conservation measures. In 2025, two years after the expedition, the government of the Marshall Islands designated the waters around Bikar and Bokak, about 18,500 square miles (48,000 square km), as the country’s first national marine sanctuary, as part of the community-led Reimaanlok conservation framework. Despite the threats that come from far away, Friedlander is optimistic.

“As relatively intact tropical marine ecosystems become increasingly rare worldwide,” he and his co-authors concluded, “remote atolls such as Bikar and Bokak serve not only as regional conservation priorities but also as globally important ecological reference systems for understanding the structure and future trajectories of tropical oceanic ecosystems in the Anthropocene.”

Elizabeth Rayne is a creature who writes. Her work has appeared in Popular Mechanics, Ars Technica, SYFY WIRE, Space.com, Live Science, Den of Geek, Forbidden Futures and Collective Tales. She lurks right outside New York City with her parrot, Lestat. When not writing, she can be found drawing, playing the piano or shapeshifting.

#6482. Stanford Scientists Discover 3 Hidden Brain Types in Children With ADHD and Anxiety

Scientists have identified three distinct patterns of brain activity in children with ADHD, anxiety, or both, revealing biological differences that traditional diagnoses often overlook.

Brain scans have uncovered three distinct patterns of disrupted brain activity in children with ADHD, anxiety, or both conditions. These patterns do not align neatly with conventional diagnoses, suggesting that children with similar symptoms may have different underlying neurological differences. Some patterns were even detectable years before children received a diagnosis.

The findings come from a Stanford Medicine-led study published October 16 in Nature Mental Health. By combining artificial intelligence with thousands of functional MRI (fMRI) scans, researchers identified three brain biotypes associated with different combinations of behavioral, emotional, and attention difficulties.

ADHD and anxiety are among the most common childhood mental health disorders, and their symptoms frequently overlap. Clinicians typically diagnose these conditions using behavioral assessments and symptom checklists, but those categories may not fully capture the neurological differences between children.

“The high overlap between ADHD and anxiety actually hinders our understanding of the neurobiology underlying traditional, symptom-based diagnoses,” said Yu Zhang, PhD, assistant professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Stanford Medicine and co-senior author of the study.

“We wanted to know whether the biological differences among children with ADHD and anxiety follow the diagnostic labels used in the clinic,” Zhang said.

The researchers found that children diagnosed with ADHD, anxiety, or both could belong to any of the three biotypes. Although particular brain patterns were more common with certain diagnoses, no biotype corresponded exclusively to a single disorder.

The researchers identified three neurological profiles, each associated with a distinctive combination of symptoms:

Each child belonged to just one biotype (each child was in only one biotype), but the three patterns appeared across all conventional diagnostic categories.

The model also identified two underlying dimensions of brain dysfunction: cognitive-behavioral dysfunction and emotion-attention dysfunction. Each involved different networks of brain regions, with the three biotypes reflecting distinct combinations of these disruptions. The findings suggest that differences in how brain circuits communicate may help explain variations in children’s symptoms.

The researchers drew on the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study, a long-term investigation of more than 11,000 U.S. children who entered the project at ages 9 or 10.

Their analysis included 3,508 children initially diagnosed with ADHD, anxiety, or both; 693 children who received one or both diagnoses later; and 1,947 children who never received either diagnosis. The researchers also examined brain scans from 224 children with ADHD or anxiety in the separate Healthy Brain Network study to validate their findings.

An AI model examined functional connectivity, which describes how activity in different brain regions is coordinated. By combining these measurements with diagnostic records and cognitive and behavioral assessments, the researchers identified brain connectivity patterns associated with ADHD and anxiety that differed from those seen in children without either diagnosis.

The researchers also detected the biotypes in initial brain scans from children who had not yet been diagnosed with ADHD or anxiety but developed one or both conditions later. This suggests that certain patterns of brain connectivity may emerge before symptoms lead to a clinical diagnosis.

“We think this means we may be able to use the biotypes as an early indicator of these conditions,” Zhang said. He identified the early appearance of these patterns as one of the study’s most surprising results.

“It could help us provide more timely intervention for these conditions and slow down or, we hope, even reverse their progression.”

The findings do not establish that brain scans can reliably predict which individual children will develop ADHD or anxiety. Further research is needed to determine whether the biotypes can serve as clinically useful biomarkers for early identification.

Beyond early detection, the researchers hope the findings could eventually help clinicians select treatments based on a child’s underlying brain activity rather than relying entirely on symptoms.

Current treatment decisions often involve considerable trial and error, particularly when medications do not produce the expected improvement.

“When doctors prescribe a new medication, it can take quite a long time, a couple of weeks or months, to see a response,” Zhang said. “If the first medication doesn’t work, they switch to a different one,” a process that can be costly, slow, and frustrating for families.

Zhang does not expect brain biotypes to replace existing diagnostic methods. Instead, he envisions using them alongside conventional assessments to provide a more detailed picture of each child’s condition.

Future clinical trials could investigate whether particular treatments improve the brain connectivity abnormalities associated with each biotype. Researchers could then examine whether these neurological patterns help predict treatment responses.

“We want to find biomarkers that can really inform the right treatment at the right time,” Zhang said.

Reference: “Deep learning of brain–behavior dimensions identifies transdiagnostic biotypes in youth with ADHD and anxiety disorders” by Yong Jiao, Xiaoyu Tong, Gregory A. Fonzo, Ian H. Gotlib, Kilian M. Pohl, Theodore D. Satterthwaite, Jing Jiang and Yu Zhang, 16 October 2026, Nature Mental Health. DOI: 10.1038/s44220-026-00740-3

The research was supported by grants from the National Institutes of Health (grant numbers R01MH129694, R01MH136197, R01MH145082, R01MH140425, U24AA021697, R01DA057567, R37MH101495 and R01MH132784), the Eagles Autism Foundation, the Stanford Knight Initiative for Brain Resilience, the Rosenkranz Foundation, the Brain and Behavior Research Foundation, and the Effie and Wofford Cain Foundation.

#6481. Are Uranus and Neptune Secretly "Rock Giants"? A Noble Gas Might Hold the Answer

For decades, astronomers have divided the planets in the outer solar system into two distinct camps. Jupiter and Saturn were the âgas giantsâ made up primarily of hydrogen and helium. Uranus and Neptune were the âice giantsâ, and were much smaller but were packed with heavier elements. A new paper from Olivier Mousis of the Southwest Research Institute and his co-authors, available in The Planetary Science Journal, explores whether we can use an isotope of a noble gas - argon-40 - to determine whether there are hidden mountains of rock under the ice giantâs thick atmospheres.

Scientists are getting excited because there has been an ongoing debate that these distant worlds are actually covered in rock. But we canât simply fly a probe out a few billion miles and drill down into their surfaces to determine that for ourselves. Instead, they decided to use proxies, such as the concentration of argon-40, as a rough measurement for how much rock there is below the atmosphere.

Understanding why the presence of one noble gas isotope leads to understanding whether rock is present or not requires a bit of a diversion into the world of bananas. Or at least, it gives me an excuse to talk about bananas in a planetary science article. Bananas are radioactive, and the thing causing their radioactivity is potassium-40 - a relatively unstable form of a very common element. When potassium-40 decays, it turns into argon-40, which, as a noble gas, hardly interacts with anything.

Fraser talks about how to plan a mission to Uranus.

Most of this radioactive decay takes place in rocks containing potassium-40, rather than bananas, so one of the most common sources of argon-40 is literally rocks. After it is created, it bubbles up out of those rocks and escapes into its host planetâs atmosphere. In fact, it makes up around 1% of the air youâre breathing right now.

On the ice giants, this same process could hold - argon-40 could form inside a rocky surface, and then bubble up into the planetâs atmosphere over billions of years. So we should be able to send a probe to measure the concentration of argon-40 in their atmospheres, and that would serve as an effective proxy for the existence of rock under the atmosphere.

Thereâs just one catch - rocks arenât really the only source of argon-40. In fact, there was already plenty of it floating around in the protosolar nebula that the Sun and all the planets eventually formed out of. Therefore, Uranus and Neptune could have âtrappedâ this leftover argon-40 before they were even mature, causing argon-40 to eventually appear in their atmosphere, but not from rocky surfaces.

Fraser talks about efforts to go back to visit the ice giants of the solar system.

According to the paper, the amount of argon collected by the early versions of Neptune and Uranus depends entirely on where they formed with regards to the âargon ice lineâ. This line, which happens around 23-35 Kelvin, the temperature that argon freezes into solid ice, or is trapped inside water ice, is the determining factor of how much primordial argon Neptune and Uranus had sucked up.

Unfortunately, thereâs still a lot of debate about where exactly in the solar system the ice giants formed. If they formed close to the Sun and eventually migrated back out to the edges of the solar system, they might not have captured much argon ice, and the majority of the argon in their atmospheres would be due to release from rocks. On the other hand, if the theories about them actively moving through the solar system soon after their creation are true, then they would likely have captured a large amount of argon-40, making it useless as an indicator of whether or not the planets have a rocky surface.

Luckily, there is a way to potentially solve this puzzle. Argon-40 has a lighter isotopic cousin, known as argon-36, which is non-radioactive, and doesnât form in decaying rocks. Measuring its level would act like a control group, allowing scientists to estimate how much of the argon present in the atmosphere would have been swallowed at birth, as we have other estimates of the ratio between argon-40 and argon-36 in the early solar system.

Itâs good these sorts of insights are coming out now, as there is currently a mission, Uranus Orbiter and Probe, which is in active development and planned to arrive in the system in the 2040s. That still gives us some time to finalize our theories about what we would expect to find there. And perhaps, once it does arrive, weâll be able to definitively answer whether or not the âIce giantsâ have a truly solid surface or not.

SwRI - SwRI team studies interior composition, origins of ice giants

O. Mousis et al - Primordial and Radiogenic Argon 40 in Uranus and Neptune

UT - Argon â The First Noble Gas Molecules Discovered In Space

UT - Webb Sees a System That Just Finished Forming its Planets

#6480. The 38 Best London Restaurants, According to Eater’s Local Dining Expert

The best meals in London, from Michelin fine dining to beloved street food, according to a longtime restaurant editor

The story of the London food scene is one that includes dim sum, Sunday roasts, curries, pizza, sinasir, rarebits, banh mi, udon, pepper pot, sweetbread suya, and natural wine. Across cuisines, neighborhoods, and price points, all these dishes and drinks place London among the very best and most diverse places to eat in the world.

This guide, which I’ve been compiling and iterating on for the better part of the last decade, aims to reflect the best food and most important restaurants in the capital. I want this map to help you navigate a city in which it is all too easy to eat poorly, but in which it is increasingly inexcusable to do so. It will showcase a mix of over three dozen restaurants, which have all done outstanding things in extraordinary times: emerging, surviving, thriving, and continuing to enrich the city and its food culture through more than half a decade of unprecedented change and tumult.

We update this list regularly to make sure it reflects the ever-changing London dining scene. Our write-ups include insider tips, as well as a rough range of pricing for each destination — ranging from $ for quick, inexpensive meals with dishes largely under $10 (or the equivalent in pounds), to $$$$ for places where entrees exceed $30.

New to the map in November 2026: A return to the 38 for Kiln, one of London’s most consistent and innovative modern Thai restaurants, which this year turns 10; Bouchon Racine, a French bistro above a Farringdon pub whose faithful homage to the traditions of simple French cooking have it booked up months in advance; and perhaps the most interesting restaurant to open in London this year: Tramps, a semi-secret, not-often-open restaurant and bar within a gallery space off City Road. Three restaurants added to the map, which collectively exhibit just a portion of the curious plurality of the London dining experience.

Adam Coghlan is a writer and editor based in London. In 2017, he launched Eater London and ran the site until it ceased daily publication in 2023.

Across cuisines, neighborhoods, and price points, all these dishes and drinks place London among the very best and most diverse places to eat in the world.
