#6472. The 8 Best Lawn Sweepers Make Clearing Leaves a Breeze

Whether you attach one to your lawn mower or buy a dedicated push-behind model, using a lawn sweeper makes it easy to keep your lawn pristine.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

For many of us, the pretty early days of colorful autumn trees have passed, and now we’re dealing with a deluge of leaves covering the ground. During my years in grounds maintenance, much of it landscaping, fall cleanup meant long days with a rake and a blower, then bagging everything we'd piled up. A lawn sweeper thankfully takes most of the bending out of that job and is much more efficient.

With this rake on wheels, it’s the device doing all the work. As it rolls, a gear in each wheel spins a shaft of brushes several times faster than the wheels turn, and the brushes flick leaves, grass clippings, and pine needles back into a fabric hopper—the collection bag stretched over a frame. There's no engine and no cord.

The range of lawn sweepers varies from 26-inch push sweepers you use like a lawn mower, suitable for a small lawn or a patio, to tow-behinds, some of them 54 inches wide, that are pulled with lawn tractors or zero-turn mowers. To find the right one for you, look at how fast a lawn sweeper’s brushes spin at a safe ground speed (the pace you drive or walk), how far the brushes adjust into the grass, and whether the hitch holds the machine level.

Here are our top recommendations spanning various categories and use cases.

With decades of experience testing and researching lawn care equipment, our Popular Mechanics test team compiled the following recommendations based on brands we know and trust. Lawn sweepers are typically suited for large properties, with the majority of our selections in this guide being the type of models you tow behind a lawn tractor.

The recommendations here are capable of clearing large amounts of grass clippings and leaves from lawns that span a half-acre or more. For quarter-acre yards, we generally recommend a leaf blower to clear leaves and a mower with a bagging attachment to collect grass clippings. That said, we still include two lawn sweeping options for smaller yards.

Adding expertise to this article is freelance writer James Fitzgerald, who started as a ranch hand, then apprenticed as a carpenter, and spent several years in residential construction. Fitzgerald followed that with time as a production tree climber and aerial lift operator, then transitioned into facilities and grounds maintenance across multiple residential and commercial properties. All of these efforts involved a great deal of landscaping. His byline has appeared in Family Handyman, Bob Vila, The Spruce, This Old House, and Forbes Home.

For this most recent update, Fitzgerald reviewed manufacturers' specifications, owners' manuals and parts lists, and consumer reviews. For tow-behinds, he gave preference to a published brush-to-wheel ratio (written like 5:1, for five turns of the brushes to each turn of the wheels) and speed limit. Those with a hitch that adjusts to the height of a tractor's hitch plate (the flat bar at the back of the tractor with a hole for the pin) were also given preference. For push sweepers, capacity, weight, and price mattered more.

If you’ve got a lawn tractor and more yard than you want to rake, this is the sweeper that is best. It's one of the pricier picks, but what more money buys you is time. Its brackets assemble for hitch plates (the flat bar at the back of the tractor with a hole for the pin) 7 to 9, 9 to 11, or 11 to 13 inches off the ground, so it rides level whether your hitch sits low or high. The hitch can be offset so that it runs to one side of the tractor, enabling you to pick up the clippings right out of your discharge chute. Picking up already-mowed leaves theoretically lets the collection hopper fit more debris, saving you further time as you don’t have to empty as often.

Its 5.6:1 gearing spins the brushes about 470 times a minute at a 3 mph cruise, fast enough to throw debris to the back of the 28-cubic-foot hopper.

It dumps with a handle you work from the seat, which is better than a rope for the leverage on a full load of wet grass. Empty it more often when the grass is wet, since a heavy load can bend the hopper's support tubes.

At 72.7 pounds, the Yard Commander's 42-inch sweeper is the lightest of the tow-behind options in this guide. Its universal hitch attaches quickly to most lawn tractors and ATVs but not to zero-turn mowers.

Four 10-inch nylon brushes sweep into a 17.79-cubic-foot hopper, which holds a little over three lawn bags' worth and empties with the pull of a string. The corrosion-resistant steel construction delivers stability and ensures use season after season. Yard Commander doesn't publish a gear ratio or a top speed.

This mid-size lawn sweeper behind a tractor is worth a look. Its 42-inch path makes it manageable to steer easily around beds and trees, and the 22-cubic-foot hopper, about four lawn bags' worth, empties with a rope from the seat. Five hitch positions let you choose the one that leaves the hitch tubes (the bars running from the hitch to the sweeper) roughly level with the ground.

Its four spiral brushes twist along the shaft, so part of each always touches the grass and it doesn't bounce and chatter over uneven ground the way straight brushes can. Sealed bearings (ones that come greased and closed) keep dirt and grass dust out of the brush shaft, so it keeps turning freely.

I like fiberglass-reinforced nylon wheels on a machine that lives outdoors, since the glass fiber stiffens them against knocks and a solid wheel can't go flat.

Ohio Steel doesn't publish a wheel size, but a retailer lists 11-inch wheels, and smaller wheels turn more often. At a 3-mph cruise, that puts its 4.5:1 gearing at about 410 brush turns a minute, so its lower ratio costs it less than the number suggests.

Width saves laps on a big lawn, and Brinly's 54-inch sweeper has both the widest path and the largest hopper in this guide, at 54 inches and 30 cubic feet. Brinly says its six Double-Helix brushes (brush strips that twist in a spiral around the shaft) pick up continuously, even through turns. Brinly lists no brush speed, but its 12-inch wheels and 5:1 gearing put it at about 420 turns a minute at a 3 mph cruise, or 560 at the 4-mph cap. A 10-position lock arm sets brush height from about 1/4 inch to 3-1/4 inches, high for deep leaves and low for clippings.

Its clevis (the U-shaped fitting at the front of the hitch that pins to your tractor) mounts two ways, for hitch plates 7 to 10 inches off the ground or 11 to 14, so it rides level on a low hitch or a high one. At nearly 62 inches across, it needs a wide gate and shed door.

Set aside a few hours for assembly. The vinyl hopper is a tight fit, so work it onto the frame a section at a time. With acres to clear and a tractor that fits its hitch, this is the one I'd want. It's the most expensive sweeper in this guide, but the width and the hopper are what the extra money will buy you.

For a lawn that doesn't justify a tractor, Agri-Fab's 26-inch push sweeper is the one I suggest. Its hopper holds 6.2 cubic feet, a little more than one lawn bag, and that’s a lot for a machine this size. Its four brushes are geared at 5:1.

Small wheels help here. Its 9.8-inch wheels turn more often than a tow-behind's, so at a brisk 3-mph walk the brushes spin about 515 times a minute, and they slow down when you do. Brush height adjusts by sliding a tube and locking it with a knob.

At 26 pounds, it's light enough to hang on a garage wall, and the hopper frame comes off if you'd rather store it flat. Upkeep is a few drops of light oil on the brush-shaft bearings twice a year, plus cleaning and lightly greasing the wheel gears every two years.

While it's simple to put together, the plastic body flexes, so be prepared that it pushes hard with the brushes low and needs a flat lawn to pick up well. On a small, level lawn, it's the push sweeper to get.

Scotts' 26-inch push sweeper is the lightest machine recommended here, and it's sized for small jobs like a townhouse lawn, patio, or a driveway after a windy night. Its hopper holds 3.6 bushels, about 4.5 cubic feet, or a little less than one lawn bag, which is the smallest hopper in this guide. The whole sweeper weighs under 22 pounds. The hopper unhooks from the frame so you can carry it to the compost pile and tip it out.

American Lawn Mower Co. makes it under the Scotts name, touting its adjustable height control for moving between grass and hard surfaces. For my own setup, it's the one that I'd likely choose. I move around the country a lot and keep my gear modular, and a sweeper this light and small is the easiest to toss into storage.

Keep in mind that it’s best suited for a light fall of leaves. Plan on more than one pass, and if light debris sails past the hopper, slow your walk until it lands inside. Leave heavy, damp leaf piles to a bigger machine.

Brinly's 42-inch sweeper is built for a thick layer of leaves. Two things lift a deep layer—how many sweeps the brushes make and how high they reach, and it ties for the most in this guide on both.

The brush roll is highly adjustable with 10 labeled height settings. This lets you tailor the sweeper to your desired height based on the density of your leaves and yard and grass type.

While not the lightest tow-behind option in this roundup, the Brinly is on the lighter end of the spectrum, which makes it easier to hitch up to your tractor and also puts less strain on it when full of wet, heavy leaves.

Continuous-contact Double-Helix brushes, geared at 5:1, according to the company, last 2.5 times longer than other brushes. Its clevis fits hitch plates 7 to 10 or 11 to 14 inches off the ground, so it rides level on a low or a high hitch.

Ohio Steel's 50-inch model is sturdy, and its heavy steel build runs across a 50-inch path, which suits a big, open lot with pine needles, cones, and sticks to clear. Against a 42-inch sweeper, the narrowest tow-behind size here, its extra 8 inches cut about one pass in six, so an hour's sweeping takes about 50 minutes.

Its brush shaft runs on sealed ball bearings, so you never have to oil them, while some sweepers' brush shafts need oil every season. The chute (the opening debris flies through into the hopper) is 9 inches across, room for a pine cone or a fist-sized clump of wet clippings. Anything bigger catches on the lip and dams everything behind it.

Its 26-cubic-foot hopper holds about five lawn bags' worth, one of the larger hoppers in this guide, so on a big lot you stop to empty it less often. Behind a 50-inch path, I'd want that capacity, since a wider sweep fills a hopper sooner.

What can be an issue is a hopper bottom that wears through where it meets the ground, so set the hitch height that keeps the hitch tubes level and the bag off the ground. Among sweepers under $400 in this guide, it's the widest.

There are a number of important considerations to make before you purchase a lawn sweeper. Below this section, we’ll cover the following topics in further detail.

Before you shop for a lawn sweeper, walk your property. Note how big your lawn is, whether you have a riding mower or lawn tractor to tow with, how steep the slopes get, how wide your gates are, and what type of debris you’ll be picking up, from leaves and pine needles to cones and sticks.

Consider how you'll use a sweeper, towed or pushed, and if you’re using a riding mower, measure the height of the hitch plate from the ground. Then weigh sweeping width (how wide a strip it clears in one pass) against hopper capacity (how much it holds before you empty it, measured in cubic feet). A wider sweeper will obviously cover more area per pass, and if you have lots of thick, dense leaf cover, you want to make sure you aren’t having to stop and empty the hopper every five seconds.

Look hardest at ground speed and the brush-to-wheel ratio, because together they set how fast the brushes sweep. This in turn affects how much debris is pulled into the hopper in relation to the speed you are moving at. The brushes and how far they adjust come next. You want to make sure you aren’t scalping your lawn with the brushes, but also make sure you can adjust them to a height sufficient to pick up debris. The wheels and weight come last, since they mostly decide grip and the load on your tractor.

A push sweeper suits a small lawn, a patio, or a strip of driveway. A tow-behind needs a tractor of some kind, either a lawn tractor or a zero-turn mower with a rear hitch. If you don't have a riding mower or lawn tractor, check out our buying guides to the best riding lawn mowers and the best zero-turn mowers.

Keep in mind the working capacity of your riding mower. A tow-behind sweeper full of wet, heavy leaves can double its dry weight and put strain on your mower’s transmission. Before you buy, find the towing capacity in your tractor's manual and compare it with the sweeper's loaded weight. One final aspect of weight to factor in is the operator’s weight, which can affect the operating capacity of the mower.

Keep a tow-behind off steep slopes. Each sweeper's operator’s manual details slopes its own way, and there is no universal numbering system. One maker's published figure is 10 degrees, which is a rise of about 2 inches per foot, so read the slope warning for the model you're considering if your lawn has a grade. Your tractor's manual sets a slope limit too, sometimes a lower one for towing, and the lower of the two is the one to follow.

To measure a grade, lay a 2-foot level on the slope pointing downhill, lift the downhill end until the bubble centers, and measure the gap under that end in inches. Half that gap is the rise per foot.

"Fits all tractors" usually means the hitch pin (the steel pin that drops through the sweeper's hitch and the hole in your tractor's hitch plate to join them) fits. What varies is height. Hitch plates sit at different heights on different tractors, and the sweeper has to ride level at whatever height yours sits. A sweeper that tips forward or back changes the height its brushes run at, so they either dig in or skim. Tipped forward, it can also drag the front of its hopper on the ground.

The level check is one you can see. Hitched up on level ground, the hitch tubes should sit roughly level with the ground.

You don't need the sweeper in hand to check fit. Before you order one, park your tractor on level ground, measure from the ground to the bottom of the hitch plate, and compare that with the hitch heights the sweeper's maker lists, checking its manual for where it measures from and how it rounds. If your measurement falls outside every height a maker lists, look for a model whose range covers your dimensions.

Height range is varied with hitch brackets that assemble differently for different heights, a clevis with more than one set of mounting holes, or a hitch with several height positions. Some add an offset hitch, so you can mow and sweep in one pass.

Push sweepers usually cover a path of about 2 feet, and tow-behinds run wider, some to 54 inches. A 54-inch path covers more than a quarter more ground per pass than a 42-inch one, which saves more than one pass in five. On a lawn that takes 20 passes with a 42-inch sweeper, a 54-inch one finishes in about 16, which means less time on the seat and fewer turns at the ends.

Wider is harder to steer around beds and trees, and a tow-behind's frame can be close to a foot wider than its path. Makers list the assembled width in their specifications, so check it, and the height, against your gate and your shed door.

Hopper capacity is measured in cubic feet, and a 39-gallon lawn bag holds a bit over 5 cubic feet. Hoppers run from a few cubic feet on a small push sweeper to 30 on some large tow-behinds, and a bigger one means fewer trips to empty it. Treat the numbers as approximate, since retailer listings don't always match the maker's figure.

Tow-behinds usually empty from the seat, with a rope or a handle that tips the hopper. Push sweepers empty by lifting the hopper off the frame or tipping the whole machine forward. Given the choice, I prefer a dump handle. A rigid handle gives you leverage on a heavy, wet load, and there's no rope to tangle in the brushes. If you get a rope dump, fasten the rope or its pull handle to the tractor and cut off any loose tail, so nothing trails into the brushes or wheels. On a push sweeper, I like a hopper that lifts off, so I can carry it straight to the compost pile.

Because the wheels drive the brushes, your ground speed sets your sweeping power. Drive too slowly, and debris won't carry all the way to the back of the hopper. Drive too fast, and you risk damaging the wheels and gears.

Manufacturers generally cap ground speed between 4 and 6 mph. What I have found to be a smart rule of thumb is to start at a 3 mph cruising pace (covering about 44 feet in 10 seconds), and then gradually speed up, staying under the maker's limit, until the material is reliably hitting the back of the hopper. A 4-mph cap works out to about 59 feet in 10 seconds, and 6 mph to 88 feet. Stop now and then and look at the load. If it heaps up at the front of the hopper, the brushes need more speed, and if light debris sails over the top, slow down.

With your top speed limited, the real sweeping power comes down to the sweeper's gearing and wheel diameter. Manufacturers express this as a ratio, such as 4.5:1.

If you tow a sweeper with 12-inch wheels at 3 mph, the wheels turn at roughly 84 revolutions per minute (rpm). With a 4.5:1 ratio, those brushes are spinning at about 380 rpm. Bump that gearing up to 5.6:1 on the exact same wheels, and your brushes will spin at about 470 rpm.

Sweepers carry anywhere from two to six brushes on the shaft, and more brushes mean more sweeps for every turn. Some makers twist their brushes into a spiral or a double helix along the shaft, so part of each brush is always touching the grass and the sweeper runs smoother over bumps.

Brushes wear out, though, and can be costly to replace, which is why some warranties exclude them. Along with checking whether the warranty covers brush replacement, check that replacements are sold for the model you buy.

Brush height is a buying question, too. Some sweepers publish their range, about 1/4 inch to just over 3 inches, with a chart matching settings to conditions. Others give only a target of about 1/2 inch into the grass and no top height. For a deep layer of leaves, look for a range that reaches past 2 inches, which generally covers heavy leaves.

A sweeper's wheels turn its brushes, so a wheel that slides instead of rolling slows the sweep, and grip on the grass is part of pickup. Most sweeper wheels are semi-pneumatic tires (rubber tires that aren't inflated) or hard nylon or plastic, often reinforced with glass fiber, and none of these can go flat.

Diameter also matters. At the same ground speed, a smaller wheel turns more often, so it spins the brushes faster at the same gearing. At 3 mph, a 12-inch wheel geared at 5:1 turns its brushes about 420 times a minute, and a 10-inch wheel with the same gearing about 500.

On a push sweeper, weight is what you shove and lift. On a tow-behind, empty weight is only the starting point, and the loaded weight is what has to stay under your tractor's rated towing capacity.

Check the brush height first. Brushes set too low drag in the grass, and the wheels skip and slip instead of turning them. Stop the mower safely and go check the sweeper. Then raise the brushes one setting and try again. If the wheels still skid, stop again and look for something wrapped around the brush shaft or jammed in a wheel. If you have to pull a wheel to clear it, follow the owner's manual and take off one side at a time, since the left and right wheel gears often aren't interchangeable.

Some, but it isn't the best job for one. Wet leaves mat down and weigh far more than dry ones, which adds to what your tractor has to pull and stop, and dropping the brushes to dig into a wet mat only makes the wheels skid. Pushing into a wet mat of leaves loads the machine the same way, and a sweeper that already needs a flat lawn or several passes on dry leaves will struggle more with wet ones. Skip the job entirely on a muddy lawn. Sweep after the surface dries if you can, and empty the hopper right away. Damp material left in the hopper damages the bag, and a stored load of damp clippings can heat up enough to catch fire.

Keep the brushes as high as they'll still sweep, which cuts drag and wear on the brushes and wheels. Agri-Fab's 44-inch manual, for example, calls for oiling the wheel bearings once a season, lubricating the brush shaft at the start and end of the season, and greasing the wheel gears every two years. Some manuals call for white lithium grease on the wheel bearings and gears, and others call for light oil, so check the owner's manual before using anything.

Store the sweeper empty and clean with the brushes off the ground. When the brushes leave debris behind at a setting that previously worked fine, it's time to replace them.

#6471. The Best Little Gifts Your Holiday Party Host Will Actually Want

Don’t show up empty-handed or with a cheap bottle of wine — bring status cocktail cherries, a beeswax candle, or a painterly placemat

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

A good host is always thinking of others, whether it’s by making guests feel welcome, accommodating everyone’s diets, or setting an Instagram-worthy tablescape to make the night feel extra special. But the holiday season is an opportunity to flip the script and show the host you’re thinking of them, too. Bringing them a gift is the cardinal way to thank the host for all their thoughtful work. The only question remains: what to give?

For those who delight in trotting out their special dinnerware for guests, there’s a world of creative and whimsical gifts out there, even if it seems like they already have the entire CB2 catalog. And if that is the case, this just means you, as the gift-giver, can allow them to indulge in the things they typically would not. Take, for instance, some unique vintage shot glasses, intricately carved chopsticks, and pearl cocktail picks. Not only do these playful takes on essentials inspire joy, but they’re also sure to be conversation starters for future gatherings. And, as the bestower of the new treasured piece, you just might secure yourself the invite for the next one.

You can never have enough serving utensils if you love to host. That moment when you toss your pasta salad, plate everyone’s green beans, or dole out your main dish is an opportunity to flex some of your more decorative yet functional kitchen tools. This ethereal stainless steel set from Leif boasts pewter star-shaped handles with sea glass.

Even Diaspora Spice Co.’s everyday spices come in bold, ready-to-gift packaging, but the equitable spice company’s new holiday spice sampler gift box is an extra colorful treat for the senses. The bundle includes samples of its beloved Nandini coriander, a rare Ceylon cinnamon, a Himalayan foothills-sourced pink garlic powder, and several more spices to inspire your host.

When it comes to gift-giving, we believe in working smarter, not harder. Case in point: Buy a set of nice-looking vintage glasses — these are labeled shot glasses by the seller, but they’re just as nice for sipping cordials — and rather than giving one lovely host a set of eight, split them up into pairs or fours and use them for multiple gifting situations. There’s always a use for little glasses like this (and they’re pretty enough to display, too).

It’s pretty fun to use a posh plaid napkin when you’re digging into some quiche or sipping on mulled wine.

It’s always fun to kick off an evening of cocktails with a caviar bump, which is what makes this Imperia Caviar bundle such a gift for the avid party host. The 30-gram tin of royal ossetra comes with a mother-of-pearl spoon and a caviar tin opener in a velvet bag, and the bundle’s compact size means you can simply slide it into your purse or jacket on the way to the function (unlike a heavy bottle of wine or olive oil, which would likely need their owns bags).

It really has been the year of the dirty martini. For those who are building a bar cart (or want to start), getting a couple of sets of proper cocktail picks can be a game-changer. Nothing wrong with a traditional wood toothpick, of course, but it really does add a lot of pizzazz to a martini to bite the olives off a pearl-emblazoned skewer.

Swooning will abound once people get a look at these beautiful walnut chopsticks featuring inlaid geometric designs. Another great example of “practical, but nicer to look at than what you might get for yourself.” Plus, you can grab a set of five on sale right now for under $20.

When it comes to cocktail cherries, one brand truly reigns supreme: Luxardo, which has been making candied cherries soaked in marasca syrup for 120 years. A classic for a reason!

Jonathan Adler is another designer to keep tabs on when it comes to playful but elevated home decor. This set of Matisse-esque coasters also has a slight lip to keep condensation from spilling, and would be prime for serving up lychee martinis the next time you gather with friends. Snag them while they’re 40% off for Black Friday.

Halen Môn is a salt nerd’s dream. The organic, hand-harvested sea salt hails from the tides of the Isle of Anglesey in Wales (Halen is Welsh for salt; Môn is Welsh for Anglesey), and has earned numerous awards for its subtle crunch and crisp mineral flavor. Any host would be thrilled to receive a bag of the stuff, but this gift set combines the salt with a charming ceramic cellar and spoon.

Matches are always a solid host gift, and a small but useful present that’s made all the better with cool packaging. The lifestyle brand State the Label, for example, has housed its matches in a folk art-inspired cottage (the striker paper is on the bottom of the house).

Those who like to entertain likely appreciate a good placemat. This set of two block-printed placemats from West Elm puts a romantic spin on the dining-table staple with painterly tones and bright hues. Who wouldn’t love to receive these dreamy accents?

Is your host a lover of ice-cold martinis? Perfect gift incoming: Quincy’s fabulous olives, which have superb flavor and are ratioed with drink-perfect brine to make exactly 14 dirty martinis per jar.

Scents are tricky. Unless you really know your host, refrain from gifting them scented candles, and opt for a beeswax pillar candle instead; they can light it sans candelabra (unless you’re sure that they own one and prefer tapers) by simply placing it on a small plate. Above all, beeswax candles make a wonderful dining companion, because they don’t emit the same stuffy, paraffin wax-based smoke as non-beeswax candles.

Sometimes, brevity is wit. Give it to someone who means business, or orders the business women special.

We all love a little Le Creuset in our kitchens, but a Dutch oven isn’t in the price range for what we’d consider an easy host gift. Enter the butter dish, a fabulous little thing to present and say “I brought you something,” presented with a kiss on the cheek and maybe a bouquet of flowers or bottle of wine.

#6470. Feast Your Eyes on Uranus at Opposition This Thanksgiving 2026

Why late November 2026 is prime Uranus observing season.

The outer planets are ever so slowly starting to sneak back into the evening sky this month. First, Saturn crossed this mark last month on October 4th, then Neptune followed suit on September 26th. Now, the planet Uranus makes the transition, crossing opposition next week.

Opposition occurs on November 25th. On âU.S. Thanksgiving-eve.â We say âoppositionâ for an outer planet, as a point at which it seems to rise âoppositeâ to the setting Sun as seen from our Earthly vantage point. Orbiting the Sun at a leisurely pace once every 84 years, Uranus has a synodic period of 370 days, meaning oppositions for the planet only slide forward about five days each year. This year sees Uranus reach opposition in the astronomical constellation of Taurus, between the Hyades and the Pleiades open star clusters.

Uranus at opposition for 2026. Credit: Stellarium.

Shout out to the Full November Beaver Moon nearby on the same date as opposition 2026, fresh off of occulting the Pleiades for the Arctic on November 24th.

Uranus reached aphelion 20 Astronomical Units (AU) from the Sun in 2009, and is now inbound toward perihelion 18.3 AU distant in 2050. In 2033, Uranus will pass the point in Taurus where it was discovered by Sir William Herschel on March 13th, 1781, between the horns of the Bull very near the constellation's border with Gemini. Uranus made spurious appearances on star charts of the era at least 20 times prior to discovery.

The discovery position of Uranus. Credit: Dave Dickinson/Starry Night

Uranus reached its southernmost point in the sky in 2007, and crossed the celestial equator multiple times from 2011-2012. Uranus crosses the ecliptic plane northward in 2029. Uranus reaches its northernmost in 2032, and then begins the long trek southward. The Moon wonât resume occulting the planet Uranus again until a cycle starting on September 29th, 2029.

The Moon occults the Pleiades on November 24th. Credit: Occult 4.2.

Observing +5.5 magnitude Uranus is as easy as sweeping the suspect field at low power, and looking for a blue-green âstarâ that obstinately refuses to snap into focus. To my eye, Uranus looks like a tiny planetary nebula or perhaps a distant fuzzy comet. In fact, thatâs exactly what Herschel thought heâd first discovered, back on that fortuitous night in 1781. He later correctly realized after following the new object for several nights that it was a distant, and therefore intrinsically large object far out in the solar system beyond Saturn, then thought to mark its outer boundary. All of this happened in his backyard garden in Bath, England. We can, however, be thankful that the name âGeorgeâ that Herschel proposed to honor his benefactor King George the III didnât stick (!)

One of Herschel's speculum metal mirrors and telescopes at the London Science Museum. Credit: Dave Dickinson

Can you see Uranus with the naked eye? Topping +6th magnitude near opposition, itâs knocking on naked eye visibility from a good dark sky site. At the eyepiece, Uranus only shows a 4â disk at around opposition, barely resolvable with a telescope and tough to tease out detail.

A fine capture of Uranus from 2017. Credit: Szabolcs Nagy.

Uranus is tipped over 98 degrees (prograde) on its side, the result of some ancient encounter with another large body early in the solar systemâs history. Currently, weâre staring nearly directly at the rotational (north?) pole/hemisphere of the planet, which will be pointed nearly directly towards us in late 2029.

Though Uranus has 29 known moons, only five are within potential reach of amateur telescopes, with +13.9 magnitude Titania being the brightest. Orbiting Uranus once every 8.7 days, Titania reaches a greatest elongation of 28â from Uranus. We once saw a sharp view of the moons observing through the Steward Observatoryâs Kuiper Telescope in the Santa Catalina Mountains outside of Tucson, Arizona. They were a surprisingly easy catch through the enormous 61â telescope.

A fine capture of Uranus and its moons. Credit: Ralph Smyth.

A planetarium program such as Stellarium and Starry Night will show you the current orientation of the moons of Uranus, to help parse them out from any nearby background stars.

The orbits an orientations of the major Uranian moons. Credit: Starry Night.

The orbits of the moons are currently nearly perpendicular to our view in 2026, though theyâre edge-on and can transit Uranus as seen from our view once every 42 years. This last occurred on 2006-2009, and will happen again starting around 2048.

Hubble captures a shadow transit of Ariel in 2006. Credit: NASA/ESA/L. Sromovsky/University of Wisconsin.

Will we return to Uranus in the coming years? To date, only one mission has seen the planet close up: NASAâs Voyager 2, which flew past Uranus and its moons in 1986. Cassini-style orbiters have been proposed, though such a mission would be a lengthy affair, needing to first make the trip to the distant ice giant then slow down to enter orbit. As it stands, such a mission would be feasible for around the 2040s time frame.

JWST's view of Uranus and its rings. Credit: NASA/JWST.

Certainly, Uranus calls out for a dedicated mission. But you can explore the planet yourself tonight as it nears opposition for 2026.

#6469. This Dietary Supplement Could Have Potential Brain Benefits, Study Finds

A supplement containing a substance naturally made by gut bacteria increased blood flow to a memory-related brain region in adults with obesity, raising new questions about its potential benefits.

When the brain works harder, it needs more blood to supply oxygen and nutrients. For people with obesity, changes in blood vessel function can affect circulation, raising questions about how well the brain responds to these demands. A new clinical trial suggests a dietary supplement could help increase blood flow during mental activity, although researchers have yet to show that it improves memory.

Researchers at the University of Oklahoma investigated urolithin A, a substance produced when certain gut bacteria break down compounds found in foods such as strawberries, pomegranates, and walnuts. The amount people naturally produce varies, and existing research suggests that production declines with age and increasing body mass index. Urolithin A is also available as a dietary supplement.

In the randomized clinical trial, published in JAMA Network Open, 50 adults with obesity, ages 40 to 64, received either 1,000 milligrams of urolithin A daily or a placebo for four weeks.

Participants taking the supplement showed a greater increase in blood flow to the brain while completing a challenging memory task. The difference was especially noticeable in the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, an area involved in holding and using information over short periods. However, researchers found no significant improvements in blood vessel function in the arm or performance on memory tests.

“The brain needs an adequate supply of blood to meet the demands of mental activity,” said first author Ana Clara da Costa Pinaffi Langley, Ph.D., an assistant professor in the Department of Nutritional Sciences at the OU College of Allied Health on the OU Harold Hamm Health Campus. “We found that urolithin A increased blood flow to the brain during a memory task, suggesting the supplement may help the brain meet its increased need for oxygen and nutrients when it is working harder. We plan to conduct more research to understand what this finding means for brain health.”

According to the researchers, this is the first human study to report an effect of urolithin A on blood vessel function in the brain. The supplement was well-tolerated, although the trial involved relatively few participants at a single research site. Longer studies with larger groups will be needed to determine whether the changes in blood flow lead to lasting health benefits.

“These findings offer an interesting starting point for understanding how urolithin A affects the brain,” said study co-author Andriy Yabluchanskiy, M.D., Ph.D., an associate professor in the Department of Neurosurgery at the OU College of Medicine. “Although we saw increased blood flow to the brain during mental activity, participants did not demonstrate measurable improvements in memory or attention. Future studies will need to determine whether taking the supplement for a longer period leads to meaningful improvements in cognitive function or other health benefits.”

The researchers ultimately hope to find ways to help people maintain their cognitive health as they age.

“The idea is to mitigate cognitive decline,” Langley said. “We want to expand the time that people are living healthier lives.”

Reference: “Urolithin A and Endothelial and Cerebrovascular Function in Middle-Aged Adults With Obesity: A Randomized Clinical Trial” by Ana Clara da Costa Pinaffi-Langley, Rafal Gulej, Zalan Kaposzta, Zsofia Szarvas, Ali Shahriari, Henry Kinnard, Bryan Ticer, Camila B. Pinto, Peter Mukli, Mihaly Muranyi, Cheryl Adams, Jeng Kong, Leah Anderson, Stefano Tarantini, Yan Daniel Zhao, Norman G. Hord and Andriy Yabluchanskiy, 9 October 2026, JAMA Network Open. DOI: 10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.38047

Research reported in this publication was supported by the American Heart Association (grant No. 24DIVSUP1282484 awarded to Dr da Costa Pinaffi-Langley) and the Reynolds Foundation.

A mysterious bronze foot found in a bog was likely once part of a monumental statue of the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius, who tried to conquer Scotland.

All that remains of a larger-than-life statue of the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius once erected in Scotland is a lower right leg. Experts have now reconstructed what the entire sculpture looked like but are still unsure why it was carefully dismantled over 1,800 years ago.

The gold-covered bronze foot and calf, also known as the Milsington leg, was discovered in a bog in 1820, according to a Nov. 12 statement from National Museums Scotland. It is the only example of a monumental Roman emperor statue ever found in Scotland and was likely made around A.D. 140.

Initially, experts thought the bronze statue had been looted from York, England, which was founded by the Romans in A.D. 71 as the town of Eboracum. But as research into the Roman frontier advanced over the years, it became clear that equestrian statues were often set up in forts along the border of the Roman Empire.

This lower leg, experts now believe, originally came from an equestrian statue of Emperor Antoninus Pius that was similar to the famous statue of Marcus Aurelius in Rome.

Antoninus Pius was Roman emperor from A.D. 138 to 161, succeeding Hadrian, who had built an enormous wall to defend the northernmost limit of the Roman Empire. To add to Rome's territory, Antoninus Pius directed the imperial governor of Roman Britain to move north, invade southern Scotland and build a second wall, called the Antonine Wall. But that wall was left undefended after Antoninus Pius died, and the Romans retreated from Scotland.

During that retreat, the Romans may have dismantled any valuable statues that they had set up, according to the statement. An examination of the Milsington leg ahead of a new exhibition showed that the bronze had no cut marks, suggesting it was removed carefully and not "brutally hacked off."

"This contrasts with examples of statues being deliberately destroyed after a battle, when an emperor's memory was condemned, or when they were chopped up for scrap," according to National Museums Scotland.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

With the Scottish provenance firmly established, National Museums Scotland curators were able to learn more about Antoninus Pius and his approach to imperial expansion.

"This really turns on its head our understanding of Rome's second attempt at conquering Scotland," Fraser Hunter, principal curator of prehistoric art and Roman archaeology at National Museums Scotland, said in the statement. "This was a big deal for the Emperor, something which was worth celebrating."

But while the boot-clad bronze leg provides a glimpse into the monuments that may have graced southern Scotland nearly two millennia ago, it raises an important question for Hunter: Where is the rest of the statue?

The Milsington leg, the Inveresk Mithras altars and other Roman-period finds are on display beginning Nov. 14 in the exhibit "Roman Scotland: Life on the Edge of Empire" at the National Museum of Scotland.

#6467. Euclid's Hunt for Strong Gravitational Lenses is Off to a Strong Start

If dark matter and dark energy were a part of our everyday lives, we would live in a perpetual state of dumbfoundedness. Imagine living in a world where 95% of the matter and energy were invisible and undetectable. It would be impossible to make sense of our surroundings.

Luckily, dark energy and dark matter aren't everyday concerns. They're interesting problems for people who are intellectally curious about Nature. But for physicisits, the questions surrounding dark matter and dark energy are much more acute. Some of them dedicate their entire lives to understanding dark matter and dark energy. They design and build special telescopes, instruments, and spacecraft to make progress toward an answer.

One of the spacecraft astrophysicists built to study dark matter and energy is the European Space Agencyâs Euclid space telescope.

This artist's illustration shows the Euclid Space Telescope doing its thing in its halo orbit at L2. The telescope is on a six-year mission to create a 3D map of the sky, revealing how dark energy and dark matter shape the Universe. Image Credit: By ESA, CC BY-SA IGO 3.0, CC BY-SA 3.0 igo, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/128347141

Dark matter and dark energy are foundational in our Universe. Dark matter doesn't interact with any light, but it's clearly there. It's some form of mass, but we don't know what. Dark matter is a placeholder term.

Dark energy is another placeholder term. It describes the force driving the expansion of the Universe. Like dark matter, we can measure its effect, but we don't know what it really is. And the puzzling thing is that dark matter and dark energy make up most of the Universe.

âIt turns out, the stuff humans are made of is relatively rare in the universe,â said Dr. Douglas Scott, professor at the University of BC's department of physics and astronomy (PHAS) and member of the Euclid collaboration. âAnd what dominates â dark matter and dark energy â is invisible so we're not used to dealing with it. But it makes the universe what it is, it drives how the universe expands and what the past and future of the universe will be. Where did these things come from? What properties do they have? Euclidâs data gives us the potential to answer those questions.â

This image reminds us that Euclid does more than study dark matter and dark energy. It's a powerful camera, after all, and can also capture stunning images of regular, baryonic matter, the kind that stars, people, and planets are made of. This image is from Euclid's Early Release Observations, and shows the Messier 78 star formation region about 1300 light years away in Orion. This is the first time Messier 78 has been imaged with such width and depth, hallmarks of Euclid's observations. Image Credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, image processing by J.-C. Cuillandre (CEA Paris-Saclay), G. Anselmi

Euclid launched in July 2023 and orbits the Sun-Earth Lagrange point 2 (L2), roughly 1.5 million kilometers away from Earth, a popular spot for space telescopes. From that perch, it uses its wide-angle, 600-megapixel camera to capture visible light, and a photometer and a near-infrared spectrometer to measure the redshift of about 10 billion sources out to redshift 2. That's roughly equivalent to about 10 billion years ago, or about 3.7 billion years after the Big Bang.

Among these sources, Euclid is especially interested in strong gravitational lenses. These are massive objects like galaxies, galaxy clusters, and dark matter halos. These objects can magnify background objects that are otherwise beyond observing. But they're critical for mapping dark matter itself, because their lensing effect is based on the total mass of these objects, not just their visible mass. So strong gravitational lenses are a way to measure the presence of dark matter. But they're not easy to find.

Euclid delivered its first data release on November 12th, called DR-1 Foundation, and it holds a whopping 1.7 million gigabytes of data. The data revealed almost 5% of the night sky in 13 months of observations. That data holds 900 million galaxies, and 60 million quasars, which are the extremely luminous cores of far-away galaxies. Euclid also found 15,000 new strong gravitational lens candidates, a massive increase in the potential number.

"Strong lenses have been difficult to find â the odds were about one in 10,000,â said Hrishabh Srivastava, doctoral student in the UBC department of physics and astronomy (PHAS). âBefore Euclid, we had less than a thousand confirmed strong lenses. Now we have 15,000 new candidates.â

There's more than one type of gravitational lens. This is a collage of some of the different types of strong gravitational lenses Euclid has found so far. The top row shows, from left to right: a classic galaxyâgalaxy lens, an Einstein ring in a face-on spiral lens, and an inclined dusty disc lens galaxy. The middle row shows an edge-on dusty lens galaxy, a lensed galaxy with visible star-forming regions, and a compound lens.The bottom row shows a galaxy group lens, a lensed quasar, and a galaxy group lens. Image Credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, image processing by N. Lines and T. Li. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO or ESA Standard Licence

Overall, Euclid is expected to find more than 100,000 strong lenses over the course of its nominal six year mission. That would increase the number of known strong lenses by two orders of magnitude, a transformational advance for dark matter science.

âI like to call these gravitational lenses ânature's own magnifying glassesâ to probe the dark matter distribution of our universe,â said Srivastava.

Strong gravitational lensing is an important tool, but so is weak gravitational lensing. They can be used together to build a fuller picture of dark matter and dark energy. The weak gravitational lensing signature is most apparent around massive galaxy clusters. Since weak gravitational lensing extends beyond a cluster's virial radius, it can help constrain a cluster's overall mass.

Finding huge numbers of gravitational lenses is clearly important in the quest to understand the Universe, but Euclid has other tasks, too. It will slowly build a 3D map of the Universe that covers greater than one-third of the sky. This map will comprise the actual tool used to measure dark matter and dark energy. The map will show how matter is distributed, and then that map can be tested against models of the Universe, especially Lambda-Cold Dark Matter, which is the standard Big Bang model of cosmology.

Lambda-CDM predicts how matter, including dark matter, is spread throughout the Universe, and how its structure is shaped by dark energy, which drives the Universe's expansion. So Euclid's 3D map can test both facets of Lambda-CDM: dark matter and dark energy. Dark energy is directly tested, and dark matter is tested more indirectly.

Euclid's test of Lambda-CDM won't be in one big grand finale, where physicists around the world wait with bated breath to find out the answer. The test is ongoing. Each new data release will generate rounds of new research, as physicists and cosmologists dig into it. It'll be fuel for the different lines of detailed research that different teams of scientists pursue. It's like a process of elimination. Eventually, hopefully, the possible answers and explanations for dark matter and dark energy will be constrained and refined until only one is left standing.

Then, in all likelihood, Nobel prizes will be awarded.

But that won't be the end of cosmology. New questions will arise, intellectual curiosity will be piqued in new ways, and the quest to understand the Universe will continue.

But Euclid and its 3D map will be in history of science textbooks for a long time.

#6466. The 8 Best MagSafe-Compatible Portable Chargers For On-the-Go Charging

A magnetic battery pack snaps onto your phone and keeps it going all day, no cable needed.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

A good portable battery pack keeps your phone alive through long travel days, packed schedules, and everything in between. If you have a MagSafe iPhone (the iPhone 12 or newer) or an Android phone that supports Qi2, a magnetic pack is the most convenient choice: it clicks onto the back of our favorite phones and starts charging, with no cable to carry.

These packs have come a long way. The first MagSafe batteries charged at a sluggish 5 watts. Many of today’s Qi2 packs deliver 15 watts, and the newest Qi2.2 models reach 25 watts while fitting twice the battery into a body about as thin as your phone. Plenty also add built-in cables, kickstands, and fast USB-C ports for topping up a second device.

All that progress means more choice, and more spec sheets that look the same. We’ve rounded up the best MagSafe portable chargers you can buy right now, from slim everyday packs to fast premium picks, so you can find the right one for you.

I’ve used MagSafe battery packs with my iPhone for years. The ones I kept using had a strong magnet and enough battery to get through a day away from an outlet. Most picks here support Qi2, which charges at 15 watts, or Qi2.2, which charges at up to 25 watts on an iPhone 16 or newer. I looked for packs around 10,000 mAh, since that size can charge most phones and then some. I also looked for a USB-C port of 30 watts or more, so the pack itself recharges quickly.

The INIU SnapGo Air packs a 10,000 mAh battery into a body just half an inch thick. It supports Qi2.2 wireless charging at up to 25 watts, and INIU says it can take an iPhone 17 Pro from empty to 50 percent in 33 minutes. That top speed works on the iPhone 16 Plus, 16 Pro Max, and newer models running iOS 26. The iPhone 12 through 15 charge at 15 watts.

For faster charging, plug in the USB-C cable attached to the pack. It delivers 45 watts, which INIU says charges an iPhone 17 Pro from 20 to 78 percent in 25 minutes. The pack also supports passthrough charging, so when it’s plugged into the wall, it charges itself and your phone at the same time. The cable doubles as a lanyard and detaches, and a digital display shows the exact battery percentage.

For $23, the LISEN Ultra Slim charges at the same 15-watt Qi2 speed as the Anker Nano, which costs more than twice as much. It’s 0.38 inches thick and weighs 3.6 ounces. LISEN says it charges an iPhone 17 to about 50 percent in an hour. Past 75 percent, it slows down on purpose to protect your phone’s battery.

LISEN lists the battery as 5,000 mAh but gives a rated capacity of 3,000 mAh. The rated number is closer to how much charge reaches your phone, so plan on a partial top-up rather than a full charge. Plugged in with a USB-C cable, it charges at up to 20 watts. It only works with the iPhone 12 through 18. LISEN recommends pairing it with a MagSafe case, since other cases can cause overheating.

The Anker MagGo 2 Pro costs twice as much as our top pick, and most of that extra money goes toward cooling. Wireless charging creates heat, and many packs slow down as they warm up. This one has a small fan and layers of graphene that Anker says keep it cool, so it can stay at its top speed of 25 watts for longer. It’s rated to charge an iPhone 18 Pro to 50 percent in 25 minutes.

Its USB-C port runs at 45 watts in both directions, fast enough to refill the pack from 0 to 80 percent in under an hour. A screen shows battery level, charging speed, temperature, and battery health, and a built-in stand folds out to prop up your phone for video.

UGREEN says the MagFlow can fully charge an iPhone 17 Pro Max more than 2.5 times before it needs a wall outlet. At 20,000 mAh, it holds twice as much as our top pick, and a digital display on the side shows how much is left.

Wireless charging runs at up to 25 watts, which UGREEN says gets an iPhone 18 Pro to 50 percent in 30 minutes. The built-in USB-C cable on the side doubles as a carry strap, and UGREEN rates it for more than 10,000 bends. The pack's USB-C port charges at up to 45 watts and refills the pack at the same rate, and a USB-A port lets you plug in older cables.

Fitting twice the battery makes the MagFlow heavier and thicker than our 10,000 mAh picks. That makes it harder to slip into a pocket, and it adds noticeable weight to the back of your phone while it charges.

The Sharge Icemag 3 has a see-through case that shows the internal components, plus a subtle RGB light. It charges wirelessly at up to 25 watts using Qi2.2, and Sharge says that gets an iPhone 17 Pro from zero to 50 percent in 30 minutes. A built-in fan keeps the pack’s surface cool, so charging stays steady. The fan doesn't lower your phone's temperature.

A fold-out kickstand holds your phone upright or sideways for video calls. The built-in USB-C cable and a second USB-C port sit on the side, so you can still hold your phone normally while it charges via cable. Unlike the previous two picks, the wired connection charges a bit slower at up to 35 watts.

The Anker Nano Magnetic Power Bank is 0.34 inches thick and weighs 4.3 ounces, about a third less than the INIU. Because it’s Qi2 rather than Qi2.2, it charges wirelessly at up to 15 watts. Its 5,000 mAh battery is half the size of our other picks, but that makes it more pocketable.

Anker’s own figures show it charging an iPhone 17 to 85 percent and an iPhone 17 Pro Max to 63 percent with the phone in Low Power Mode. That makes it a backup for a long day, not a full refill. A graphene layer inside spreads heat, so the pack stays cool. The USB-C port charges a phone at up to 20 watts, and the pack comes in six colors with a two-year warranty.

If you take your phone on hikes or to the beach, the TORRAS MiniMag Pro is the magnetic pack to get. TORRAS rates it IP54, so it should be protected from dust and splashes from any direction; however, it isn't meant for underwater use.

Inside is a semi-solid-state battery that TORRAS says passed puncture, crush, and drop testing. An aluminum frame wraps the body, and a digital display shows the remaining charge.

Wireless charging tops out at 15 watts, and with a USB-C cable, the pack charges a phone at up to 30 watts. With passthrough charging, one cable plugged into the wall charges the pack and your phone together overnight.

The iPhone Air gave up battery capacity to get its thin body, and Apple’s answer is a battery pack built just for it. On the Air, Apple says it adds up to 65 percent more charge. The pack is shaped around the Air's camera bump, so it doesn't fit other iPhones.

While it fits the Air perfectly, wireless charging tops out at 12 watts. For faster top-ups, leave the battery attached and plug your phone into a 25-watt or higher adapter; the phone and battery charge together. The pack also has no battery readout. Instead, a single hidden light glows green while it charges and orange when it runs low.

Check the box for Qi2 or Qi2.2. Qi2 packs charge wirelessly at up to 15 watts, while Qi2.2 packs reach 25 watts, which Apple says can bring an iPhone 17 Pro to 50 percent in about 30 minutes. Packs sold as "magnetic" or "MagSafe-compatible" without Qi2 certification often charge at just 7.5 watts.

The iPhone 12 through 15 charge at 15 watts even on a Qi2.2 pack, so if you own one, a cheaper Qi2 pack will charge it just as fast. For 25 watts, you need a newer phone, such as the iPhone 16 series and later models running iOS 26.

For most people, I recommend a pack around 10,000 mAh, the size of our top pick. Don't expect two full charges, though. Some power is lost in the battery cells and in the circuits that convert it for your phone. Anker says its 10,000 mAh pack delivers about 5,500 to 6,500 mAh to your phone. A 5,000 mAh pack is thinner and lighter, but it works best as a midday top-up. A 20,000 mAh pack can recharge a phone several times, but the extra weight and thickness make it harder to carry.

Every magnetic pack has a USB-C port, which refills the pack and can charge a second device. Look for one rated at 30 watts or higher. At 45 watts, a pack can fast-charge a phone over a cable and refill itself quickly. Anker says the MagGo 2 Pro reaches 80 percent in 52 minutes. If you want to charge the pack and your phone overnight from one outlet, look for passthrough charging.

Faster wireless charging produces more heat, and many packs cut their charging speed as they warm up. The Anker MagGo 2 Pro and Sharge Icemag 3 use small fans to maintain speed. Thick cases trap heat too. Anker recommends a case no thicker than 2.4 mm.

Most magnetic packs are designed around iPhones. Anker and LISEN don't recommend their packs for Android phones, and Apple’s own battery fits only the iPhone Air. If you use a case, make sure it's MagSafe-compatible, or the magnet won't hold well.

#6464. Scientists Uncover a Natural Molecule That Makes Muscles Stronger and More Resistant to Fatigue

A molecule released during exercise could help muscles fight the weakness and fatigue that make staying active so difficult for many people with type 2 diabetes.

Exercise does more than burn calories and build strength. It triggers a complex series of chemical signals that help muscles become stronger, more efficient, and more resistant to fatigue. But for people with type 2 diabetes, muscle weakness and declining endurance can make it difficult to stay active, creating a cycle that may worsen their condition.

Researchers at the University of Leeds have identified a molecule that could help break that cycle. Known as L-β-aminoisobutyric acid (L-BAIBA), this naturally occurring compound acts as a key signal that helps muscles respond to exercise.

The researchers found that it plays an important role in reshaping muscle fibers, improving metabolism, and enhancing strength and endurance. It also helps protect muscles against damage and weakness associated with type 2 diabetes, raising the possibility of future treatments that preserve muscle function and make physical activity more manageable.

Published in Nature Communications, the research was led by Professor Lee Roberts and funded by Diabetes UK and the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council (BBRSC).

Exercise prompts muscles to adapt so they can better handle future demands. Scientists are still investigating how the body coordinates these adaptations, and Roberts’ team wanted to understand whether those processes could inform treatments for chronic disease.

L-BAIBA was already known for its effects on metabolism. In research published in 2014, Roberts helped show that BAIBA could boost the fat-burning effects of exercise. L-BAIBA is now sold as a nutritional supplement, although the new findings concern its biological role and potential as a future treatment.

The latest study extends that earlier work by identifying L-BAIBA as a regulator of muscle remodeling. Roberts, Professor of Molecular Physiology and Metabolism at the University of Leeds, said, “Our research identifies L-BAIBA as an exercise-induced signal that helps muscles adapt, improve their metabolic capacity and ability to contract, and ultimately enhances physical performance.

“This gives us exciting new insight into how exercise benefits the body and highlights a promising target for future therapies aimed at preserving muscle function in chronic conditions such as diabetes.”

L-BAIBA’s protective effects could be particularly valuable for people with type 2 diabetes, who can experience muscle loss, declining strength, and impaired metabolism. Weakness and fatigue can make exercise harder, creating a barrier to an activity that helps manage the condition. Future treatments targeting L-BAIBA could help people stay active by improving their muscles’ resistance to fatigue.

The need for better ways to manage type 2 diabetes is growing as the condition becomes more common among younger adults. Cases among people under 40 are now increasing faster than those among people over 40. The condition can lead to serious complications, including heart attacks and strokes, and develops through a complex mix of factors, with risk influenced by age, ethnicity, genetics, and living with overweight or obesity.

Anna Morris, Assistant Director of Research Strategy and Partnership at Diabetes UK, said: “Exercise plays an important role in managing type 2 diabetes, but for many people muscle weakness and fatigue can make staying active a real challenge. This research helps us better understand how muscles adapt to exercise and identifies a potential new target for improving muscle health. While these findings are still at an early stage, they could help shape future approaches that support people with type 2 diabetes to remain active and live healthier, longer lives.”

Reference: “The metabokine β-aminoisobutyric acid mediates exercise performance and skeletal muscle adaptation through a PGC1α-BAIBA-PPARδ axis” by Helene N. Daou, Nicole T. Watt, Shaimaa A. Gad, Amanda DV MacCannell, Aysha Ali, Chew Cheng, Raquel L. Fernando, T. Simon Futers, Sumeet A. Khetarpal, Harrison Gallagher, Luis D. Chinait, Anselmo S. Jeremy Bentham, the "godless" philosopher who founded modern utilitarianism, had severe dental and jaw problems, a CT scan of his skull reveals.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The great and "godless" English philosopher Jeremy Bentham, whose remains have been on display at a U.K. university for over 150 years, suffered from severe dental problems, according to X-ray scans of his skull.

The scans were conducted with CT (computed tomography) scanning equipment to create a digital 3D model of his head and highlight Bentham's lengthy "presence" at University College London (UCL) as it celebrates its 200th anniversary.

The scans revealed that Bentham was missing many teeth and had advanced arthritis in his lower jaw when he died of natural causes at the age of 84. During the scanning process, project leader Tannis Davidson, curator of UCL's Grant Museum of Zoology, saw how thin the jawbone had become. "He must have been in excruciating pain," she told Live Science.

Bentham's utilitarian philosophy inspired UCL's founders; it was only the third university in England, after Oxford and Cambridge, which was founded as London University in 1826 and opened to students in 1828.

As a young man, Bentham had declared that he would donate his body to science after his death. This was a radical idea at the time; in the U.K., dissection after death was looked down upon, even if it was for scientific purposes, and it was reserved for the worst criminals. After Bentham died in 1832, his remains were fashioned into an auto-icon — a supposed replica of himself — to memorialize him in the way a tombstone might, Davidson said.

Except for brief visits across Europe and to the Met Breuer in New York City, this auto-icon has been in a display case at UCL since the 1850s, where it can be seen by students as they pass by.

To make the auto-icon (which is not a mummy), Bentham's body was dissected and studied. Then, his skeleton was dressed in his clothes, which were padded with straw. His severed head was badly disfigured during an attempt to preserve it with sulfuric acid, so a wax reconstruction based on paintings and death masks was attached to the body.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Bentham's real head was displayed at the feet of the clothed skeleton that had a lifelike wax head; the real head's eyes were replaced with highly detailed glass eyes, which can be seen in the scans. According to UCL lore, the real head was stolen in 1975 and held ransom for a few days by rivals from King's College London, after which it was locked away.

Davidson explained that Bentham had coined the term "auto-icon" to mean "self-representation" and was setting an example for others. "He imagined a future where people were making auto-icons to keep their dead relatives around," she said.

The CT scans of the real head show that Bentham had dental damage and jaw arthritis, and that his brain had been removed before it was preserved—although some of his dura mater, a layer of connective tissue that covers the brain and spinal cord, was preserved. Davidson said the brain extraction was done to keep with Bentham's instructions that his head be mummified in the same way as Māori heads, which had their brains removed. The scanning process is shown in a short film called "Bentham Revealed."

Jeremy Bentham's "auto-icon" on display at University College London in 2008.

Bentham wrote about his dental problems several times, Davidson said, but it is not clear if he understood that he also had severe arthritis in his lower jaw, which must have made the problems with his teeth much more painful. In addition, modern ideas about cleaning teeth had not been established by Bentham's time. "Dentistry 200 years ago was a very different kettle of fish than it is today," Davidson said.

Bentham was a polymath who hoped to improve the lives of ordinary people through social reform. He wrote extensively about subjects as varied as law, economics, education and animal rights, and he believed that society could be engineered to produce better outcomes through legislation and the objective measurement of "utility."

His most famous idea was the panopticon in 1791, a ring-shaped prison with one warden to watch all of the prisoners, which he proposed as a humane alternative to Australia's penal colonies. Today, however, it is a symbol of state control and surveillance. Bentham also invented a "felicific calculus" to numerically assess the benefits and drawbacks of any given action, based on variables like its intensity, duration, certainty, purity and extent.

Bentham's philosophy put him at odds with the established Church of England; he called himself an "unbeliever," while critics called him "godless."

This rift with the church may have played a part in Bentham's wishes for his remains. Davidson suggested that the auto-icon may have been a means for Bentham to avoid being buried with traditional Anglican rites. "Maybe this was a way he could 'stick it to them' a little bit," she said.

Tom Metcalfe is a freelance journalist and regular Live Science contributor who is based in London in the United Kingdom. Tom writes mainly about science, space, archaeology, the Earth and the oceans. He has also written for the BBC, NBC News, National Geographic, Scientific American, Air & Space, and many others.

#6462. ESA's Hera Probe Uses "Superhuman" Vision to Inspect NASA's Asteroid Crash Site

Around four years ago, humanity intentionally hit an asteroid. The Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) was by pretty much all measures a resounding success when it struck the asteroid moonlet Dimorphos going more than 22,000 kilometers per hour. However, we still donât know just how much of a success it actually was - DART was a one-way mission with no real way to track the results of the impact close up. Enter Hera, the European Space Agency (ESA) mission that recently arrived in the binary asteroid system. Now, in a press release, ESA has provided some of the best pictures of the binary system since that fateful day four years ago.

The lack of accurate measurement isnât for lack of trying. Ground-based observatories have been watching 151m wide Dimorphos and its parent asteroid, 780m wide Didymos very closely over the last four years. They could tell that Dimorphos slowed its orbit around its larger companion by about 33 minutes. But some scientists were surprised by the magnitude of the change in orbit, based on the theoretical math done before the mission.

To help clear up any ambiguity about the math underlying this planetary defense mission, Hera is equipped with three main imaging tools. Its standard âeyesâ are the Asteroid Framing cameras, which handle both black-and-white photography and navigation. The press release showcases an image from this system showing Didymos from roughly 28.5km away, with features down to roughly 2.7m per pixel.

Fraser talks about Hera's final insertion into the binary asteroid system.

In the image, you can clearly see the âspinning topâ shape of the larger asteroid in the pair. Didymos spins at a relatively rapid speed for its size, completing a rotation every 2.2 hours. That energy is strong enough to pull boulders and gravel towards the middle of the asteroid, causing a build-up of material that makes it look fatter in the middle than at its poles.

However, seeing an asteroid in black in white isnât as scientifically useful as seeing it in âcolorâ. That is what Heraâs second imaging system, the HyperScout H instrument, is designed to do. It monitors the asteroid over 25 different color bands. With that information, HyperScout H can absorb and reflect light with different unique patterns - essentially it can spectroscopy. Comparing the results to lab experiments on meteorite samples on Earth will help determine what Didymos and its smaller companion are actually made up of.

But why stop at simple hyperspectral imaging when you can also have heat vision? The Thermal Infrared Imager (TIRI), supplied to ESA by Japanâs Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) gives Hera âSuperman-likeâ heat vision according to the press release. TIRI maps the temperature of the surface of the asteroids, and since solid rock dissipates heat much more slowly than porous or fragmented rock, it will also give a good indication of how solid Didymos really is.

Fraser talks about some of the results of the DART test.

Crucially, Dimorphos itself, the actual subject of the original DART test, is surprisingly absent from many of the pictures in this first round of releases. In the visible light images, Dimorphos is tucked almost entirely into the shadow of Didymos, appearing as a tiny sunlit spec beneath Didymos in one of the images. But with TIRIâs âSupermanâ view, the entire 151m wide asteroid is clearly in focus, glowing a shade of cool purple in the infrared. Cameras arenât the only thing Hera is carrying either. It will eventually launch two CubeSats, Juventus and Milan, to study the asteroid binary very closely. They will use ground-penetrating radar and even touch down on the surface of Dimorphos in an effort to understand what itstruly made of.

But ultimately the overarching purpose of the mission is to get a better idea of how effectively we can move an asteroid out of the way if we need to. DART appeared to be a success on the surface. Understanding what really happened to Dimorphos is what Hera, with all its cameras and companion spacecraft, was literally designed for. And weâre just at the earliest phases of that process. The next step is a major release of even sharper images planned for a live event at the Berlin Museum of Natural History on November 25th. Asteroid watchers, and space enthusiasts more generally, should mark their calendars for our first high-resolution view of one of the biggest impacts weâve had on another body in the solar system to date.

Hera surveying asteroids with superhuman vision

#6460. A Study of 50,000 Children Reveals the Real Impact of Daily Iron Pills

A major scientific review involving more than 50,000 children and adolescents reveals that daily iron supplementation can significantly reduce the risk of iron deficiency anemia.

A daily iron supplement can substantially reduce the risk of iron deficiency anemia in children and teenagers, but it does not appear to improve growth or protect against common illnesses. These findings come from a major Cochrane review of 114 studies involving more than 50,000 participants.

Led by researchers at Cornell University’s Joan Klein Jacobs Center for Precision Nutrition and Health, the review examined daily iron supplements taken alone or combined with folic acid and other vitamins and minerals. Many of the studies were conducted in Asia and involved children younger than five.

The strongest evidence showed that iron alone probably reduces the risk of iron deficiency anemia compared with receiving no treatment or a placebo. Combining iron with folic acid probably offers similar protection, although that conclusion was based on just one study. Supplements containing iron alongside other vitamins and minerals may also help. Evidence suggests that iron supplementation can reduce anemia and iron deficiency more broadly, but confidence in several findings remains limited.

Iron is essential for producing hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that transports oxygen from the lungs throughout the body. When iron levels become too low, the body cannot produce enough healthy hemoglobin, potentially leading to iron deficiency anemia.

“Iron deficiency remains one of the most common nutritional problems affecting children worldwide,” says first author Dr Kripa Rajagopalan. “Our review shows that daily iron supplements do what they are meant to do, which is reduce iron deficiency anemia, without any measurable impact on the common illnesses parents and health workers worry about.”

Although iron supplements helped prevent iron deficiency anemia, the researchers found no improvement in children’s height or weight relative to others of the same age and sex. Iron alone also had no measurable effect on the occurrence of cough, fever, or respiratory illness.

Adding folic acid to iron made little to no difference in rates of diarrhea or respiratory illness. Results for other supplement combinations were less conclusive, with evidence ranging from moderate to very low certainty.

Daily iron supplementation may cause stool discoloration, but iron alone appears to have little or no effect on vomiting or diarrhea. Its relationship with constipation remains uncertain. When iron was included in supplements containing other vitamins and minerals, vomiting was probably more common than with otherwise identical supplements that lacked iron.

“While the evidence base supports the use of daily iron supplements where needed, some adverse effects do occur. Stool discoloration and, in some formulations, vomiting were more common with iron, and the certainty of evidence for several outcomes, including anemia and iron deficiency themselves, was low or very low,” explains senior author Dr Saurabh Mehta.

Uncertainty about longer-term outcomes has persisted for years. The World Health Organization’s guidelines, last updated in 2016, identified gaps in evidence concerning the long-term effects of iron supplementation in children. The new review brings together a much larger body of research, although the strength of the evidence still varies across outcomes.

Anemia affects an estimated 874 million children and women worldwide. Young children face a particularly heavy burden, with approximately 40% of children younger than five affected in 2019. Iron deficiency accounts for roughly half of these cases.

Preventing anemia is a central objective of the global health strategy for women, children, and adolescents through 2030. Iron supplementation is already widely used to prevent and treat anemia, particularly among adolescents and women in populations where iron deficiency is common.

“These findings give decision-makers a stronger evidence base for guidance on iron supplementation in children and adolescents,” says co-author Dr Julia L. Finkelstein. “The data supports continued use of iron supplementation where iron deficiency is a concern.”

The researchers caution that their findings do not justify giving every child or adolescent a daily iron tablet. Decisions about supplementation should account for individual nutritional needs, local rates of iron deficiency and anemia, and the specific supplement formulation being used.

Reference: “Daily iron supplementation for prevention or treatment of iron‐deficiency anaemia in infants, children, and adolescents” by Kripa Rajagopalan, Laura Hackl, Juan Pablo Peña-Rosas, Maria Nieves Garcia-Casal, Mochammad Rizal, Neel H Mehta, Michael Roudik, Saiful Islam, Meghan M Trumbull-Kennedy, Nabila Reem Khondakar, Juan VA Franco, Julia L Finkelstein and Saurabh Mehta, 17 November 2026, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. DOI: 10.1002/14651858.CD013227.pub2
